body_standards: Kindergarten – Me and My Community (Draft)
Inquiry Process: Students act as social scientists as they ask questions, think critically, solve problems, and share conclusions.
C3 Indicators (K-2):
• Constructing Compelling and Supporting Questions: D1.1, 2, 3 • Gathering and Evaluating Sources: D2. His. 9, 10, 13, 17; D3. 1 • Communicating and Critiquing Solutions: D2. His. 16; D4. 1
Overarching Kindergarten Themes:
• American Ideals • Work and Commerce • Connections • Shared Traditions
Civics
Theme: American Ideals
Civic and Political Institutions:
D2.Civ.1.K-2. Describe roles and responsibilities of people in authority.
D2.Civ.3.K-2. Explain the need for and purposes of rules in various settings inside and outside of school.
D2.Civ.6.K-2. Describe how communities work to accomplish common tasks, establish responsibilities, and fulfill roles of
Authority.
Sample C3 Indicator Connections
Students will understand that children and adults have rights and responsibilities at home, at school, in the classroom, and in the community.
Civic Virtues and Democratic Principles: Applying Civic Virtues and Democratic Principles
D2.Civ.7.K-2. Apply civic virtues when participating in school settings.
D2.Civ.8.K-2. Describe democratic principles such as equality, fairness, and respect for legitimate authority and rules.
D2.Civ.9.K-2. Follow agreed-upon rules for discussions while responding attentively to others when addressing ideas and making decisions as a group.
D2.Civ.10.K-2. Compare their own point of view with others’ perspectives.

Students will explain the benefits and challenges of cooperation and rules within communities. Students will understand how ensuring that everyone’s voice is heard supports the classroom community. Students will identify ways to address a need or a goal as a group.
Rules, Processes, and Laws
D2.Civ.11.K-2. Explain how people can work together to make decisions in the classroom.
D2.Civ.12.K-2. Identify and explain how rules function in public (classroom and school) settings.

Students will understand that people make and change rules for many reasons. Students will identify examples of rules in the school and neighborhood community and explain why they exist. Students will describe incentives for following rules and consequences for breaking rules.
Economics
Theme: Work and Commerce
Economic Decision Making
D2.Eco.1.K-2. Explain how scarcity necessitates decision making.
D2.Eco.2.K-2. Identify the benefits and costs of making various personal decisions.
Students will be able to differentiate between needs and wants. Students will be able to explain why people earn, spend, and save money.
Exchange and Markets
D2.Eco.3.K-2. Describe the skills and knowledge required to produce certain goods and services.
D2.Eco.4.K-2. Describe the goods and services that people in the local community produce and those that are produced in other communities.
D2.Eco.5.K-2. Identify prices of products in a local market.
D2.Eco.6.K-2. Explain how people earn income.
Students will identify economic activities and resources in the local community. Students will describe ways in which people exchange money for goods.
Geography
Theme: Connections
Geographic Representations: Spatial Views of the World
D2.Geo.1.K-2. Construct maps, graphs, and other representations of familiar places.
D2.Geo.2.K-2. Use maps, graphs, photographs, and other representations to describe places and the relationships and interactions that shape them.
D2.Geo.3.K-2. Use maps, globes, and other simple geographic models to identify cultural and environmental characteristics of places.
Students will describe where things are located. Students will identify familiar places both in a community and on a map. Students will understand the function of a map.
Human-Environment Interaction: Place, Regions, and Culture
D2.Geo.4.K-2. Explain how weather, climate, and other environmental characteristics affect people’s lives in a place or region.
D2.Geo.5.K-2. Describe how human activities affect the cultural and environmental characteristics of places or regions.
D2.Geo.6.K-2. Identify some cultural and environmental characteristics of specific place.
Students will be able to describe the environmental characteristics of a community.
History
Perspectives Indicators are not assessed in kindergarten in this scope and sequence and will have opportunities for assessment within the K-2 grade-band in grades 1 and 2.
Theme: Shared Traditions
Change, Continuity, and Context
D2.His.1.K-2. Create a chronological sequence of multiple events.
D2.His.2.K-2. Compare life in the past to life today.

Students reference time in the past, present, and future to explain how they have observed change (classroom, community, school, stories). Students will be able to use sequence and chronological terms when describing past events.
Causation and Argumentation
D2.His.14.K-2. Generate possible reasons for an event or development in the past.
D2.His.16.K-2. Select which reasons might be more likely than others to explain a historical event or development.
Students will identify cause and effect.
body_examples: Overview

The focus of kindergarten is to provide students with opportunities to explore topics that affect them and their personal environments. These include basic citizenship skills such as rule making and compliance, and how these change in different settings (school, home, community). Students will engage in learning about themselves, their schools, their cities/towns, and local communities. They will also develop an awareness of the similarities and differences among individuals in the classroom as well as within the school and community. Students will have the opportunity to compare how life in the past is different from today, with respect to their own experiences within their home, classroom, and community.
Sample Content Connections

• Children have classroom responsibilities. • Considerate classmates are good citizens. • Children and adults have responsibilities at school and at home. • People can be citizens of a school, neighborhood, state, the United States, and/or a home country. • Communities have rules and routines. • Communities and organizations can identify and elect leaders. • Leaders serve in various roles within the community. • Students can be leaders. • Belonging/acceptance in a group.

• People use honesty, mutual respect, social responsibility, and cooperation and pay attention to other perspectives when interacting with others. • People demonstrate respect for the rights of others. • Individuals have the same basic human rights. • People share common characteristics. • People are unique and different. • People learn from families. • Teachers and others help students learn. • People have various strengths and abilities. • People can have different opinions. • Communities can have problems and issues to be addressed. • People can work together to resolve conflicts and problems (executive function skills). • Children communicate with individuals and in groups by identifying feelings that might lead to interpersonal conflicts (executive function skills).

• Rules are different in different places. • Taking turns is respectful. • Classrooms are organized for student learning. • A school community helps children learn. • Many people work in schools and have different jobs and responsibilities. • Members of the classroom and school deserve respect. • Citizens are members of communities. • Children can help create classroom rules.
Resources
Civics for All: From the NYC DOE, comes this resource-rich guide of lesson plans and projects covering American Ideals, Rights and Responsibilities, and Role of the Individual.

C3 IDM - Rules: This inquiry engages kindergartners in exploring the various ways people interact with and act upon rules and laws in society. The compelling question “Are all rules good rules?” assumes that while students generally enter school with some concept of rules and what it means to follow or break them, they may not yet understand who makes rules and how they change.

History’s Mysteries - How do Communities Make Good Decisions?: In this unit, students will solve three mysteries using evidence from primary sources including, 1) “What does it mean to belong to a group?”, 2) What does it mean to be a citizen?”, and 3) How do groups make decisions?” Students will act as investigators to solve the mysteries, which helps students understand themselves and their connections to their communities, including the ideas and process of voting and why it is important.

Learning for Justice - Part of a Community Online: This lesson focuses on helping young children learn to participate in different kinds of digital communities. Students will solidify and work on what they know about being part of any community.

National Endowment for the Humanities - The Statue of Liberty: The Meaning and Use of a National Symbol: Students will learn the history of the Statue of Liberty and the evolving meaning of its symbolism. The focus is to understand symbols as students study the Statue of Liberty, complete research on a national symbol, and use their research to communicate a message of their own.

PBS Learning Media - America, Our Country/Arthur: In these episodes from the PBS KIDS series ARTHUR, students examine the United States of America - the reasons it was founded, its citizens, and the symbols that represent its values.

PBS Learning Media: Together We Can is a unique live-action music video series that supports children as they move through the developmental stages of “me” (a focus on the self), to “we” (a focus on the self and immediate other), to “us” (a focus on their wider surroundings). Through fun, upbeat, and engaging songs, this series explores ideas and concepts about American Democracy and Civics.

PBS Learning Media – Xavier Riddle - Talking About Life Lessons: Xavier Riddle and his friends explore values and skills such as compassion, perseverance, responsibility, and gratitude in these video clips supported with teacher materials.

• Family members care for and help each other. • Families have basic needs and wants (safety, economic decisions, etc.). • Family members make choices to meet their needs and wants. • People in neighborhoods rely on each other for goods, services, and assistance. • Needs (food, rent) are different than wants (toys). • Scarcity is the condition of not being able to have all of the goods and services that a person wants or needs

• Recognize and count using different coin values. • Vermont has specific economic activities and resources, such as maple sugaring, skiing, and eco-tourism. • Family members have different jobs and responsibilities. • People pay for goods and services. • People work in neighborhoods and have different jobs and responsibilities (police, store owners, sanitation workers, firefighters).
Resources

C3 IDM - Needs and Wants: This annotated inquiry focuses on the economics concept of scarcity by developing an understanding of needs and wants and goods and services through the compelling question, “Can we ever get everything we need and want?” The distinctions between these constructs serve as the necessary components of an examination of the choices people must make when faced with potential limitations.
PBS Learning Media - City Island: Short videos, with catchy tunes to introduce concepts like “What is Money?”, “Garbage,” and “Messy Jobs.”

PBS Learning Media - Garbage: In this media-rich lesson featuring LOOP SCOOPS videos, students consider how the concept of "needs" vs. "wants" can help them think about ways to protect Earth's natural resources by reducing, reusing, and recycling materials.
PBS Learning Media - $martpath Good Boy! (Goods vs. Services): This 5-minute video is supplemented with teacher support resources.

• Communities have unique features and special purpose buildings (homes, schools, businesses, places of worship, libraries, parks, police/fire station, museums, hospitals). • Each student has their own physical address. • Buildings within a community have a physical address. • The purpose of an address. • Communities have landmarks, monuments, and architecture. Purpose of a map: • Define vocabulary that defines location in space (e.g., near, far, below, above). • Create a simple map and use it to find something.
• Environmental characteristics include climate and weather. • Physical features of a community can be changed by weather and climate.
Resources
Vermont FEED - Maple in Every School: Sample of activities to bring to the school to extend the students' maple education, including “Sugar Maker in the Classroom” and “Meet a Tree.”

C3 IDM - Paper Maps: This inquiry leads students through an investigation of electronic and paper maps as representations of the physical world. In examining the different ways in which the two mediums reflect place and positionality, students should consider the utility and relative value of different geographic representations. Through interaction with the formative performance tasks and featured sources, students build their knowledge and understanding so that they are able to develop an argument that answers the compelling question “Do We Still Need Paper Maps?”

National Geographic - Mapping the Classroom: Students practice using the language of location and then apply that language when creating a map of their classroom. They use the map to locate hidden items in the classroom.

KidCitizen - A Bird’s Eye View: Wondering with Maps: In this interactive lesson, students analyze a historic map and photos to learn how maps are more than just a way to represent a place on paper; maps also are sources that can be analyzed for how they are constructed and what they communicate.
National Geographic - Places in the Park: Students explore a map of a park and use map symbols, a map key, and cardinal directions to analyze it.

Shelburne Farms - How Are We Connected?: This downloadable resource cultivates an awareness and appreciation of what sustains us: our food, fiber, and relationships. This thread provides an opportunity to deepen our connection with our local food system. Beginning with our air, soil, water, and space, we begin the exploration of food, fiber, family and friends. We weave, knead, bake, and create products that we use and eat, and discover the joy of living with gratitude and in relationship to the world around us.

Shelburne Farms - Who Lives Here?: A downloadable resource that introduces children to the people, plants, and animals of their place. By asking and exploring the question, “Who lives here?” children discover how our human, natural, and agricultural communities are interdependent. Children will develop a strong understanding and sense of community and place, as well as begin to grasp how they are interdependent—no matter where they live.

C3 IDM - Maps and Globes: This inquiry leads students through an investigation of maps and globes as tools that represent the physical world in different ways. In the inquiry, students consider how each tool represents locations, what purposes each tool serves, and what advantages and disadvantages each tool offers. The study of maps and globes provides the foundation for students to develop an understanding of how and why humans interact with geography and geographic features across time and space. The manner in which students gather, use, and interpret evidence should increase their geographic reasoning and allow them to make and support their arguments in response to the compelling question, “Which is better, a map or a globe?”

• Events can be identified as past, present, or future. • Concepts of time measurement include: o Days o Weeks o Months o Years • Key Sequence and Chronological Terms • Visual Timelines • Timeline illustrating key events in a story or a historical event

• Outcome – what happens after people make a choice or do something alone or together. • Observation – listening and looking to learn about people and places. • Evidence – things you see or hear to show that something is true.
Resources

C3 IDM - Holidays: This inquiry encourages kindergartners to expand their study of self and others by deepening their understanding of the role of traditions, holidays, and symbols in establishing cultural identity and unity. The compelling question “What makes holidays special?” reflects an enduring conversation about how and why people engage in ritual and tradition. It is respectful of kindergartners’ intellectual efforts as they are likely to be interested in knowing more about traditions and holidays and are likely to have a meaningful entry point into the discussion based upon personal experiences.

C3 IDM - Identity: This inquiry leads students through an investigation of self by recognizing that all humans have both unique and similar characteristics. By investigating the compelling question “Is everyone unique?” students begin to see how they are similar to and different from their classmates. The study of similarities and differences among individuals provides the foundation for students to demonstrate their understanding of and respect for others.

History’s Mysteries - How Do We Celebrate Our Shared Traditions?: In this unit, students will solve four historical mysteries using evidence from primary sources including 1) “Where is the history in a name?”, 2) “What shared traditions make your family special?”, 3) “Why do we have a day off from school?”, and 4) “How does a tradition become a holiday?” Students will explore naming traditions, family traditions, civic versus religious holidays, and lastly, the story of Juneteenth and how it has become a holiday celebrated across America.

History’s Mysteries - What is the Difference Between Then and Now?: In this unit, students will explore three mysteries, 1) “What is the difference between then and now?”, 2) “Where do people work?”, and 3) “How is work different now than in the past?” Students will explore primary source images from the Library of Congress to solve historical mysteries with evidence.

iCivics - How Do We Celebrate Our Shared Traditions?: Traditions can be large or small. Kids may be familiar with certain traditions. This unit allows them to explore more. They will have the opportunity to identify traditions that are important to their family, learn about naming traditions, and discuss holidays.

iCivics - What Is the Difference Between Then and Now?: In this unit, students analyze primary images from the past and compare them to those from today. Students will have the opportunity to learn how people, work, and familiar objects have changed over time.

KidCitizen - Community Helpers: In this interactive lesson, students will learn how community helpers have changed and stayed the same over time by exploring a photograph of a man delivering ice to a schoolhouse around 1900 and investigate who community helpers are.
Learning for Justice - What Is a Family?: This lesson provides a framework that will help students talk about their own and others’ families in safe, caring ways.

PBS Learning Media Habitats and Discoveries: Images of the Past: In this lesson, your students will participate in a hands-on observation challenge that will encourage them to look closer at the habitats around them.

PBS Learning Media - The Fred T. Korematsu Institute - How Are We Defined as Americans?: In this lesson, the students will explore what it means to them to be an American. They will reflect on their own identities and family histories to better understand their experience. Individually and as a group, students will develop a definition of what it means to be an American and add to that definition throughout the year.

body_standards: Grade 1 – People, Places, and the Environment (Draft)
Inquiry Process: Students act as social scientists as they ask questions, think critically, solve problems, and share conclusions.
C3 Indicators (K-2):
• Constructing Compelling and Supporting Questions: D1.1, 2, 3 • Gathering and Evaluating Sources: D2. His. 9, 10, 13, 17; D3. 1 • Communicating and Critiquing Solutions: D2. His. 16; D4. 1
Overarching Grade 1 Themes:
• Roles and Responsibilities • Economic Choices • Geography’s Influence on Culture and the Environment • Past and Present
Civics
Theme: Roles and Responsibilities
Civic and Political Institutions:
D2.Civ.1.K-2. Describe roles and responsibilities of people in authority.
D2.Civ.3.K-2. Explain the need for and purposes of rules in various settings inside and outside of school.
D2.Civ.5.K-2. Explain what governments are and some of their functions.
D2.Civ.6.K-2. Describe how communities work to accomplish common tasks, establish responsibilities, and fulfill roles of
Authority.
Sample C3 Indicator Connections

Students will identify local community and government leaders that have roles and responsibilities to provide services for their community members. Students will be able to explain how communities have rules and people in charge to keep things fair and help everyone get what they need.
Civic Virtues and Democratic Principles: Applying Civic Virtues and Democratic Principles
D2.Civ.7.K-2. Apply civic virtues when participating in school settings.
D2.Civ.8.K-2. Describe democratic principles such as equality, fairness, and respect for legitimate authority and rules.
D2.Civ.9.K-2. Follow agreed-upon rules for discussions while responding attentively to others when addressing ideas and making decisions as a group.
D2.Civ.10.K-2. Compare their own point of view with others’ perspectives.

Students will understand that children, families, and communities exhibit cultural similarities and differences. Students will be able to identify examples of freedom, respect, and safety in their community and explain how these contribute to the common good. Students will understand that culturally, ethnically, and racially diverse people help to shape a community.
Rules, Processes, and Laws
D2.Civ.11.K-2. Explain how people can work together to make decisions in the classroom.
D2.Civ.12.K-2. Identify and explain how rules function in public (classroom and school) settings.

Students will identify examples of how individual actions (such as volunteering or voting) and government decisions (like making laws or providing services) help create order and promote peace in their community. Students will be able to identify characteristics of effective rules and participate in a process to establish classroom rules. Students can participate in problem solving, decision making and conflict resolution within their home, school, and community. Students will understand that outcomes to conflict or disagreements based on different beliefs, culture, and values can be achieved through compromise and cooperation. Students will describe how individuals can bring about change.
Economics
Theme: Economic Choices
Economic Decision Making
D2.Eco.1.K-2. Explain how scarcity necessitates decision making.
D2.Eco.2.K-2. Identify the benefits and costs of making various personal decisions.

Students will be able to identify choices and decisions for various uses of money (spending, saving, sharing, contributing). Students will be able to use cost-benefit analysis (i.e., weigh positives and negatives) of two choices to make a decision.
Exchange and Markets
D2.Eco.3.K-2. Describe the skills and knowledge required to produce certain goods and services.
D2.Eco.4.K-2. Describe the goods and services that people in the local community produce and those that are produced in other communities.
D2.Eco.5.K-2. Identify prices of products in a local market.
D2.Eco.6.K-2. Explain how people earn income.

Students will be able to identify prices of goods in a local market. Students will be able to describe the goods and services produced in the local community. Students will be able to identify sources of income. Students will identify how goods and services are exchanged within Vermont communities.
Global Economy
D2.Eco.14.K-2. Describe why people in one country trade goods and services with people in other countries.
D2.Eco.15.K-2. Describe products that are produced abroad and sold domestically and products that are produced domestically and sold abroad.
Students will be able to explain why people in one country trade for goods in another country.
Geography
Theme: Geography’s Influence on Culture and Environment
Geographic Representations
D2.Geo.1.K-2. Construct maps, graphs, and other representations of familiar places.
D2.Geo.2.K-2. Use maps, graphs, photographs, and other representations to describe places and the relationships and interactions that shape them.
Students will understand how physical features and man-made structures are represented on a map.
Human-Environment Interaction: Place, Regions, and Culture
D2.Geo.4.K-2. Explain how weather, climate, and other environmental characteristics affect people’s lives in a place or region.
D2.Geo.5.K-2. Describe how human activities affect the cultural and environmental characteristics of places or regions.

Students can explain how Vermonters are impacted by their environment and ways that individuals can support a healthy Vermont environment. Students will understand how and why environments change and how people adapt in different ways to their environments.
Human Population: Spatial Patterns and Movements
D2.Geo.7.K-2. Explain why and how people, goods, and ideas move from place to place.
D2.Geo.8.K-2. Compare how people in different types of communities use local and distant environments to meet their daily needs.
D2.Geo.9.K-2. Describe the connections between the physical environment of a place and the economic activities found there.

Students will understand that one’s community does not provide all of the resources that most members need in their daily lives. Students will be able to describe patterns of movement (e.g., people, goods, ideas, etc.).
Global Interconnections: Changing Spatial Patterns
D2.Geo.10.K-2. Describe changes in the physical and cultural characteristics of various world regions.
D2.Geo.12.K-2. Identify ways that a catastrophic disaster may affect people living in a place.

Students will examine and understand the varying communities that they belong to (e.g., family, school, town, etc.), and how they may change over time. Students will identify, respect, and explain the diverse cultures of their community and communities in the United States. Students will explain physical changes in their community over time.
History
Theme: Past and Present
Change, Continuity, and Context
D2.His.1.K-2. Create a chronological sequence of multiple events.
D2.His.2.K-2. Compare life in the past to life today.
D2.His.3.K-2. Generate questions about individuals and groups who have shaped a significant historical change.

Students will understand that there were significant historical individuals and events that had an impact on Vermont. Students will understand and identify the ways in which the lives of people in the past are similar to and different from people today (food, clothing, housing, jobs, education, leisure activities). Students will be able to describe similarities and differences between families long ago and families today. Students will be able to describe how documented and recorded changes over time are ways to learn about the past and wonder about the future.
Perspectives
D2.His.4.K-2. Compare perspectives of people in the past to those of people in the present.
D2.His.6.K-2. Compare different accounts of the same historical event.

Students will understand that children, families, and communities have similarities and differences. Students will be able to examine their own self- identity and how it fits with the identity of the family, school, and local community. Students will be able to explain that people can have different viewpoints.
Causation and Argumentation
D2.His.9.K-2. Identify different kinds of historical sources.
D2.His.10.K-2. Explain how historical sources can be used to study the past.

Students will be able to explain how historical sources can be used to study the past. Students will be able to create a timeline to identify a sequence of events in a student’s life or community. Students will be able to explain ways that students can take informed action to help address issues and problems at school or in the community (See Civics - Rules, Processes, and Laws).
body_examples: Overview

In grade 1, students will learn how they are connected to the world around them and develop a deeper understanding of how diverse cultures, values, and beliefs help to shape the world in which we live. Students will further develop a sense of purpose and empathy regarding their role and the role of other citizens within the community and world. As a global citizen, it is developmentally appropriate for students to identify similarities and differences from others (cultural, likes and dislikes, gender, skin color, hair, and eye color). Best practice is having materials and visuals that are representative of people, cultures, and the community in which they live. They will have the opportunity to look for ways that they can be civic-minded and make change happen within their own classroom, school, and community. Students will develop an understanding of how basic economic concepts influence people, places, and the environment. They will learn that people not only use the environment to meet their needs and wants but also that the environment often dictates where and how people choose to live. Students will continue building group skills, including roles, rules, voicing an opinion, and conflict resolution skills with adult support. They will enhance their knowledge of spatial awareness of their surroundings by furthering the use of geographic representations, tools, and terminology to process information about the world around them. Students will continue to compare life in the past to life today as they study the contributions of historical figures and how those figures have helped shape and change various communities and environments across the globe.
Sample Content Connections

• Different people serve in appointed and/or elected roles in governments. • Leaders have different roles and responsibilities. • Governments represent the needs of the people, create and enforce laws, and help to resolve conflicts. • Governments provide services (education, roads, parks, public safety). • Civic identity is shaped by symbolic figures, places, and events. • People elect officials to represent them. • Citizens help to form their government. • Voting determines who will be president and vice president. • The president is the leader of the country, and the vice president is second in charge. • Individuals work together to respect and uphold the rights of the self and others in the community. • Learners in the classroom community have rights (feeling safe, belonging, learning).

• Civic virtues include honesty, mutual respect, cooperation, attentiveness to multiple perspectives, empathy, and courage. • Democratic principles include equality, freedom, liberty, rights, deliberation, and consideration for the common good. • Rights can include individual rights and group rights (common good). • The United States is comprised of diverse cultural groups. • Cultural groups share traditions, beliefs, religions, and holidays. • A school is made up of diverse people. • People can belong to different groups. • People speak a native language. • People share ethnicity, culture, and religion.

• There are differences between a rule and a law. • Various people make laws/rules. • There are consequences for not following laws/rules. • Laws/rules are not the same everywhere. • Various people enforce laws/rules. • There are differences between rights (freedoms of speech and religions) and responsibilities (paying taxes, obeying the law). • People can bring about change in the classroom and/or community.
Resources

American Bar Association - Taking a Stand: Students will understand that citizens take stands on issues and explore ways to advocate for those issues. Pearl Moscowitz’s Last Stand is utilized in the lesson; it can be accessed through a video reading from the Cayton Children’s Museum.

C3 IDM - Friendship: This inquiry leads students through an investigation of early social interactions and behaviors. By investigating the compelling question “Do I have to like everyone?”, students evaluate friendship, what is a friend, how to be a friend, and how to respond when you dislike someone or they dislike you. Students will develop a deeper understanding of friendship(s). The formative performance tasks build on knowledge and skills through the course of the inquiry and help students create their own understanding of friendships and how to treat everyone fairly. Students create an evidence-based informative argument about whether or not they need to like everyone and appropriate behaviors.

C3 IDM - Global Citizen: This first grade annotated inquiry highlights the idea that even primary-age children can begin thinking about their civic roles in their communities and beyond. Those roles can be made real and vital to young children by exploring the traits or characteristics that represent responsible citizenship. Those traits – respecting others, behaving honestly, helping others, making and obeying rules and laws, being informed, and sharing needed resources – will be familiar to students through their experiences in their home and school lives.

C3 IDM - The President: This inquiry engages first graders in exploring the meaning and purpose and function of government through the compelling question “Is the president the most important person in government?” Assuming that most first graders know who the president is, this inquiry is designed to help students explore the different levels of governmental leadership and the idea that other authority figures exist in addition to the president. In learning about the levels of government and the issues each deals with, students should consider their own ideas for desired change within their communities (e.g., more recreational space, better roads, more variety in school lunches) and develop a commitment to civic participation.

iCivics - How Can Perseverance Help Me Be a Good Citizen?: The way students respond when things are challenging can be the difference between success and failure. But it’s not easy to practice a civic virtue like perseverance. This unit introduces students to behaviors they can use to work through challenges and offers the real-life examples of Wilma Rudolph and Katherine Johnson demonstrating perseverance for students to explore.

iCivics - How Do Communities Make Good Decisions?: In this unit, students will be introduced to citizenship and leadership. Students will work together to create a classroom book on the rights and responsibilities of citizenship. Students will have the opportunity to practice citizenship by voting, recounting, and coming together for the common good.

iCivics - What Makes a Good Leader?: In this unit, students will explore leaders in their community and identify leadership traits. Students will then learn about President George Washington and identify the qualities that made people believe he would be a good first leader for the United States. Finally, students will learn about the life of Ona Judge, and examine one way in which leaders stand up for important things.

iCivics - Private i History Detectives Civic Virtues Collection: In the new Private i History Detectives Civic Virtues Collection, students learn about civic virtue champions and practice civic virtues in their own lives and in the classroom. Throughout these units, students will discover the untold stories of important and influential figures who lived out civic virtue in their own lives. They will also gain the skills they need to understand each other’s ideas and have opportunities to bring their own experiences into the learning.

KidCitizen - Children in Action: From recycling materials during World War II to wearing masks during the COVID-19 pandemic, children have helped meet community goals during times of need. In this interactive episode, students draw upon their observations and reflections to explore how children have contributed to recycling efforts in the past and present.

KidCitizen - Congress and Milk: Congress is a group of people who work together to make laws for our country. They are elected by the people to represent their interests and make decisions about important issues. We will explore one way that Congress affects children's daily life at school.

National Park Service - National Parks Legacy: Nature and Culture…NPS Protects Both!: This lesson teaches students how the National Park Service protects both nature and culture as students engage with the changing landscapes of Yellowstone national Park and Mesa Verde.

PBS Learning Media - Arthur’s Park Game: Students practice taking action to improve our world by playing ARTHUR’s Park, a digital game. In order to create a new park in an empty lot, Arthur has to make a speech to raise awareness, hold a bake sale to make money, and then equip the park. As students play each round, set in a board game format, they accumulate stars that allow them to “buy” what they need for the new park. They also recognize the importance of making a plan to achieve one’s goals.
PBS Learning Media - My Vote Counts Lesson Plan: In this lesson from the PBS KIDS series ARTHUR, students learn about elections and to voice their preferences by voting.

PBS Learning Media - Stand Up, Sit In, Speak Out: In this lesson from the PBS KIDS series ARTHUR, students examine activism and how ordinary people can be part of powerful collective movements that bring change. Students watch “Arthur Takes a Stand” and discuss taking action against things they believe are unjust. They map out the characters’ actions, noting that multiple voices bring power and opportunities for change. Then, they listen to a story about the reasons people protest and are introduced to important movements in our country’s history. Finally, they explore different ways people take action and brainstorm a list of issues in their own community that they would like to change.

PBS Learning Media – Xavier Riddle: Talking About Life Lessons: Xavier Riddle and his friends explore values and skills such as compassion, perseverance, responsibility, and gratitude in these video clips supported with teacher materials.

PBS Learning Media – You, Me, and Community: This collection includes resources related to civics & government, geography, economics, and history. All resources are available in English, and some are available in Spanish. No student is too young to learn how to become civically engaged. Introduce young learners to basic civics concepts—including making their voice heard and exploring the process of voting.

Choices and Decisions • Sources of income • Needs and wants • Identify multiple forms of U.S. money • Means of transaction • Volunteering • Different jobs in different communities • Scarcity • Opportunity costs

• Goods (maple syrup, cheddar cheese) and services (firefighter, teacher) • Sources of income • Value • People can be consumers and producers. • Local economic activities aid the national economy (e.g., VT maple syrup). • Economy is a system for using resources and distributing goods and services within a community. • Money is a means of exchange. • Trade allows consumers to have items not made in Vermont.

• States and countries have different resources. • Geography and environment connect in the production of goods and services. • Local goods and services export to Global markets (e.g., VT maple syrup). • Examples of products made in the United States (possible exports) • Examples of products bought here but made outside of the country (imports)
Resources

California State University - Expanding Children’s Economic World: A Curriculum Guide: This guide provides focus questions, activities, and assessments on topics such as “The Jobs People Do” and “Goods and Services.”

C3 IDM - Economic Choices: This first-grade inquiry features an investigation of economic decision making through the context of how families manage their money. In examining the costs and benefits associated with making decisions about spending and saving money, students should be able to develop an argument with evidence to answer the compelling question “What choices do we make with our money?”

C3 IDM - Economic Interdependence: This inquiry is an initial exploration into the concept of interdependence through the lens of community economics and the idea of a community as a diverse, mutually supportive web of needs and wants, workers and consumers, and problems and solutions. The compelling question, “What makes me become we?” challenges students to consider interdependence and groups to think about how a community is just a bunch of me- people living in a shared space but also a collective “we” that interacts, grows and contracts, and tries to solve issues. (This is a 2nd grade inquiry that can be adapted for younger students, as needed).

PBS Learning Media - Needs vs. Wants: In this media-rich lesson featuring a LOOP SCOOPS video, students are introduced to the concept of “needs” vs. “wants,” and begin to consider the relationship between consumer goods and happiness.

Vermont Historical Society - My Sheep Farm Activity: William Jarvis (1770-1859) was a successful merchant and the United States Consul to Portugal and well known in both New England and Washington, DC. Jarvis played an important part in introducing Merino sheep to the United States, and subsequently in the development of the sheep herds in this country. The success of raising Merino herds in Vermont led to "merino mania."

Map Identifications • Physical and political maps • Physical features (e.g., roads, routes, interstates) • Continents • Oceans Map Skills • Create a map as a representation of a space (e.g., playground, neighborhood, or town common). • Identify and use map key features. • Positional word use

• Physical environment affects the way people live and how they adapt to their physical environment (e.g., dressing for winter). • Children can take care of or hurt the environment in different ways (e.g., recycling, Green Up day, littering).

• People move for different reasons (e.g., climate, job opportunities, family connections). • Commuting/transportation • Vermont’s exports include different products. • Agricultural products include apples, maple syrup, milk, and cheese. • Forest products include wood and paper products. • Manufactured goods (#1 export) include computer/electronic products and machinery.

Culture and Community • People in communities have multiple perspectives. • Communities can be made up of diverse social and ethnic groups. • Heritage, songs, symbols, celebrations, and folklore help to build culture. • Contributions and impact of various cultural groups in the community (e.g., variety of foods and celebrations). Physical Changes to Communities • Flooding, drought, and farming impacts (e.g., runoff, erosion) • Development
Resources

America, Our Country/Arthur: In these episodes from the PBS KIDS series ARTHUR, students examine the United States of America—the reasons it was founded, its citizens, and the symbols that represent its values.

History’s Mysteries - Why Do People Move?: This four-mystery/lesson inquiry unit helps students learn about push and pull factors, refugees, and the Great Migration by exploring primary and secondary sources to answer historical questions.
National Geographic - Exploring Maps and Models of Earth: Students compare miniature models to real things. Then they explore maps and globes as miniature versions of places and the Earth.

National Geographic - Mapping Storybooks: Students use a map and cutouts of a story's characters to follow their actions through space and time. They retell the story in their own words, using the map and positional vocabulary.

National Geographic - The Sun, Earth, and Cardinal Directions: Students record the position of the sun in the morning and afternoon and make connections to the directions east and west. They practice moving north, south, east, and west and use cardinal directions to read a map.

PBS Learning Media - Animals, Maps, and Habitats, Oh My!: In this STEM activity from CYBERCHASE, students watch a video in which a habitat has been disturbed by the construction of a bike path. They then use X and Y coordinates to locate items on a map and find a solution to the problem posed in the video.

PBS learning Media - Reduce, Reuse, Recycle: In this media-rich lesson featuring LOOP SCOOPS videos, students consider how the concept of "needs" vs. "wants" can help them think about ways to protect Earth's natural resources by reducing, reusing, and recycling materials.

Important Vermonters: (examples include Ethan Allen, Ira Allen, Thomas Chittenden, Brigham Young, Joseph Smith, Ann Story, Annette Chase Dimcock, Lucy Terry Prince, Calvin Coolidge, Phineas Gage, Wilson “Snowflake” Bentley) How to Compare Present and Past: • People • Events • Observances • Sequential order • Folklore/Folktales • State holidays • Religious holidays and cultural recognitions Key Sequence and Chronological Terms Basic Time-related Vocabulary: • Before/After • First, next, then, last • Beginning, middle, end • Now, later • Yesterday, today, tomorrow • Past, present, future • Family history can be shared (names, family trees, letters, old photographs, etc.)

• Family histories can be recorded. • Family histories may have started in other places (states, countries, etc.). • Records of history have changed over time and with technology. • Historical sources (letters, artifacts, photographs, maps, newspapers, etc.) inform us about broad aspects of the past.

• Causes/effects of life (personal/family) events can be used to study the present and the past. • Artifacts, letters, maps, photographs, newspapers, primary and secondary sources provide evidence to study the past to learn the truth about events. Community Action Examples: • School Clean-Up Day: o Action: Students pick up litter around the playground or school grounds. o Lesson: Teaches responsibility for shared spaces and environmental care. • Kindness Campaign: o Action: First graders create posters promoting kindness or perform small acts of kindness, like writing “kind notes” to classmates or teachers. o Lesson: Promotes empathy and social-emotional awareness. • Food Drive Participation: o Action: Students bring in canned goods for a local food pantry. o Lesson: Raises awareness of hunger and the importance of helping others in need. • Cards for Community Helpers/Veterans: o Action: Students make thank-you cards for firefighters, police officers, healthcare workers, or veterans. o Lesson: Encourages appreciation and connection to community roles. • Recycling Initiative: o Action: Start or help with a classroom recycling program. o Lesson: Teaches environmental responsibility and the importance of reducing waste.
Resources

C3 IDM - Family Stories: This inquiry leads students through an investigation of their families as a way to begin understanding the concepts of past and present. By answering the compelling question “What do family stories tell us about the past?” students learn about change over time. Through the use of family artifacts (e.g., photographs, marriage licenses, family trees, keepsakes), students learn that such items can reveal information about how life in the past differs from life in the present and how their families have changed over time.

KidCitizen - Capture the Flag: By investigating primary sources displaying the American flag, we will explore the various ways people use the flag to show characteristics such as pride, loyalty, and unity for the nation. In this episode, students will engage in careful observation to identify flags and note details of the variety of places in which American flags are used.

KidCitizen - How have community helpers changed and stayed the same over time?: The importance of community helpers is a building block of civics understanding. In this episode, children investigate who community helpers are, and how they have changed over time through exploration of a rich photograph (from the Library of Congress) of a man delivering ice to a schoolhouse in 1899. Children explore the photograph by revealing it in sections, observing the details they find (See), and working with in-game character Ella to figure out what jobs the helpers are doing. Children collect elements of the photograph to their journal and use what they have collected to help them decide what the jobs are (Think), and then to connect those jobs with community helpers today (Wonder).

KidCitizen - Rosa Parks: A Proud Daughter: In this episode, children analyze a greeting card to learn about Rosa Parks and her family. The greeting card offers a familiar resource for exploring family traditions. The front of the card has an image and some simple writing. The inside of the card has a poem, and the back of the card features Rosa Parks’ handwritten note to her mother. Children observe the details of the card and analyze clues to figure out what family tradition was being celebrated. Working with in-game mentor Ella, children use parts of the card as evidence to support their ideas as they generate hypotheses about the card’s recipient, sender, and the feelings the sender wanted to express. Children explore the handwritten note on the card and practice deciphering the message by looking for familiar letters or words.

PBS Learning Media - A Qyah Juneteenth Lesson Plan - MOLLY OF DENALI: Based on the animated story “A Qyah Juneteenth” from the PBS KIDS series MOLLY OF DENALI, this lesson helps students deepen their comprehension of informational text by asking questions. In the video, Trini is excited as the Juneteenth holiday approaches, but Molly and

Tooey don’t know anything about it and have many questions. They sit down with Grandma Dorena, who answers their questions about the holiday and slavery. In the lesson, students listen to informational texts, monitoring their understanding and asking questions as they arise.

PBS Learning Media - Looking for Lincoln Throughout His Life: In this interdisciplinary lesson, students gather different facts about Lincoln through a variety of hands-on activities. Students will tell a story about their own lives by using classroom items. They will also create a timeline of Lincoln's life and their own.

Vermont Historical Society - This Place in History: Since 2016, the Vermont Historical Society has recorded a weekly video series with a local news station. Over 200 videos highlight historic places across the state. Follow the links to access organized lists of the short videos by subject, such as “Famous Vermonters” and “Agricultural History,” or use the This Place in History Map to search for videos by location.
