body_standards: Grade 2 – The Americas (Draft)
The Inquiry Process: Students act as social scientists as they ask questions, think critically, solve problems, and share conclusions.
C3 Indicators (K-2):
• Constructing Compelling and Supporting Questions: D1.1, 2, 3 • Gathering and Evaluating Sources: D2. His. 9, 10,12,13, 17; D3. 1 • Communicating and Critiquing Solutions: D2. His.16; D4. 1
Overarching Grade 2 Themes:
• Rules and Laws • Resources • Environmental Connections • Relationships
Civics
Theme: Rules and Laws
Civic and Political Institutions:
D2.Civ.1.K-2. Describe roles and responsibilities of people in authority.
D2.Civ.3.K-2. Explain the need for and purposes of rules in various settings inside and outside of school.
D2.Civ.6.K-2. Describe how communities work to accomplish common tasks, establish responsibilities, and fulfill roles of
Authority.
Sample C3 Indicator Connections

Students will be able to describe the significance of national traditions and symbols (e.g., flag). Students will be able to identify how government can look different at different times and in different places. Students will identify where rules, laws, and agreements can come from. Students will be able to identify a level of government and describe the role it serves. Students will be able to describe ways that people show support for their country (i.e., patriotism).
Civic Virtues and Democratic Principles: Applying Civic Virtues and Democratic Principles
D2.Civ.7.K-2. Apply civic virtues when participating in school settings.
D2.Civ.8.K-2. Describe democratic principles such as equality, fairness, and respect for legitimate authority and rules.
D2.Civ.9.K-2. Follow agreed-upon rules for discussions while responding attentively to others when addressing ideas and making decisions as a group.
D2.Civ.10.K-2. Compare their own point of view with others’ perspectives.

Students will be able to describe different national identities across the Americas. Students will be able to identify how a nation’s identity may be influenced by the beliefs and values of various cultures. Students will be able to explain how different societies share similarities (e.g., traditions, symbols, etc.).
Rules, Processes, and Laws
D2.Civ.11.K-2. Explain how people can work together to make decisions in the classroom.
D2.Civ.12.K-2. Identify and explain how rules function in public (classroom and school) settings.
Students will identify how individuals have brought about change in their community and in North America over time.
Economics
Theme: Resources
Economic Decision Making
D2.Eco.1.K-2. Explain how scarcity necessitates decision making.

Students will be able to explain what resources are and how they are used. Students will be able to identify resources as renewable or non- renewable. Students will be able to explain how environments are impacted by production and resource use.
Exchange and Markets
D2.Eco.3.K-2. Describe the skills and knowledge required to produce certain goods and services.
D2.Eco.4.K-2. Describe the goods and services that people in the local community produce and those that are produced in other communities.
Students will be able to explain the difference between producers (e.g., farmers) and consumers (e.g., shoppers).
The National Economy
D2.Eco.13.K-2. Describe examples of capital goods and human capital.
Students will be able to identify economic activities that use resources in the local region (e.g., maple syrup production, skilled and trained labor).
The Global Economy
D2.Eco.14.K-2. Describe why people in one country trade goods and services with people in other countries.
D2.Eco.15.K-2. Describe products that are produced abroad and sold domestically and products that are produced domestically and sold abroad.
Students will describe how geography plays a large role in regard to economic production.
Geography
Theme: Environmental Connections
Geographic Representations: Views of the World
D2.Geo.2.K-2. Use maps, graphs, photographs, and other representations to describe places and the relationships and interactions that shape them.
D2.Geo.3.K-2. Use maps, globes, and other simple geographic models to identify cultural and environmental characteristics of places.

Students will be able to use geographic tools (e.g., maps, lobes, maps, diagrams) to locate places in the Americas. Students will be able to describe unifying characteristics of regions. Students will be able to use major geographic descriptors (equator, continent, province, bodies of water) to differentiate locations in the Americas.
Human-Environment Interaction: Place, Regions, and Culture
D2.Geo.4.K-2. Explain how weather, climate, and other environmental characteristics affect people’s lives in a place or region.
D2.Geo.5.K-2. Describe how human activities affect the cultural and environmental characteristics of places or regions.
D2.Geo.6.K-2. Identify some cultural and environmental characteristics of specific places.

Students will be able to explain that people in the Americas have adapted to and modified their environment in different ways to meet their needs. Students will be able to explain the importance of water to communities and ecosystems in the Americas. Students will be able to explain the role of oceans in shaping climate and supporting life in the Americas.
Human Population: Spatial Patterns and Movements
D2.Geo.7.K-2. Explain why and how people, goods, and ideas move from place to place.
D2.Geo.8.K-2. Compare how people in different types of communities use local and distant environments to meet their daily needs.
D2.Geo.9.K-2. Describe the connections between the physical environment of a place and the economic activities found there.
Students will explain how the physical environment influences settlement patterns. Students will be able to explain how geography creates a need for global trading.
Global Interconnections: Changing Spatial Patterns
D2.Geo.10.K-2. Describe changes in the physical and cultural characteristics of various world regions.
D2.Geo.12.K-2. Identify ways that a catastrophic disaster may affect people living in a place.

Students will be able to explain what makes up culture. Students will be able to explain how and why cultures change over time. Students will be able to identify how different groups have worked to protect the land and natural resources.
History
Theme: Relationships
Change, Continuity, and Context
D2.His.1.K-2. Create a chronological sequence of multiple events.
Students will be able to develop a chronological sequence of events in the Americas.
Perspectives
D2.His.4.K-2. Compare perspectives of people in the past to those of people in the present.
D2.His.6.K-2. Compare different accounts of the same historical event.

Students will be able to explain how perspectives and accounts of different historical events can vary. Students will be able to describe how a community may consist of multiple cultures. Students will be able to identify, respect, and explain the diverse cultures of their community and communities in the United States.
Causation and Argumentation
D2.His.14.K-2. Generate possible reasons for an event or development in the past.
D2.His.16.K-2. Select which reasons might be more likely than others to explain a historical event or development.
Students will be able to use different types of sources to support an argument. Students will be able to use historical evidence/sources to create an explanation about an event(s) in the past.
body_examples: Overview

In grade 2, students will expand on their understanding of the concept of community by exploring past and present neighboring communities in Central America, North America, South America, and the Caribbean. Students will explain continuities and differences among cultures, governments, traditions, and available resources to investigate how individuals work together while acknowledging different perspectives and cultivating empathy. Students will learn how culture spreads across borders and compare and contrast Vermont/local community governments, customs, and traditions to others in the Americas. Students will explain current and historic patterns of human settlement and compare the ways various cultural groups connect and interact across the Americas. Students will describe how resources vary across geography and climates and discuss how resources can be categorized as renewable and non-renewable.
Sample Content Connections

• Symbols of civic and political institutions in: o Flags o National holidays o Songs and pledges • The U.S and Vermont have Constitutions, which are the basis for their laws: o Voting o Compromise o Town meeting o Multiple government levels o Branches of government • How governments serve citizens: o Create order - laws (driving, noise, etc.) o Establish laws that protect people’s rights – free speech, religious freedom, no national language o Citizen’s needs - clean water, safety, schools o Tribal governments o Some countries in the Americas have governments like the U.S. (e.g., elect leaders).

• Cultural influences: religion, traditions, values, belief systems, food, customs • Pledge of Allegiance/patriotic songs • Examples of values from different cultures • Examples of beliefs from different cultures • Freedom • Individualism • Patriotism • Equality • Tolerance • Democracy • Family • Opportunity • Ways of participating/being a citizen in one’s school and community in modern times may include voting and participating in the election process, attending public meetings, and writing letters to representatives. • American Indians today may be citizens of their tribal nations, the states they live in, and the United States. • Indigenous people • Tribal nations • Examples of structures, rules, and laws of different societies in North, Central, and South America
• How communities can be improved over time: Building of parks, playgrounds, libraries • Helping others: Green Up Day, food banks, clothing drives, blood drives, fundraisers
Resources

Canadian First Nations: This PBS Learning Media activity allows students to explore a map of Canada and the distribution of Native American groups across it, fill out a chart about the major groups, and answer questions about the map.

Children in Action (Kid Citizen): In this interactive episode, students draw upon their observations and reflections to explore how children have contributed to recycling efforts in the past and present.

Congress and Milk (Kid Citizen): Students learn how Congress has affected their lives by passing laws to include milk in school lunches, and they match different types of food to a school lunch poster from long ago.

Community Helpers (Kid Citizen): The importance of community helpers is a building block of civics understanding. In this episode, children investigate who community helpers are, and how they have changed over time through exploration of a rich photograph (from the Library of Congress) of a man delivering ice to a schoolhouse in 1899.

Educating for American Democracy: Various grade 2 resources, including “Children’s Lives: Comparing Long Ago to Today” and “Historical Figures and Activists”. Primary Sources Spotlight Kits are primary source collections organized
around compelling questions to spotlight key history and civics content in K-12 social studies. Each kit includes diverse primary sources, captions, context, and a collection summary.

Famous Latinos and Latinas: From fighting for justice to being groundbreaking thinkers, artists, athletes, and more, Latinas and Latinos have been breaking boundaries in the United States for centuries. Check out the information below to learn more about famous Latinos and Latinas, from actors to activists.

Haudenosaunee Wampum Belts: In this activity, students will learn about the Great Law of Peace that created unity between the Haudenosaunee nations, and how that unity and peace translated over the creation of the Hiawatha Wampum Belt, and peace with the Europeans. Students will then have the opportunity to create their own Wampum belt to represent unity within their family and community.

How Can Being Civic-Minded Help Me Be a Good Citizen? (iCivics): In this inquiry-based unit, students will examine how they can be civic-minded and make decisions for the common good. Then they will examine the lives of Clara Barton and Robert Smalls to explore the ways they demonstrated civic mindedness.

How Can Generosity Help Me Be a Good Citizen? (iCivics): In this inquiry-based unit, students will learn how they can practice generosity to help others. Using historical examples, they will analyze primary sources to discover how children showed generosity to help during the World Wars and investigate how over 100,000 people showed generosity to bring the Statue of Liberty to New York City.

Latin Independence Days: Much like the United States’ independence is celebrated on the 4th of July, Latin American countries honor their own independence movements. Many of these movements occurred in the Age of Revolutions, a period from the late 1700s to the mid-1800s when several countries fought for and gained their independence.

PBS Learning Media – Xavier Riddle: Talking About Life Lessons - Xavier Riddle and his friends explore values and skills such as compassion, perseverance, responsibility, and gratitude in these video clips supported with teacher materials.

• Limited resources (natural, human, capital) • Renewable resources are resources that can be created, re-purposed (recycled materials into new materials) or re-grown (forests, crops). • Nonrenewable resources are finite (natural gas, coal, oil). • Different countries have different resources. • How resources are made or used can impact local environments. (e.g., several of South America’s top industries—including beef production, fishing and forestry—have a negative effect on the environment and may not be sustainable)

• Impacts on production: technology, innovations, trade, culture, labor, knowledge, etc. • Major social, cultural, and economic changes took place in American Indian cultures as a result of the acquisition of goods and technologies from Europeans and others.

• Examples of the importance of skill development and learning lead to individual and community growth: o Skills needed by Native Americans in the past compared to skills needed in workplaces today. • American Indian knowledge and related innovations, goods, and technologies (e.g., agriculture) have had enormous global impact.

• Examples of productivity in North America and Vermont: o Agriculture o Manufacturing o Tourism o Transportation • Produced in South America: o The warm, wet climate is perfect for two of South America’s most important exports: coffee and cacao, which is the source of cocoa, the base ingredient in chocolate. o Brazil is the world’s largest exporter of coffee and beef. o Ecuador is a major producer of cacao. o Grazing animals such as alpacas, llamas, sheep, and vicuñas thrive in the cold climate regions of South America. These animals are bred for their meat and their wool, which is used in high-quality textiles exported throughout the world. • Major tourist areas in Central America.
Resources

Conserving Non-Renewable Resources: This PBS Learning Media resource lets students learn why it is important to be careful when using non-renewable resources in this video from CYBERCHASE. Students discover that most electricity currently comes from burning gas, oil, and coal, which are all resources that cannot be replaced once they are consumed. Refer to the accompanying discussion questions, renewable energy coloring book from Solar1, and teaching tips for ideas

on using this video with students and to help them consider ways to use electricity wisely. Discussion questions and vocabulary terms are available in Spanish in the Support Materials. (See also resources in Geography.)

Economic Interdependence: This C3 IDM inquiry is an initial exploration into the concept of interdependence through the lens of community economics and the idea of an economy as a diverse, mutually supportive web of needs and wants, workers and consumers, and problems and solutions. The compelling question “What makes me become we?” challenges students to consider interdependence among individuals and groups and think about how a community is not just a bunch of individual “mes” living in a shared space but also a collective “we” that interacts, grows and contracts, and tries to solve issues. This inquiry builds on students’ first-grade knowledge and challenges them to understand that through businesses, town organizations, and local governments, a community meets the needs and wants of its people, finding strength in collective efforts to address problems.

Global Trade Inquiry: This C3 IDM inquiry leads students through an investigation of economic systems by focusing on the context of trade among world communities. Trading is one of the oldest forms of economic interaction among humans, yet it is also among the most complex. In examining the reasons for international trade and the exports of world communities, students should be able to develop an argument supported by evidence to answer the compelling question, “Why do countries need each other?”

Human Impact on the Environment: This PBS Learning Media collection of resources shows real-world life impact on the environment. Lessons/activities include a focus on ocean litter, air pollution, climate change, and food waste and offer the opportunity for a lens to economics, geography, as well as life and earth sciences.

• Equator, provinces, states, countries, continents • Physical geography vs. political geography (e.g., boundaries and borders) • Time zones • Map vs. Globe • Continent vs. Country • Identify and locate the major continents and oceans in and bordering the Americas using maps and globes: o Locations of North America, Central America, and South America • Identify the U.S land/water borders including: o Canada, Mexico, Atlantic Ocean, Pacific Ocean, and Gulf of Mexico • Regions of the U.S. (i.e., Southeast, Northeast, Great Plains, Southwest, Rocky Mountain, and Pacific Northwest) and their climate, physical features, and population • Identify major physical features of the U.S., including: o Rivers – Colorado, Mississippi, Ohio, Rio Grande, Amazon, Hudson o Mountains – Alaska Range, Appalachian, Rockies o Bodies of Water – Great Lakes, Gulf of Mexico, Atlantic Ocean, Pacific Ocean o Desert – Great Basin o Landforms – Grand Canyon, Great Plains o Man-made – Panama Canal

• Environmental characteristics of a community: o Climate and weather patterns, landforms, natural resources, and natural hazards • Ocean effect on: o Climate differences, storms, hurricanes, fishing industry, transportation • Importance of water: o Farming/agriculture, drinking and everyday use, ecosystem support, conservation, and anti-pollution efforts • Past cultural adaptations/modifications: o American Southwest – pueblos and irrigation systems o Amazon – stilt-houses and crops that thrive in wet environment o Andes Mountains – terraced living and farming

• Geographic features, such as bodies of water, topography, climate, land, and natural resources, often affect where people settle and how these people sustain themselves: o Aztecs, Mayans, Incas, Iroquois, Abenaki, Mohawk, Plains (nomadic) • Cultural Spread: o Internet, air travel, social media, television, movies, music, video calling • Imports and Exports • United States exports: o Petroleum, cars, liquified natural gas (world’s largest exporter), consumer goods • Main United States imports: o Consumer goods, industrial supplies, capital goods

• Culture can include, but is not limited to: o Characteristics like values, norms, beliefs, and ways of behaving. • Culture can be defined as the main characteristics shared by a group of people at a particular time and in a particular place that are learned and passed down by rules, traditions, and stories. • The belief systems of various indigenous, religious, and racial groups often influence art, music, customs, and cultural traditions in a nation. • Communities from around the world interact with other people and communities and exchange cultural ideas and practices. • Indigenous cultures: o European conquest, disease spread, cultural assimilation, farming practices
Resources
Map Skills/General:
Cardinal Directions and Maps: Students listen to a poem that uses cardinal directions. They use a compass rose to help describe locations of places on a world map.

Central American Studies Curriculum Project: Cultural Identity Preservation Through Storytelling (California Subject Matter Project, Ethnic Studies Initiative): In this mini-unit students will learn about the migrant stories of their families, their school community, and/or local area through the cultural practice of storytelling through oral tradition and
artwork. Students will create or retell a migrant story through a written narrative, accompanying art piece, and oral presentation.
Classroom Map: Introduce young students to the concept of maps as representations of places with this classroom map.

Cultural Diversity: This C3 IDM is grade-leveled for third graders but can be amended to engage second graders in expanding their understandings of diverse cultures. The compelling question “How does our culture make us similar and different?” is intellectually respectful of students who, by their nature, are interested in people and their similarities and differences. It allows for engagement with several social studies disciplines as students examine diverse cultures and histories around the globe.

Map Skills for Students (National Geographic): This collection features map activities designed to strengthen spatial thinking skills for students. Spatial thinking allows students to comprehend and analyze phenomena related to the places and spaces around them and is one of the most important skills students can develop as they learn geography and various science disciplines.

Mapping the Storybooks: Students use a map and cutouts of a story's characters to follow their actions through space and time. They retell the story in their own words, using the map and positional vocabulary.

Measuring Distances on a Map: Students use a map scale to measure distance between cities and other places on a map of your state. They create and exchange quizzes and use an interactive map to check their answers.
Park Map: Introduce young students to the concept of maps as representations of places with this park map.

PEI Activity 1: Continents and Oceans (ESRI Canada): In this activity, students explore the vast continents and the deep, mysterious oceans using the PEI Atlas. Students start by learning how to navigate the PEI Atlas, learning how to zoom in and out to see the world from different perspectives, from a bird's eye view of the entire world to a closer look at the intricate coastlines of continents. Next, students learn how to label the continents and the world's oceans using the sketch tool. (May be suitable for class-led activity for Grade 2)

PEI Activity 2: Geography Shapes the World (ESRI Canada): In this activity, students explore landform regions around the world and world heritage sites using the PEI Atlas and the activity sheet. Students start by learning how to navigate the PEI Atlas in 3D and how to zoom in and out to see the world from different perspectives. Next, students learn how to use the measure tool to measure distance and coordinates and create an elevation profile. (May be suitable for class-led activity for Grade 2.)

PEI Activity 3: Exploring Cultural Regions (ESRI Canada): In this activity, students explore data layers to understand if cultural regions have a connection to the physical world using the PEI Atlas and the activity sheet. Students start by learning how to navigate the PEI Atlas data tools. Students learn how to change the look of data and see the table behind the data on a map. Next, students learn how to compare different data layers to look for connections and analyze them. (May be suitable for class-led activity for Grade 2.)
Reading a Resource Map: Students read a natural resource map and use a chart to determine the origins of goods that people use.
Using a Grid with a Zoo Map: Students use a map grid to describe and find locations on a zoo map and a city map. They use a grid to create a message.

Why do People Move? (iCivics): People move for many different reasons, such as for jobs or to be closer to family. In this inquiry-based unit, students will learn all about moving. They will start by learning about the push and pull factors that cause animals to move. While learning new vocabulary, listening to stories, and examining primary source materials, students will better understand reasons why humans move. The unit ends with stories of the push and pull factors that influenced the Great Migration.

Why do We Need Maps? (iCivics): This inquiry-based unit puts kids on the map! Key vocabulary and primary source information allow kids to study different map projections and learn how maps have changed over time. The 1904 World’s Fair Map will be the guide to practice their newly acquired map skills.
North America:

Let’s Discover Canada (ESRI Canada): In this activity, you will discover the Capital cities in Canada, areas of interests, and measure distances between places. The purpose of this quick exercise is to engage with a map of Canada in order to begin the discovery of this large, complex land mass. (May be suitable as a class-led activity.)
North America overview video (National Geographic): Short Destination World video.

U.S. States and Territories (photos from National Geographic): The creators of Molly of Denali worked with Alaska Native elders to ensure its authenticity from the ground up, so watching the series is a solid source of information about Alaska Native traditions for little kids. PBS LearningMedia also has classroom resources to accompany episodes of the show like "Grandpa's Drum."
Central America:

Beauty and Eco-Relationships in the Natural World of Central America: In this lesson, students learn about three different animals — a bird, a frog, and a butterfly (the Motmot of El Salvador, the Exquisite Spike-Thumb Frog Plectrohyla exquisita of Honduras, and the Owl Butterfly from Guatemala). All these creatures are indigenous to Central America and help us understand the region’s ecosystems. Using visual art, the lesson gives students the opportunity to explore in- depth facts about each animal, while integrating an arts component where students are encouraged to draw the animals and design their own books about the animals to scaffold learning.

Comparing Cultural Holidays: What comparisons can you draw from the artistic and cultural traditions of Halloween and the Day of the Dead?: In this lesson, students will explore the holiday traditions, music, and art of Halloween and Día de los Muertos. Students will create an altar in memory of a loved one.
Elementary Booklist
Elementary Level Poetry

Geography is History: Locate the Countries of Central America: This interactive map lesson provides students with clues based on the history and geography of Central America so that they can find and remember the location of each country.

Maya Skies: Calendars, Seasons, and Time: The Maya of Mesoamerica have been tracking the Sun's movements in the sky for thousands of years. Today, more than seven million Maya people live in regions of Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, Belize, El Salvador, and other countries. More than two thousand years ago, the Maya created a complex calendar system to organize the events of their world and developed sophisticated mathematics, inventing the zero. They applied their knowledge and observations to time their ceremonies and agricultural cycles. The Maya built extensive cities with monumental architecture, including pyramids that they used to track the stars and predict seasons.

Native American Representation in STEM: Indigenous Innovation: Explores Native scientific legacies. Use this guide to increase awareness of Indigenous knowledge in the subjects of science, technology, engineering, and math. Culturally sensitive activities and resources connected to Native Americans and STEM are provided. In many schools, lessons about Indigenous Peoples are presented only through social studies. This often defines Native Americans by their encounters with others, rather than by their own accomplishments. In truth, Indigenous Peoples in the Americas have

been innovative and successful managers of their lands and resources for tens of thousands of years. Native innovation is anchored in a deep understanding of how tools and technologies are best suited to the environment

Pancho Rabbit and the Coyote: A Migrant’s Tale: Pancho Rabbit and the Coyote: A Migrant’s Tale by Duncan Tonatiuh is one of the best books we’ve seen for children on the experiences of families forced to migrate to the U.S. to survive. In a child-friendly format, the story addresses the push factors, the hardships caused by family separation, the dangerous journey through Mexico, and crossing the border. The Consortium of Latin American Studies Programs (CLASP), on behalf of the Américas Award, produced an extensive teaching guide to accompany the book written by Katrina Dillon in 2015.

Smithsonian in the Classroom: Native American Dolls: Smithsonian Institute. “Developed in collaboration with the Smithsonian Center for Education and Museum Studies, this lesson plan presents the firsthand perspectives of five Native American doll makers from around the United States. Students examine full–color images of dolls from the museum's collection in order to learn more about the diverse cultures, communities, and environments the dolls represent”.
South America:
South America overview video (National Geographic) Short Destination World video.

The Great Inka Road: How Can a Road System Be an Example of Innovation?: The Inka Empire thrived in South America in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. To support the empire, the Inka built a vast road system for transportation, communication, and integration. This lesson highlights Inka engineering accomplishments that allowed the Inka to manage their vast and disperse empire, and how their legacy has relevancy in the present day. Explore a variety of sources to learn about the engineering of the Great Inka Road system and the Q'eswachaka suspension grass bridge. **El Grand Camino** what is happening currently along the route?

• Describe periods of time in terms of: o Decades o Centuries • Timelines can reflect key historical events. • Past: o First Americans o European arrival o Colonial founding: Jamestown, Plimoth/Patuxet, Williamsburg o Mayan and Aztec Calendars • Present: Examine change/differences within the Americas of things that students are currently familiar with: o Transportation o Communication o Food o Homes/shelter o Clothing o Resources • Persons of influence in the past: o Pocahontas, Tecumseh, Sacagawea, Columbus, Cortes, Champlain, Hudson, Ahuitzotl, Montezuma II, Mog, Grey Lock, Ethan and Ira Allen • Contemporary leaders: o Activists, presidents, scientists; student’s choice if they can define person(s)/groups as leaders

• It is okay to have different perspectives as long as harm is not caused. • Evidence can be used to validate perspectives. • Discuss how different experiences shape perspective; share evidence of experience from multiple viewpoints (Native Americans, colonists). • Discuss how different languages, cultures, traditions can affect ways in which people see the world, both now and in the past.
Use of: • Primary and secondary sources • Photographs • Maps • Journal entries
Resources

Anishinaabe/Ojibwe/Chippewa: Culture of an Indian Nation: This lesson provides information and activities about one American Indian Nation, the Anishinaabe, called Ojibwe in Canada and parts of the U.S., and Chippewa other regions of the U.S., and engages students in research on its history, location, and past and present culture. By focusing on one Native American tribe, students will acquire a differentiated and accurate understanding of one of the many diverse peoples and cultures living throughout the lands that are now referred to as North and South America, in addition to recognizing elements of a common history of conquest and displacement by Europeans that affected all Native American peoples

Canada - Core Knowledge: This unit introduces the geography and people of Canada. Students learn about Canada’s government, major population centers (including Montreal, Quebec City, and Toronto), and the country’s vast wilderness and natural resources. They are introduced to Canada’s indigenous peoples and to its French and British heritage, which

lie behind the country’s two official languages. Students explore the strong influence of French culture in Quebec. They also consider similarities and differences between Canada and the United States and learn how Canada’s history and relationship with Britain (the United Kingdom) are different from those the U.S. has with that nation.

C3 IDM - Holidays: This inquiry encourages learners expand their study of self and others by deepening their understanding of the role of traditions, holidays, and symbols in establishing cultural identity and unity. The compelling question “What makes holidays special?” reflects an enduring conversation about how and why people engage in ritual and tradition. It is respectful of students’ intellectual efforts as they are likely to be interested in knowing more about traditions and holidays and are likely to have a meaningful entry point into the discussion based upon personal experiences.

C3 IDM - Identity: This inquiry leads students through an investigation of self by recognizing that all humans have both unique and similar characteristics. By investigating the compelling question “Is everyone unique?” students begin to see how they are similar to and different from their classmates. The study of similarities and differences among individuals provides the foundation for students to demonstrate their understanding of and respect for others.

Colonial Williamsburg: Varied resources from Historic Trades and Skills to Created Equal, which help students get a look at the colonial Virginia settlement; other resources include the Art Museum for CW Kids.

The Earliest Americans - Core Knowledge: This unit introduces students to some of the different native peoples who populated America many years before the arrival of European explorers. Students learn how some of the earliest Americans arrived in North America as early as thirty thousand years ago along the Pacific Coast, whereas others traveled from Asia across Beringia, the land bridge. Over time, native peoples migrated throughout the North American continent and into Central and South America. Students explore how these early peoples adapted to their environments and developed unique cultures. Chapters focus on the Inuit, the Ancestral Pueblo and Mound Builders, and specific Native American peoples of the American Southwest, Southeast, and Eastern Woodlands.

Educating for American Democracy: Various grade 2 resources, including “Children’s Lives: Comparing Long Ago to Today” and “Historical Figures and Activists”. Primary Sources Spotlight Kits are primary source collections organized around compelling questions to spotlight key history and civics content in K-12 social studies. Each kit includes diverse primary sources, captions, context, and a collection summary.
Ethan Allen Homestead Museum: Curated collections with themes including Abenaki Heritage, Women in early Vermont, Homesteading and Artisan Crafts, and Slavery in early Vermont.

Exploration of North America - Core Knowledge: This unit focuses on English, French, and Spanish explorers who crisscrossed the Americas in search of new finds, whether gold, riches, or a passage through the continent from east to west. After reviewing the explorations of Columbus, students learn about Ponce de León’s search for the Fountain of Youth, De Soto’s long march to the Mississippi, Coronado’s quest for cities of gold, the founding of St. Augustine, and the development of settlements around Spanish missions. The focus then shifts to the explorers who undertook perilous voyages to find the Northwest Passage, a shortcut across North America to Asia, including John Cabot, Samuel de Champlain, and Henry Hudson. Throughout the unit students reinforce their map skills and geographic knowledge and also learn about the interactions of the explorers with Native Americans, including Popé and the Pueblo Revolt.

History’s Mysteries - How do We Celebrate Our Shared Traditions?: In this unit, students will solve four historical mysteries using evidence from primary sources including 1) “Where is the history in a name?”, 2) What shared traditions make your family special?”, 3) Why do we have a day off from school?”, and 4) “How does a tradition become a holiday?” Students will explore naming traditions, family traditions, civic versus religious holidays, and lastly, the story of Juneteenth and how it has become a holiday celebrated across America.

History’s Mysteries - What is the Difference Between Then and Now?: In this unit, students will explore three mysteries, 1) “What is the difference between then and now?”, 2) “Where do people work?”, and 3) “How is work different now than in the past?” Students will explore primary source images from the Library of Congress to solve historical mysteries with evidence.

KidCitizen - Community Helpers: In this interactive lesson, students will learn how community helpers have changed and stayed the same over time by exploring a photograph of a man delivering ice to a schoolhouse around 1900 and investigate who community helpers are.
Learning for Justice - What is a Family?: This lesson provides a framework that will help students talk about their own and others’ families in safe, caring ways.

Native American Cultures Across the U.S.: Children's literature, movies, and other media often perpetuate generalized stereotypes, whether positive or negative, in their representations of Native American peoples. Teaching children about the First Americans in an accurate historical context while emphasizing their continuing presence and influence within the
United States is important for developing a national and individual respect for the diverse American Indian peoples and is necessary to understanding the history of this country.

Native American Dwellings: Statistics in Schools: In this activity, students will look at historical images to learn about three types of Native American dwellings — teepees, pueblo adobe structures, and hogans. Students will make observations about the types of dwellings in the images. Then students will discuss their observations as a class.

PBS Learning Media Habitats and Discoveries: Images of the Past: In this lesson, your students will participate in a hands-on observation challenge that will encourage them to look closer at the habitats around them.

PBS Learning Media - The Fred T. Korematsu Institute - How are We Defined as Americans?: In this lesson, the students will explore what it means to them to be an American. They will reflect on their own identities and family histories to better understand their experience. Individually and as a group, students will develop a definition of what it means to be an American and add to that definition throughout the year.

Plimoth Patuxet Museum: Teacher tools and resources to help students understand multiple perspectives and challenge stereotypes of past history. Teachers will need to cull from the site to find primary and secondary sources that are grade appropriate.
Project 562: Explore and discuss the photos from Project 562, which includes images of contemporary Native life from over 562 federally recognized tribes.
Redesign Your Thanksgiving Curriculum: This collection of resources from the National Education Association ranges from articles to lesson plans, advice, and books.

Teaching Native American History and Culture: This infographic from NAPTAC covers some key information to inform teaching Native American history and culture as well as creating a more inclusive environment for Native students.
Teotihuacan: City of Water, City of Fire: This virtual exhibit invites students to explore recent archaeological finds made at the site, while placing them in historical and cultural context.
Toolkit for Decolonizing Thanksgiving: This toolkit now has two parts and assembles resources, including books, that will help reframe the story of Thanksgiving.
Vermont Classroom Blueprint: Vermont Office of the Secretary of State. A K-12 ‘blueprint’ providing resources and lesson plans for active civic engagement in your classroom.

Critical Proficiency (K-12): Students act as social scientists as they ask questions, think critically, solve problems, and share conclusions.
Priority Performance Indicators (3-5):

• Constructing Compelling and Supporting Questions: Explain why compelling and supporting questions are important and how associated ideas can be open to different interpretations. (D1. 1-3) • Gathering and Evaluating Sources: Compare information from different sources and use differences between fact and opinion to determine the credibility of the source. (D2. His. 10, 12; D3. 1-3) • Communicating and Critiquing Solutions: Use evidence from multiple sources to develop a claim or argument about the past. (D2. His. 16; D4. 1)

• Identity • Resources • Environmental Connections • Relationships

Students will identify similarities and differences between types of governments in Africa, Asia, Europe, and Oceania. Students will be able to identify how government can look different at different times and in continents/ areas/civilizations in Africa, Asia, Europe, and Oceania.

body_examples: Overview

In grade 3, students will expand on their understanding of the concept of community and widen their global lens by exploring interactions between groups of people in Africa, Asia, Europe, and Oceania. Students will explain continuities and differences among cultures, governments, traditions, and resources to investigate how individuals work together while acknowledging different perspectives and cultivating empathy. Students will learn how culture spreads across borders, and students will compare and contrast Vermont/local community customs and traditions to others in the world. Students will explain current and historic patterns of human settlement and compare the ways various cultural groups connect and interact. Students will describe how resources vary across geography and climates and discuss how resources can be categorized as renewable and non-renewable.
Sample Content Connections

Different Types of Governments: United States and Vermont • Democracies; both follow the three-branch system (executive, legislative, judicial), have elected officials, and written constitutions • Governor vs. President; laws- state vs. federal Africa • Example: South Africa o Type: Democracy (similar to U.S.) o Structure: President, Parliament, Constitutional Court o Difference: President is chosen by Parliament, not directly by voters • Example: Eritrea o Type: One-party authoritarian state o Difference: Citizens do not vote freely; limited political freedom Asia • Example: India o Type: Parliamentary Democracy o Difference: Voters elect a parliament, and parliament selects the prime minister • Example: China o Type: One-party Communist state o Difference: No free elections for national leaders; all major decisions made by the Communist Party

Europe • Example: United Kingdom o Type: Constitutional Monarchy + Parliamentary Democracy o Structure: Monarch (King/Queen) + Prime Minister + Parliament o Difference: Monarch has ceremonial role; real power lies with elected leaders • Example: Russia o Type: Technically a federal republic, but functions more like an authoritarian state o Difference: Elections occur, but critics say power is heavily controlled by the president Oceania • Example: Australia o Type: Parliamentary Democracy and Constitutional Monarchy o Structure: Prime Minister + Parliament + ceremonial monarch (King of England) o Similarity: People vote for representatives; courts are independent • Example: Fiji o Type: Parliamentary Republic o Past military coups; now functions more democratically

Government Examples by Region and Time Period Africa • Ancient Egypt (Old Kingdom) – Pharaoh was considered a god and ruled with total power (theocracy/monarchy). • Mali Empire (1200s–1400s) – Emperor (Mansa) ruled with help from advisors and local leaders. • Modern South Africa – Today has a democratic government with a president and parliament. • Shows a shift from monarchy and empire to democracy. Asia • Ancient China (Qin Dynasty) – Emperor had absolute power; used strict laws (legalism). • Mughal Empire (India) – Ruled by emperors with regional governors. • Modern Japan – Constitutional monarchy with elected parliament and a ceremonial emperor. • Government changed from absolute monarchy to constitutional democracy.

Europe • Ancient Greece (Athens) – Early form of direct democracy. • Medieval Europe – Feudal monarchies, with kings and nobles holding power. • Modern Germany or UK – Democracies with parliaments and prime ministers. • Shift from feudal/royal rule to parliamentary and democratic governments. Oceania • Traditional Polynesian societies – Led by chiefs or elders with tribal leadership systems. • Colonial Australia – Governed by British-appointed officials. • Modern Australia & New Zealand – Parliamentary democracies with elected leaders. • Change from tribal governance to colonial rule, then to modern democracy.

Africa • Nelson Mandela (South Africa) • Led the fight against apartheid (racial segregation) • Became the first Black president of South Africa • Worked for equality and reconciliation • Wangari Maathai (Kenya) • Started the Green Belt Movement • Helped women plant millions of trees and protect the environment Asia • Mahatma Gandhi (India) • Led nonviolent protests to gain India’s independence from Britain • Inspired civil rights movements worldwide • Malala Yousafzai (Pakistan) • Advocated for girls' education despite being attacked • Won the Nobel Peace Prize at age 17 Europe • Florence Nightingale (UK) • Revolutionized modern nursing and improved hospitals during war • Oskar Schindler (Germany/Poland) • Saved over 1,000 Jewish people during the Holocaust by employing them in his factories

Oceania • Eddie Mabo (Australia) • Fought for the land rights of Indigenous Australians • Led to a major legal change in how Indigenous land ownership was recognized • Kate Sheppard (New Zealand) • Led the women’s suffrage movement • Helped New Zealand become the first country to give women the right to vote (1893)
Resources

Children’s Rights - C3 IDM: The third-grade annotated inquiry focuses on the concept of universal human rights and fair treatment of all people through the compelling question “Do people around the world care about children’s rights?” This question highlights the idea that human rights, including the right to have one’s basic needs met, are to be universally ensured and protected. Around the world there are many instances of human rights violations, but there are also individuals, groups, and nations who work to protect and defend human rights. The focus on children’s rights—the idea that children have unique rights that apply to them as nonadult members of the global citizenry—offers students an opportunity to examine the idea that they have rights and to understand that they can have an impact on the world.

Discovering My Identity - Learning for Justice: “In this lesson, students will describe aspects of their identities such as race, gender, ability, religion and more. Then after exploring Marley Dias' Black Girls Books campaign, students will analyze book illustrations and write their own book review noting how characters are similar and different from them.”

Leadership and Government - C3 IDM: “This inquiry is an exploration into governments around the world; it examines how the fundamental principles of governments vary in different world communities with diverse political systems. In

uncovering the idea that the role of citizens varies in governments around the world, students develop an argument supported by evidence that answers the compelling question ‘Does it matter how leaders are chosen?’”
Vermont Classroom Blueprint - Vermont Office of the Secretary of State: A K-12 ‘blueprint’ providing resources and lesson plans for active civic engagement in your classroom.

• Encourages Production: Proximity to, and availability of, resources and technology • Limits Production: Taxation or government control, tariffs, war/conflict, cultural norms, market access • Regional Production Considerations: o Africa – Positive: Natural resources support exports; Negative: environmental damage o Asia – Positive: Access to trade routes and workforce; Negative: pollution o Europe – Positive: strong economies; Negative: historical overuse of natural resources (coal) o Oceania – Positive: Clean farming; Negative: environmental impact of farming

Then vs. Now: Regional Examples Africa • Past: Ancient Ghana and Mali traded gold and salt across the Sahara. • Now: Countries like Nigeria export oil, and Ivory Coast exports cocoa. • Comparison: Then and now, Africa relies on natural resources, but modern economies are more connected to global markets. Asia • Past: Ancient China produced silk, porcelain, and tea, traded via the Silk Road. • Now: China and India produce electronics, clothing, and software for global markets. • Comparison: Asia still leads in mass production, but goods have shifted from hand-made luxury items to high-tech and industrial goods. Europe • Past: Feudal Europe focused on local farming and craft production (blacksmiths, weavers). • Now: Europe is known for automobiles, fashion, and finance (e.g., Germany, France, UK). • Comparison: Europe shifted from rural agriculture to urban, technology- based economies.

Oceania • Past: Indigenous groups in Australia and the Pacific produced and consumed local goods (fish, tools, woven goods) within small communities. • Now: Australia and New Zealand produce wool, dairy, minerals, and participate in global trade. • Comparison: There’s a shift from self-sufficiency to globalized production, though traditional practices are still preserved in some communities.

• Bartering – Trading goods and services without using money; still practiced in rural parts of Asia and Africa • Currency – Money used to buy goods and services; Euro, Rand, Yen, Australian dollar • Goods – Physical items produced or sold; Rice (Asia), wine (Europe), gold (South Africa), wool (Oceania) • Services – Activities people do for money; tourism, tech support • Resources – Natural materials used in production; oil, timber

Geography and Specialization Africa • Geography: Rich in minerals (gold, diamonds), oil reserves, and tropical climates. • Specialization: Mining (South Africa), oil production (Nigeria), cocoa farming (Ivory Coast). • Impact: Natural resources are key to exports, but reliance on them can make economies unstable. Asia • Geography: Large rivers (Yangtze, Ganges), fertile plains, monsoon climate, mountains. • Specialization: • India – agriculture (rice, tea). • China – manufacturing (gunpowder, textiles). • Middle East – oil and gas (Saudi Arabia, Iran). • Impact: Geography supports both farming in some areas and energy production in others. Europe • Geography: Access to rivers and seas, moderate climate, fertile land, and natural resources. • Specialization: • Germany – automobiles and machinery.

Europe (continued) • France/Italy – wine and cheese (from climate and farming conditions). • Scandinavia – fishing and forestry. Impact: Physical features support high-tech industry and trade through ports. Oceania • Geography: Island geography, deserts (Australia), fertile coastlines. • Specialization: • Australia – mining (iron ore, coal), sheep farming, wheat. • New Zealand – dairy and wool. • Pacific Islands – tourism and fishing. • Impact: Remote locations can make trade harder, but natural beauty boosts tourism.
Resources

Global Trade - C3 IDM: “This inquiry leads students through an investigation of economic systems by focusing on the context of trade among world communities. Trading is one of the oldest forms of economic interaction among humans, yet it is also among the most complex. In examining the reasons for international trade and the exports of world communities, students should be able to develop an argument supported by evidence to answer the compelling question: ‘Why do countries need each other?’”

Globalization - C3 IDM: This inquiry engages third graders in expanding their understandings of our increasingly interconnected world. The compelling question “Is sharing and trading across cultures always a good thing?” is intellectually respectful of third graders who have personal experience with sharing and trading and typically have been told that sharing and trading are positive ways to interact. This inquiry explores that assumption in ways that allow
students to engage with several social studies disciplines as students uncover political, economic, and social connections across cultures and analyze the implications of those connections.

Understanding Economics - Core Knowledge: This 5-lesson unit “Understanding Economics” will provide an overview of the following content: Every society must answer basic economic questions: What will the society produce? How will society produce it? How will society distribute it? The answers to these questions are shaped by many factors, including access to resources, access to technology, and cultural values. Similarly, individuals also make economic decisions about what to buy, where to buy it, when to save, how much to save, and so on. These decisions are informed by the availability of goods and services, prices, and personal values.

Where in the World… Does All This Stuff Come From? - National Council for Social Studies: With labels removed from products, students identify on a world map where products are made around the world. This Inquiry was geared to middle school students but can easily be scaled down for elementary classrooms.

Types of Characteristics That Can Unify a Region 1. Cultural – shared religion, language, customs, or history 2. Physical/Geographic – similar climate, landforms, or location 3. Political – similar governments, alliances, or borders 4. Economic – shared trade, industries, or resources Key Locations by Region Africa • Countries: Egypt, Nigeria, South Africa, Kenya, Ghana • Cities: Cairo, Lagos, Johannesburg, Nairobi • Landforms: Sahara Desert, Nile River, Mount Kilimanjaro, Congo River Asia • Countries: China, India, Japan, Russia, Saudi Arabia • Cities: Beijing, New Delhi, Tokyo, Mecca, Bangkok • Landforms: Himalayas, Ganges River, Yangtze River, Arabian Desert Europe • Countries: United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, Spain • Cities: London, Paris, Rome, Berlin, Madrid • Landforms: Alps Mountains, Danube River, Mediterranean Sea

Oceania • Countries: Australia, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Fiji • Cities: Sydney, Wellington, Port Moresby Landforms: Great Barrier Reef, Outback, Southern Alps (New Zealand) Key Concepts: • Climate, landforms, natural resources, isolation vs. access Impacts on Culture: • Clothing, housing, economy, transportation, food, religion (spiritual ties to land)

Movement of language, food, religion and traditions • Colonization – Indian traditions found in East African countries like Kenya and Tanzania Urban growth, deforestation, pollution • Rapid urbanization in China has led to air and water pollution due to industrial development. Changing Environments Affect Human Settlements: • Environmental changes like droughts, floods, and rising sea levels can cause people to move. • Desertification in the Sahel region of Africa pushes people to leave rural areas and move to cities or other countries. Geography and the Environment Africa • Geography: Sahara Desert, Nile River, savannas, tropical rainforests • Cultural Impact: • The Nile River allowed for farming and led to the rise of powerful civilizations like Ancient Egypt. • The Sahara limited movement but also helped create trans-Saharan trade routes—leading to the spread of Islam and the rise of empires like Mali. • Diverse environments led to many ethnic groups and languages each adapted to local climates.

Asia • Geography: Himalayas, Gobi Desert, monsoons, rivers (Yangtze, Ganges) • Cultural Impact: o Monsoons shaped farming and religious practices (e.g., in India, monsoon rains are linked to spiritual beliefs about nature). o Mountain ranges isolated areas, allowing unique cultures like Tibet or Japan to develop. Europe • Geography: Mountains (Alps, Pyrenees), rivers (Danube, Rhine), Mediterranean Sea, temperate climate • Cultural Impact: • The Mediterranean Sea allowed for trade and cultural exchange among Greeks, Romans, and others—spreading art, architecture, and religion. • Mild climate helped support agriculture, leading to population growth and early urbanization. • Natural barriers like the Alps influenced the development of different languages and political boundaries. Oceania (Australia, New Zealand, and Pacific Islands) • Geography: Isolated islands, ocean-dependent cultures, coral reefs, deserts (Australia)

• Cultural Impact: o Pacific Islanders became expert navigators, using stars and waves to explore vast ocean distances—forming a rich tradition of oral history and storytelling. o Aboriginal Australians developed deep spiritual connections to land features ("Dreamtime" stories tied to the landscape). o Isolation led to unique ecosystems and cultural traditions not found anywhere else in the world.

Adaptations and Modifications Africa • Adaptation: Nomadic herders in the Sahel move seasonally to find grazing land for animals. • Modification: Building irrigation systems along the Nile River to grow crops in dry areas. Asia • Adaptation: People in mountainous areas like the Himalayas build homes on slopes and use terraced farming. • Modification: In Japan, people build earthquake-resistant buildings to stay safe in natural disasters. Europe • Adaptation: In colder regions like Scandinavia, people wear heavy clothing, build insulated homes, and rely on indoor heating. • Modification: The Dutch built dikes and canals to control flooding and reclaim land from the sea in the Netherlands. Oceania • Adaptation: Indigenous groups in Australia adapted to desert life by learning to find water and hunt with traditional tools. • Modification: People in New Zealand cleared forests for sheep farming and built cities in coastal areas.

Positive and Negative Impacts Africa • Example: Building dams on the Nile River (like the Aswan High Dam) • Positive View: Helps control floods, creates electricity, improves farming. • Negative View: Disrupts natural flow, affects fish and farmland downstream, and floods ancient sites. • Example: Rainforest clearing in Central Africa • Positive View: Creates farmland and jobs. • Negative View: Destroys ecosystems, affects global climate, and displaces Indigenous peoples. Asia • Example: Rice farming in Southeast Asia using terrace systems • Positive View: Efficient use of land, supports large populations, sustainable over time. • Negative View: Can lead to soil erosion and water use issues if mismanaged. • Example: Urban development in China and India • Positive View: Economic growth, new infrastructure, housing. • Negative View: Air and water pollution, loss of green spaces, displacement of rural communities. Europe • Example: Industrial Revolution (18th–19th centuries) • Positive View: Innovation, jobs, and economic growth.

Europe (continued) • Negative View: Air and water pollution, overuse of coal, environmental damage. • Example: Wind farms in Northern Europe • Positive View: Clean energy, reduced carbon emissions. • Negative View: Some people believe they spoil landscapes or affect bird populations. Oceania • Example: Mining in Australia • Positive View: Boosts economy, provides jobs and resources. • Negative View: Harms sacred Aboriginal lands, pollutes rivers, damages ecosystems. • Example: Traditional fishing by Pacific Islander communities • Positive View: Sustainable, culturally important, respects marine life. • Negative View: Overfishing by foreign companies now threatens their way of life.
Resources

Building the Pyramids of Ancient Egypt - PBS Learning Media: In this interactive lesson supporting literacy skills, students learn how historians think the pyramids were built and why they were built—as doorways to the afterlife for the pharaohs. Students develop their literacy skills as they explore a social studies focus on ancient Egyptian society and how those at the top organized the rest of the population in order to build these amazing structures. During this process, they read informational text, learn and practice vocabulary words, and explore content through videos and interactive activities.

Confucius: A Life - PBS Learning Media: Students will read a short history of Confucius. They will explore some principle elements of Confucius’s teachings. Finally, they will read three quotes from The Analects and correctly identify the Confucian principles they show. Teacher notes are included.

Cultural Diversity - C3 IDM: This inquiry engages third graders in expanding their understandings of diverse cultures. The compelling question, “How does our culture make us similar and different?” is intellectually respectful of students who, by their nature, are interested in people and their similarities and differences. It allows for engagement with several social studies disciplines as students examine diverse cultures and histories around the globe.

Examining Changes to the Environment Through Pictures and Data - Statistics in Schools: Students will examine how human actions and population changes can affect the environment. Students will examine a series of photographs that compare famous landmarks (Times Square, the Saltair Pavilion in Utah, Laguna Beach, and Niagara Falls) across time, and then they will identify human-generated changes in the physical environment, such as the addition of bridges and roads. Students will also examine U.S. Census Bureau population and housing data to see how population changes can contribute to changes in the physical environment. In addition, students will describe the impact of these changes on the environment. (Suggested grades 4-6)

5-Minute Challenge: Center of Population Story Map Scavenger Hunt - Statistics in Schools: What is the center of population and how has the evolution of infrastructure and technology influenced population movement throughout the decades? For this activity, students use a story map, an interactive web tool with maps, text, and photos to learn about the nation’s centers of population and test their knowledge about their findings.

Fun with Geography - National Geographic: Get ideas for how to have fun with geography in your daily life. Lessons include “Draw a Map of an Imaginary Island,” “Learn About Seasonal Celebrations,” and "Explore a Line of Latitude.”

Geography - C3 IDM: This inquiry engages third-grade students in exploring world geography through the compelling question, “Where are we?” This question sparks students’ intellectual curiosity through the study of geographic location and the impact of humans on their environment. Working with evidence from sources, students should understand that, although we can be in different ‘places, our impact on Earth is worth considering.

Interactive Human Migration Map - PBS Learning Media: Using archeological, genetic, and climate data, scientists have pieced together an outline of the human odyssey—the journey that took our species from Africa to all corners of the globe. Experience this 200,000-year migration using an interactive human migration map.
MapMaker: Cities of the World - National Geographic: This Interactive map is for grades 5+ but can be teacher-led as a whole class visual exercise.

Remote Sensing Classroom - Earth Resources Observation and Science Center - USGS: Fun and engaging educational lessons allow students to look at satellite imagery and perform the same analysis as the remote sensing scientists at EROS. Students of all ages can learn how remote sensing scientists use Landsat satellite data to track changes to the Earth’s surface over the years. There’s games and puzzles to test student skills. “Tracking Changes to the Earth’s Surface” and “Land Change with Landstat” are two of the many interactive geography opportunities.

Where is Gina the Geographer? Statistics in Schools: Students will participate in an online scavenger hunt based on a story that a geographer named Gina, who loves to travel, has escaped to an undisclosed location. It is their mission to bring her back to the school. Students must follow a series of clues about the location including landmarks, weather, and population—and use a U.S. Census Bureau data tool called State Facts for Students to answer questions that lead them one step closer to finding Gina. (Suggested grades 4-5)

World Mountains - Core Knowledge: In this 4-lesson unit, students review their skills of using maps and globes and then apply those skills in learning about major mountains and mountain ranges. They explore the Himalayas and Urals in Asia; the Atlas Mountains in Africa; the Andes in South America; the Appalachians and Rockies in North America; and the Alps and Caucasus in Europe. Students also study the tallest mountains on each continent.

World Rivers - Core Knowledge: This 7-lesson unit prepares students to use maps and globes to locate the continents, major oceans, and important world rivers. Students explore the benefits and dangers of rivers. They learn why ancient civilizations and modern cities were established near rivers, and how rivers are often associated with major historical events. Rivers studied include the Ganges, Indus, Yellow (Huang He), Yangtze (Chang Jiang), Tigris, Euphrates, Nile, Niger, Congo, Amazon, Orinoco, Mississippi, Mackenzie, Yukon, Murray, Darling, Volga, Danube, and Rhine.

Ancient Civilizations (Before 500 CE) • Africa: Rise of Ancient Egypt and Nubia • Change: Development of centralized governments, writing (hieroglyphs), and religious systems. • Asia: Maurya and Gupta Empires in India; Han Dynasty in China • Change: Spread of Buddhism; advances in science, art, and infrastructure. • Europe: Roman Empire • Change: Legal systems, engineering, and spread of Christianity. • Oceania: Indigenous societies (e.g., Aboriginal Australians, Māori) • Change: Development of oral traditions, navigation, and land-based spirituality. Medieval Era (500–1500 CE) • Africa: Mali Empire (Timbuktu as a learning center) • Change: Growth of Islamic scholarship, trade networks (gold/salt) • Asia: Tang and Song Dynasties in China; Islamic Caliphates • Change: Technological innovation (printing, gunpowder), cultural flourishing • Europe: Feudal system and the Crusades • Change: Rise of monarchies, tension between religious and political power • Oceania: Continued development of tribal societies • Change: Polynesian migration and settlement of remote islands

Early Modern Period (1500–1800 CE) • Africa: Transatlantic slave trade • Change: Population displacement, disruption of kingdoms • Asia: Mughal Empire in India; Ming Dynasty in China • Change: Cultural and architectural achievements, increased European contact Europe: Age of Exploration, Scientific Revolution • Change: Colonization, global trade, rise of modern science • Oceania: First European contact (e.g., Captain Cook) • Change: Introduction of new diseases, early colonization efforts

Cultural Attributes • Africa – Strong community and family ties; oral traditions; deep connection to land and ancestors • Asia – Influence of religions like Buddhism, Hinduism, Islam, and Confucianism; respect for elders and social harmony • Europe – Long history of individual rights, secularism, and democratic institutions • Oceania – Strong spiritual connection to nature (e.g., the Māori concept of whakapapa – ancestral connection to land); importance of tribal and kinship networks

Trade Networks and Cultural Exchange • Cause: Development of major trade routes (e.g., the Silk Road, Trans-Saharan trade, Indian Ocean trade). • Interaction: Merchants, scholars, and travelers from Asia, Africa, and Europe interacted through trade and religious pilgrimage. • Effects: • Spread of religions like Islam, Christianity, and Buddhism. • Exchange of goods (e.g., spices from Asia, gold and salt from Africa, textiles from Europe). • Growth of cities like Timbuktu, Malacca, and Venice as commercial hubs. • Advancements in science, navigation, and mathematics through knowledge- sharing. Colonialism and Imperial Expansion • Cause: European powers’ desire for resources, markets, and strategic control during the Age of Exploration and Industrial Revolution. • Interaction: Europe colonized large parts of Africa, Asia, and Oceania (e.g., Britain in India and Australia; France in West Africa). • Effects: • Disruption of local economies and traditional systems. • Introduction of European languages, legal systems, and education. • Resistance movements and eventual independence movements (e.g., India’s independence in 1947, Ghana in 1957). • Lasting economic and political inequalities.

Migration and Labor Movements (continued) • Cause: Economic opportunities, forced labor (slavery), indentured servitude, and war. • Interaction: o Africans forcibly taken to the Americas and Caribbean through the Atlantic slave trade. o Indians and Chinese migrated as indentured laborers to colonies in Africa, Oceania, and the Caribbean. • Effects: o Cultural blending (e.g., Indo-Fijians, Afro-Caribbeans in Europe). o Racial and ethnic tensions but also enriched cultural landscapes. o Formation of global labor systems and economic dependency Environmental and Cultural Impacts • Cause: European colonization and industrialization, followed by global economic integration. • Interaction: • Introduction of new crops and animals (e.g., maize to Africa, sheep to Oceania). • Exploitation of natural resources for global markets. • Effects: • Environmental degradation in colonized regions. • Shifts in dietary habits, agriculture, and traditional ways of life. • Revival movements aimed at preserving indigenous cultures (e.g., Maori language revitalization in New Zealand).
Resources

AIA Lesson Plans - Archaeological Institute of America: This page provides links to four lesson plans for elementary appropriate simulated digs: a layer cake dig (K-2), a transparent shoebox dig (K-2), a shoebox dig (grades 3-5), and a schoolyard dig (grades 3-5). The page also includes photographs, record sheets, and a list of resources and national standards addressed in these activities; artifacts are used by archaeologists to make inferences about past civilizations and cultures.

Ancient India - Core Knowledge: This 6-lesson unit introduces students to the early Asian civilization of ancient India. Students will explore the geography of India, the Ganges and Indus Rivers, and the development of the first civilization in the Indus valley, where present-day western India, Pakistan, and northeastern Afghanistan are located. The importance of settling near a river to be able to farm near a relatively reliable source of water is also reinforced. In the unit’s six chapters, students will study the culture and beliefs associated with ancient India. They will learn about the Aryan invaders, who came to the Indus valley from other parts of Asia, and whose beliefs became interwoven with those of the Indus people, resulting in the development of a new religion called Hinduism. Students will investigate three important Hindu deities, Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva; the most important Hindu holy books, the Vedas; the castes, or different social levels, that Hindus have divided themselves into; and Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights. Students will also explore Buddhism, which began in this region as well. They will learn about the Buddha, what he taught, and how Buddhism spread to other lands. They will study one of the Buddha’s Jataka tales and how such stories helped him spread his teachings, and they will also examine the life of King Asoka, the ancient king who put Buddha’s teachings into practice.

The Vikings - Core Knowledge: This 8-lesson unit begins by providing geographical information on Scandinavia, homeland of the Vikings, meaning ‘pirates’ in the early Scandinavian languages—a name they were given because of their brutal raids on many places in Europe. Their expertise as sailors and shipbuilders—and their fierce raiding spirit— enabled them to trade, conquer, and explore over a vast area. Students learn about the voyages of Eric the Red and his son, Leif Eriksson. Students are introduced to Norse mythology, including stories of Odin, Thor, and Loki.

Critical Proficiency (K-12): Students act as social scientists as they ask questions, think critically, solve problems, and share conclusions.
Priority Performance Indicators: (3-5)
Constructing Compelling and Supporting Questions: Explain why compelling and supporting questions are important and how associated ideas can be open to different interpretations. (D1. 1-3)
Gathering and Evaluating Sources: Compare information from different sources and use differences between fact and opinion to determine the credibility of the source. (D2. His. 10, 12; D3. 1-3)
Communicating and Critiquing Solutions: Use evidence from multiple sources to develop a claim or argument about the past. (D2. His. 16; D4. 1)
Overarching Grade 4 Themes:
• Foundations • Evolving Economies • Defining Boundaries • Division
Civics

Critical Proficiency (K-12): Students act as productive citizens by understanding the historical foundations, and principles of our democracy through multiple lenses, and by acquiring the ability to become engaged in civic and democratic processes.
Theme: Foundations
Priority Performance Indicator (PPI)
Sample PPI Connections

Civic and Political Institutions Explain the origins, function, key provisions and structure of the United States and Vermont Constitution, including the roles and responsibilities of citizens, organizations, and governments within a democratic system. (D2. Civ. 1-6)

Students will be able to identify the structures, functions, and powers granted by the Vermont and United States constitutions. Students will be able to identify ways the constitution(s) has changed to meet the needs and wants of society over time.
Sample PPI Connections

Civic Virtues and Democratic Principles Identify and apply core civic virtues and democratic principles that guide personal beliefs, as well as those of government, societies, and communities. (D2. Civ. 7, 8, 9, 10)
Students will be able to describe how participating in a democratic system can take on different forms in the United States over time (e.g., from pre-colonial times through the Civil War).

Rules, Processes, and Laws Identify and apply core civic virtues and democratic principles that guide personal beliefs, as well as those of government, societies, and communities. (D2. Civ. 7, 8, 9, 10)
Students will be able to explain how the United States Constitution sets the foundation for national laws, and how local and national governments work together.
Economics
Critical Proficiency (K-12): Students make sound economic decisions through understanding the interactions between humans, governments, economic systems and both the national and global marketplaces.
Theme: Evolving Economies
Sample PPI Connections
Economic Decision Making Identify the incentives (positive/ negative) that influence economic decisions and the benefits and costs of such decisions. (D2. Econ. 1, 2)
Students will be able to explain how natural resources have influenced economic development in the United States over time (e.g., from pre-colonial times through the Civil War).
Sample PPI Connections

Exchange and Markets Explain the role of business in an economic system, including resources that are needed for production, the purpose of specialization, mediums of exchange, and the value of investments. (D2. Econ. 3, 4, 5, 6, 9)
Students will be able to explain how trade impacted people and goods, in the United States over time (e.g., from pre- colonial times through the Civil War)
Sample PPI Connections
The National Economy Explain how the economy fluctuates and how the government can affect changes through interest rates and purchase of goods and services. (D2. Econ. 10, 11, 12, 13)

Students will be able to identify economic policy decisions that have been made in the United State over time (e.g., from pre-colonial United S through the Civil War). Students will be able to explain the ways that the government pays for the services and goods it provides (e.g., taxation).
