body_examples: Overview

In grade 4, students will examine change and continuity in Vermont and United States history from pre-colonial times through the Civil War. Students will understand the concept of movement and its impact on people, goods, and ideas; learn how natural resources have influenced economic development; and examine the conflicts and compromises that resulted from migration and settlement. This learning will allow students to understand the tensions and factors that led to the fight for independence, the establishment of the United States, and subsequent Vermont statehood. Students will prepare for their role as responsible and informed citizens by examining the Vermont Constitution and the United States Constitution, including the determinants of power and its effects; exploring the development, structure, and function of the United States government as well as the role of individual rights and responsibilities; examining the choices made by various groups of people on the development of the United States through the Civil War; and learn how events, people, and ideas shaped and influenced our democratic system. Grade 4 provides the framework for further study of Vermont and United States History in Grade 7, civics in Grade 8, and United States History/American Government in high school.
Sample Content Connections

Vermont Constitution and United States Constitution: frameworks/branches, structures, powers (executive, legislative, judicial), similarities and differences, amendment process, Bill of Rights • Democracy • Republic • Common Good

• Governing Bodies – Native American Councils, New England Town Meetings, Virginia House of Burgesses, Continental Congress • Documents – Mayflower Compact, Declaration of Independence, Articles of Confederation, United States Constitution, State Constitutions • Participation – Suffrage, Dissent, Movements, Rebellion
• Local, state, national laws • Federal system • State system • County, towns, municipalities, etc.
Resources

A Lesson Plan for Independence Day, the Fourth of July - Center for Civic Education: In this lesson, students will examine some of the fundamental ideas about government that are contained in the Declaration of Independence and the Preamble to the United States Constitution. Students should be able to explain those ideas and identify which ideas the class holds in common.

Assessing Access - Learning for Justice: Students will apply the principles of American democracy to people with disabilities by analyzing how individuals and groups in American society have struggled to achieve the liberties and equality promised in the principles of American democracy.

Becoming a State - Vermont History Explorer: This three-day lesson introduces the students to the conflicts between the Yorkers and the New Hampshire Grants by asking the students to pretend they are settlers or investors who receive charters and patents for new towns in Vermont. The students divide the towns and investigate the natural resources on their land. After writing their own constitution, the students learn about Vermont’s Constitution and see the official document that made Vermont the 14th state.

BRI, JR - Bill of Rights Institute: Character, History, and Civics for Younger Learners: Ten lessons that are primary source based, inquiry-based, content-area literacy instruction focused, modular, and time-friendly. Each lesson contains: paper-based worksheets, a tie to their BRI Jr. Principles & Virtues Framework, performance-based assessments, Lexiled readings, games and/or simulations, and an optional video component.

Constitution Lessons: Select by grade level. The Center for Civic Education has developed constitution-focused lesson plans with topics such as “What Basic Ideas About Government are Included in the Preamble to the Constitution?” and “What Should the Representative Do?”

Declaration of Independence - C3 IDM (5th grade inquiry that may need support): This inquiry asks why countries declare their independence. As an integral early step in the process of becoming independent, a declaration of independence functions as an argument for why people should be free. This inquiry focuses on the argument made in the United States Declaration of Independence. With a firm understanding of the American colonists’ argument for
independence, the inquiry shifts to students conducting research on declarations of independence in other parts of the Western Hemisphere.

Elementary Curriculum: Colonial America to Reconstruction - The Gilder Lehrman Institute for American History: This curated suite of resources for elementary school educators will help expand your knowledge of important topic areas in the elementary curriculum through a selection of six curated topics, such as Colonial America and the United States Constitution. You will find lesson plans, student activity sheets, videos for students, interactive maps and timelines, recorded lectures, and free professional development courses.

Government and Citizens - C3 IDM: This inquiry is an exploration into government that begins by looking at the historical roots of democracy in the United States and then focuses on state government. The inquiry features a case study of a piece of legislation, initiated by a class of New York State elementary school students that resulted in yogurt becoming the official state snack of New York. In examining the idea that we have a voice in our government, especially through state representation, students develop an argument supported by evidence that answers the compelling question, ‘Why does New York have a state snack?’”

How Did Opposition to Laws Fuel the American Revolutionary War? - iCivics Education: What happens when people don’t have a say in the laws? In this inquiry-based unit, students will explore how the American colonies’ resistance to laws fueled the American Revolutionary War. They will analyze different points of view about the Stamp Act, investigate colonial reactions to the Intolerable Acts, and determine when exactly the American Revolutionary War began.

Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness. National Archives: Students will learn about the Declaration of Independence, its important sections, and some of the American ideals it contains. Students will explore primary sources about the American Revolution and the Founders and investigate copies of the Declaration of Independence from the National Archives. This Civics for All of U.S. distance learning program is available for groups of 10 or more students free of charge. Each program will be led by one of the educators located at National Archives sites, the Center for Legislative Archives, and Presidential Libraries across the country. After submitting a program request, the educator will be connected to an available National Archives educator to confirm the reservation. It is required that the requesting educator or another educator from the institution be present during the student distance learning program to observe the session and support classroom management. Programs are also offered as regularly scheduled interactive webinars. Registration is required, but there is no minimum attendance prerequisite. Questions? Please contact civics@nara.gov.
Vermont Classroom Blueprint - Vermont Office of the Secretary of State: A K-12 “blueprint” providing resources and lesson plans for active civic engagement in your classroom.

Natural Resources and Economic Growth • Timber in New England colonies • Fur trading • Farming and agriculture - subsistence farming, trade, slavery • Cotton in Antebellum South • Coal and iron ore • Gold Rush • Whaling

Impacts of Trade • Indigenous trade networks - cultural exchange, created alliances • European Mercantilism- growth of port cities, urbanization, reliance on exports • Triangular trade - Middle Passage; increase in demand for slave labor • Technology - Cotton gin; industrialization; railroads; Erie Canal and Trade expansion • Spread of disease • Indian Removal Act - value of land for farming • Manifest Destiny - displacement of indigenous tribes and Mexican landowners, minerals, land for farming

Policy Decisions • Trade and barter • Mercantilism • Colonial paper money • Continental Congress Finances • First Bank of the United States 1791-1811 • Second Bank of the United States 1816-1836 • Hard Money vs Soft money Debate • Civil War Financing • National Banking Act • Purpose of taxes- Amendment 16

International Trade • European Mercantilism and colonial trade • Triangular trade • Cotton trade and the Southern economy • Slavery/Middle Passage • Clipper ships and global trade • Blockades during the Civil War
Resources

From Slavery to Freedom in Colonial Times - PBS Learning Media: Learn the story of Venture Smith, an African boy who was enslaved and brought to America in 1737. In this interactive lesson, students will explore the differences between slavery in the North and South as they learn about Smith’s journey from slavery to freedom.

General Store Activity - Vermont History Explorer: This activity was developed for the Vermont History Museum's History for Homeschoolers class focused on agriculture, and in connection with the General Store within the Freedom & Unity exhibit. During this activity, students act as if they are Vermont farmers in the 1830s. They will barter their goods for others with the same value within their community.

Manhattan Purchase - C3 IDM: On the surface, the compelling question for this inquiry, “What's the real story behind the purchase of Manhattan?" that asks students to explore the background to the story of the sale of Manhattan to the Dutch in 1626 for $24 of beads and trinkets. A closer look at the story reveals a range of myths and unknowns including who was involved in the transaction, what the transaction actually meant, and what was exchanged.

Seaclass - Mystic Seaport Museum: This digital learning opportunity can support educator learning about the whaling industry with content including, “Why Whaling? The Impact and Industry Explained” and “Women in Whaling: Hidden Histories of the Sea.”

Teaching the Erie Canal - Erie Canalway National Heritage Corridor: Interdisciplinary lessons (math, reading, PE, social studies, art, music, science) including mapping, “Cooking on the Erie Canal,” and making a canal boat.

The Beaver Trade and the Purchase of Manhattan - PBS Learning Media: Learn about the extensive fur trade between the Dutch and Native Americans that sustained the early settlements of New Netherland in this video from Dutch New York; Teaching Tips and Discussion Questions included.

The Panic of 1837 - C3 IDM: Students investigate the compelling question, “How Did Cotton Sow the Seeds of Panic?” Students identify the market forces of demand and supply during the boom and bust of the cotton industry in the United States during the time surrounding the Panic of 1837. They learn how economic and political forces impacted the treatment of enslaved persons in the United States during the lead up to The Panic of 1837. The depth of this inquiry is in the reflection on what role reliance on enslaved people as labor played in the economic growth of the United States. This emphasizes that individual and institutional choices can lead to the exploitation of individuals and groups.
Mapping Movement and Patterns • Triangle trade • Revolutionary War battles • Civil War battles • Westward expansion • Underground railroad • Political maps • Tribal lands

Shifting Populations • Native American tribes and settlement patterns • Colonial settlements • Impact of slavery • Westward expansion • Manifest Destiny • Social movements • Native American removal • Civil War allegiances

Technological Change, Westward Expansion, and Legislation • Technology – Cotton gin; increase in demand for slave labor • Westward expansion and pioneers • Northwest ordinance • Missouri Compromise • Compromise of 1850 Migration and Settlement Conflicts and Compromises • Native American resistance to European settlement – Powatan Wars, Pequot War; William Penn’s Treaty with the Lenape • Colonial Expansion – Bacon’s Rebellion; Proclamation of 1763 • Westward Expansion – Northwest Indian War; Land Ordinance of 1785, Northwest Ordinance of 1787 • 19th Century and Indian Removal – Seminole Wars; Indian Removal Act (also controversy/conflict) • Sectional Conflicts • Texas Annexation and Mexican American War • Missouri Compromise • Compromise of 1850 • Bleeding Kansas

Movement and Resources • Pre-colonial: Indigenous groups moved seasonally and traded regionally; sustainable use of land and wildlife; preservation of ecosystems • Colonial: settlers moved from inland from coastal areas; deforestation, land clearing, over hunting, introduction of non-native plants • Westward Expansion: westward move for land and opportunity; soil depletion and transformation of prairies to farmland • Cotton Boom: Enslaved labor in plantation South; soil depletion and land clearing for plantations • Gold Rush: migrants to western territories; mining disrupted rivers, damaged land, polluted water • Industrialization: expansion of transportation and trade; increased demand for fossil fuels; pollution; altered landscape to build railroad track and urban areas Conflicts and Compromises • Native American resistance to European settlement - Powatan Wars, Pequot War; William Penn’s Treaty with the Lenape • Colonial Expansion – Bacon’s Rebellion; Proclamation of 1763 • Westward Expansion – Northwest Indian War; Land Ordinance of 1785, Northwest Ordinance of 1787 • 19th Century and Indian Removal – Seminole Wars; Indian Removal Act (also controversy/conflict) • Sectional Conflicts
• Texas Annexation and Mexican American War • Missouri Compromise • Compromise of 1850 • Bleeding Kansas
Resources

Chief Joseph of the Nez Perce Speaks for the Indians - PBS Learning Media: Students review and answer questions about a Nez Perce chief’s various speeches he gave in the mid 1800s in order to gain insight about how the United States government and white settlers were affecting American Indian lives.

“Does Where You Live Matter?” C3 IDM: This annotated inquiry focuses on physical geography in general and on the relationship between early (pre-1700) Native American nations and their environments in particular through the compelling question “Does where you live matter?” The compelling question highlights the idea that geography is not a neutral entity. Environments can exert an influence on human existence, but they are not immune from change—human activity can modify the physical landscape. (While this inquiry focuses on New York, there were no state boundaries at that time, so it is still relevant for Vermont learners.)

Florida Footprints: A Feral Land (1704-1845) - PBS Learning Media: By the 18th and 19th centuries, Florida had been known to the Europeans for hundreds of years, but this area was far from tame. Spanish, French, British, American and Native Americans fight for control over “A Feral Land” once known as La Florida. Lesson includes video, maps, timelines and discussion questions.

How Does a Map Show the Relationship Between People and the Environment? - iCivics Education: In this lesson, students will think about how a map can show the relationship between people and the environment. The lesson begins with students learning new vocabulary to support the lesson. They will analyze a natural resource map of Maryland and list the vast resources available. Using historical maps and contemporary images, students will look for evidence of how
the growing population of the area has impacted the environment and make observations about the natural resources available over time.

Louisiana Purchase Debate - PBS Learning Media: Students read information and excerpts from primary sources about the Louisiana Purchase and create arguments “for” or “against” the purchase. Students engage in a debate about the Louisiana Purchase.

Manifest Destiny and the American Indians - PBS Learning Media: Students study the change in tribal lands over time. Students read about the Manifest Destiny of the 1800s and write a short opinion essay about the effects of Westward Expansion.

North America’s Great Waters: Explorers and Traders - PBS Learning Media: In this lesson, students will explore the expeditions of four French explorers. After viewing three short videos about Samuel de Champlain, Louis Jolliet and Jacques Marquette, and René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de la Salle, students will analyze a painting that shows Champlain leading a fleet of canoes on an expedition and then read journal entries that describe Jolliet and Marquette’s expeditions. The lesson will conclude with students creating a game that encompasses the travels, settlements, and expansion of French territory in North America during the 1600s.

The New Nation - PBS Learning Media: Six lesson plans focused on Alexander Hamilton, Thomas Paine, and Benjamin Franklin; the lessons provide an overview and a procedure which includes vocabulary, additional resource materials, and necessary background for the educator.

The Vermont 250th in the Classroom - Vermont 250th Commission: This document provides varied lessons and resources to engage students in learning about the founding of the nation and the critical role that Vermont and Vermonters played in the War for Independence and the legacy they left on America; suggested grade levels have also been provided for elementary, middle, and high school students.

Westward Expansion, 1790-1850: Interactive Map - PBS Learning Media: Students can explore the territorial and population changes in the United States between 1790 and 1850 and consider the factors and resources that shaped and enabled westward expansion. After 1787, the newly established United States began to take an active part in the
exploration of North America. Cities grew up in land that was once frontier, gradually shifting the center of population westward. Support materials provided.

What Strategies Did Native Nations Use To Protect Their Sovereignty During the American Revolutionary War? - iCivics Education: In this inquiry-based unit, students will become more familiar with Native history and people. They will learn about some elements of Native sovereignty and its importance in American history. Students will be reminded about the key ideas of the American Revolutionary War and learn a little bit about how the Americans talked about Native people in the Declaration of Independence. The unit ends with students learning about strategies the Native nations used to protect their land and sovereignty during the American Revolution.

Pre-Colonial and Early Colonial Era Indigenous Leaders and Societies • Iroquois Confederacy – A powerful alliance of Native tribes with a sophisticated political system that influenced democratic ideas in colonial America. • Pocahontas – Played a diplomatic role between the Powhatan Confederacy and English settlers in Virginia. Explorers and Settlers • John Smith – Early leader of Jamestown who helped stabilize the colony through strict discipline and negotiations with Native tribes. • Anne Hutchinson – Religious dissenter who challenged Puritan orthodoxy and promoted ideas of religious freedom and women's roles in society. Colonial Period and Revolutionary Era Patriots and Founders • Benjamin Franklin – Key figure in diplomacy, science, and political thought; helped secure French support during the American Revolution. • Phillis Wheatley – Enslaved African American poet whose writings challenged racial assumptions and supported the American cause.

Groups That Shaped Revolution • Sons of Liberty – Organized protests and resistance against British taxation (e.g., Boston Tea Party). Daughters of Liberty – Supported the boycott of British goods and helped produce homemade goods to aid colonial self-reliance. Early Republic Leaders and Thinkers • Alexander Hamilton – Shaped the United States financial system and advocated for a strong federal government. • Thomas Jefferson – Principal author of the Declaration of Independence; expanded United States territory through the Louisiana Purchase. African Americans and Abolitionists • Richard Allen – Founded the African Methodist Episcopal Church and advocated for Black community leadership and education. Westward Expansion and Reform Movements Pioneers and Settlers • Lewis and Clark – Led the Corps of Discovery (1804–1806), mapping new territory and fostering United States expansion westward. • Sacagawea – Shoshone woman who guided and interpreted for Lewis and Clark, crucial to the expedition’s success.

Reformers and Movements • Frederick Douglass – Former enslaved person who became a leading abolitionist, speaker, and writer advocating for freedom and equality. • Sojourner Truth – African American abolitionist and women's rights advocate who used powerful speeches to inspire action. • Temperance Movement – Led largely by women’s groups, it sought to reduce alcohol consumption and address social issues tied to it. Civil War Era Political Leaders • Abraham Lincoln – 16th President who preserved the Union and issued the Emancipation Proclamation. • Stephen Douglas – Advocated for “popular sovereignty” regarding slavery; debated Lincoln in famous debates. Military and Social Leaders • Harriet Tubman – Former enslaved woman who led dozens to freedom via the Underground Railroad and later served as a spy for the Union. • Clara Barton – Pioneering nurse who founded the American Red Cross and transformed battlefield medicine during the Civil War.

Groups That Influenced Change • Abolitionists – Groups like the American Anti-Slavery Society worked to end slavery through publications, speeches, and organizing. • Women’s Rights Activists – Figures like Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott helped launch the women’s suffrage movement (Seneca Falls Convention, 1848).

• Spread of Revolutionary ideas • Slavery and Abolitionist movement • Native American perspectives on land ownership; westward expansion • Settlers on religious freedom • Women’s Rights advocates • States rights vs. federal power Pre-Colonial and Early Colonial Period Event: European colonization and land settlement • Native American perspective: Colonists were intruders disrupting long- held land, trade, and spiritual practices. • European settler perspective: They believed they were bringing “civilization,” Christianity, and making productive use of land. American Revolution Event: Declaration of Independence and the war for independence • Patriot perspective: They fought for liberty and self-rule from British tyranny. • Loyalist perspective: Believed remaining loyal to the Crown was the best way to maintain order and protect property. • Enslaved African American perspective: Some saw British promises of freedom (e.g., Lord Dunmore’s Proclamation) as a better chance for emancipation.

Westward Expansion Event: Louisiana Purchase and frontier settlement • White settlers' perspective: Saw expansion as opportunity, freedom, and part of "Manifest Destiny." • Native American perspective: Saw it as encroachment, land loss, broken treaties, and violence. Trail of Tears (1830s) Event: Forced relocation of Native American tribes • United States government perspective: Believed relocation would reduce conflict and allow for American expansion. • Cherokee Nation perspective: Viewed it as unjust, brutal displacement from ancestral lands—despite legal attempts to stay. Civil War Era Event: Slavery and sectional conflict • Northern abolitionist perspective: Slavery was immoral and a violation of American ideals of liberty. • Southern slaveholder perspective: Slavery was essential to their economy and way of life; many claimed it was protected by the Constitution. • Enslaved person’s perspective: Viewed slavery as brutal oppression and hoped for freedom through escape or Union victory.

Women’s Rights Movement (Antebellum Era) Event: Seneca Falls Convention (1848) • Women reformers’ perspective: Believed women deserved equal rights, including suffrage and property rights. • Traditional male (and some female) perspective: Believed women’s role was in the home and that equality would disrupt social norms.

Conflicts Leading to the American Revolution French and Indian War (1754–1763) • Conflict: Britain and France (with Native allies) fought over land in North America. • Result: Britain won but incurred heavy debt, leading to new taxes on colonists. Proclamation of 1763 • Conflict: Banned colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains to avoid Native conflict. • Colonial response: Colonists resented the restriction on land they felt entitled to after helping in the war. Stamp Act (1765) • Conflict: Required colonists to buy stamps for legal documents and newspapers. • Colonial reaction: "No taxation without representation!" — led to protests, boycotts, and the Stamp Act Congress. Boston Massacre (1770) • Conflict: British soldiers fired into a crowd of colonists, killing five. • Impact: Sparked outrage and used as propaganda by groups like the Sons of Liberty.

Tea Act and Boston Tea Party (1773) • Conflict: Gave the British East India Company a monopoly on tea sales. • Colonial response: Colonists dumped tea into Boston Harbor in protest. Intolerable Acts (1774) • Conflict: Harsh laws passed to punish Massachusetts for the Tea Party (e.g., closed Boston Harbor). • Effect: United the colonies in opposition; led to the First Continental Congress. Battles of Lexington and Concord (1775) • Conflict: British troops tried to seize colonial weapons; first armed conflict of the revolution. • Effect: “The shot heard 'round the world” — beginning of armed resistance. Compromises (Attempts to Avoid War) Petition to the King (1774) • What: The First Continental Congress asked King George III to repeal the Intolerable Acts. • Result: Ignored by the King, which deepened colonial frustration.

Olive Branch Petition (1775) • What: Final attempt by the Second Continental Congress to avoid war, pledging loyalty to the Crown but asking for peace. • Result: Rejected by King George III, who declared the colonies in open rebellion. Declaratory Act (1766) (after repeal of Stamp Act) • What: Parliament repealed the unpopular Stamp Act but declared it still had full authority to govern the colonies. • Result: Temporarily calmed tensions but reminded colonists that Britain still claimed power over them. Pre-Civil War Conflicts and Compromises Slavery in New Territories • Conflict: As the United States expanded west, debates erupted over whether new states should allow slavery. • Example: Bleeding Kansas (1854–1856) – Violent clashes between pro- and anti-slavery settlers after the Kansas-Nebraska Act allowed residents to vote on slavery.

Abolitionist Movement vs. Slaveholders • Conflict: Growing abolitionist voices in the North (like Frederick Douglass, William Lloyd Garrison, Harriet Tubman) called for the end of slavery, while Southern leaders defended it as essential. • Example: Publication of Uncle Tom’s Cabin (1852) by Harriet Beecher Stowe stirred anti-slavery sentiment and angered the South. States’ Rights vs. Federal Power • Conflict: Southern states believed they had the right to govern themselves, especially on issues like slavery and tariffs, while the federal government increasingly intervened. • Example: Nullification Crisis (1832–1833) – South Carolina tried to nullify federal tariffs; President Jackson responded with threats of force. Dred Scott Decision (1857) • Conflict: Supreme Court ruled that African Americans could not be United States citizens and that Congress couldn’t ban slavery in the territories. Impact: Angered Northerners, delighted pro-slavery Southerners, and deepened sectional divides. Missouri Compromise (1820) • What: Missouri entered as a slave state, Maine as a free state; slavery banned in territories north of the 36°30′ line. • Goal: Maintain balance between free and slave states. • Result: Temporarily calmed tensions.

Compromise of 1850 • What: • California admitted as a free state • Stricter Fugitive Slave Law • Popular sovereignty (states decide on slavery) in Utah and New Mexico • Result: Delayed conflict but increased Northern resistance, especially to returning escaped slaves. Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) • What: Overturned Missouri Compromise by allowing popular sovereignty in Kansas and Nebraska. • Result: Led to Bleeding Kansas and greater North-South hostility
Resources

A Sailor’s Life for Me - USS Constitution Museum: The War of 1812 is often referred to as our country’s second war of independence. As a young nation, the United States' economy, territory, and rights of individual citizens were again threatened by the British. A Sailor’s Life for Me! presents life at sea during the War of 1812 for those serving aboard USS Constitution, one of the few naval vessels in America’s young navy, and now a national symbol, through interactive games, primary sources, and Museum resources.

American Indians in a Changing World -The Gilder Lehrman Institute for American History: Students will examine and analyze photographs of, poems by, and documents about American Indian experiences as European Americans migrated across the United States. They will use the knowledge gained through their analysis to write their own songs, poems, and letters.

Betrayal - C3IDM: This inquiry leads students through an investigation of leaders during the American Revolution. By investigating the compelling question ‘Is betrayal always bad?’ students evaluate the actions of King George III and George Washington. The formative performance tasks build on knowledge and skills through the course of the inquiry and help students understand the motives of patriots and loyalists.

Elementary Curriculum: Colonial America to Reconstruction - The Gilder Lehrman Institute for American History: This curated suite of resources for elementary school educators will help expand your knowledge of important topic areas in the elementary curriculum through a selection of six curated topics, such as Colonial America and the American Revolution. You will find lesson plans, student activity sheets, videos for students, interactive maps and timelines, recorded lectures, and free professional development courses.

Frederick Douglass: Orator, Editor, and Abolitionist - PBS Learning Media: Students explore what it means to speak out for your beliefs, or to right a wrong. After watching a short video, they will reflect on Douglass’s courage and the importance of literacy in his activism. They will read excerpts from Douglass’s autobiographies and examine an 1850 etching of Douglass being pulled away from a stage prior to giving a speech. Finally, they will reflect on Douglass’s importance as both a historical figure and as a role model for their own lives.

“Heroes of the American Revolution”- C3 IDM (5th grade inquiry that may require support): This inquiry leads students through an investigation of the American Revolution and the varying impacts of individuals who could be deemed heroes based on their impact. The compelling question, “What defines a hero?” allows students to consider all the actions of an individual and if they think that they are worthy of the title of hero.

“New France” - C3 IDM (5th grade inquiry that may require support): This inquiry focuses on the emergence, growth, and collapse of the New France colony in North America. French explorers, missionaries, traders, and settlers established an important presence in North America, beginning with Jacques Cartier’s explorations in 1534 and continuing through the 19th century. The development of the fur-trading industry, along with a relatively stable relationship with Native peoples in North America, peaked around 1710.

Pre- 1860 Disunion - American Battlefield Trust: This lesson allows students to look at pre-War cultures and economies of the Northern and Southern states and includes the actions of John Brown at Harper’s Ferry.

The Mexican-American War - PBS Learning Media: In this clip from Latino Americans, students will learn about the Mexican-American War. Until the mid 1800s, the region that is now the western United States was part of Mexico. Meanwhile, inspired by the notion of Manifest Destiny, United States leaders tried to buy and later went to war over this expanse of land. The result was that not only land, but people and long-standing settlements also became part of the United States.

Sojourner Truth: Abolitionist and Women’s Rights Activist - PBS Learning Media: In this lesson, students will learn about Sojourner Truth’s egalitarian spirit in the face of institutional discrimination. After viewing a video about her life, students will examine an 1864 photograph of Truth and read excerpts of her most famous speech. The lesson concludes with students choosing a new name for a current-day exemplar of perseverance.

Vermont History Kits - Vermont History Museum: History Kits can be reserved from the Museum for a minimal fee, with topics such as “Abenaki in Vermont,” “Vermont in the Civil War,” and “Vermont in the Revolutionary War.”

Critical Proficiency (K-12): Students act as social scientists as they ask questions, think critically, solve problems, and share conclusions.
Priority Performance Indicators Priority Performance Indicators: (3-5)
Constructing Compelling and Supporting Questions: Explain why compelling and supporting questions are important and how associated ideas can be open to different interpretations. (D1. 1-3)
Gathering and Evaluating Sources: Compare information from different sources and use differences between fact and opinion to determine the credibility of the source. (D2. His. 10, 12; D3. 1-3)
Communicating and Critiquing Solutions: Use evidence from multiple sources to develop a claim or argument about the past. (D2. His. 16; D4. 1)
Overarching Themes:
• Emerging Governance (see History PPIs) • Expanding Networks • Shaping Civilizations • Building Societies
Civics

body_examples: Overview

In grade 5, students will explore how people moved, traded, and interacted with others in early civilizations. They will learn how geography, power, wealth, and religion shaped the growth and culture of these societies. Students will focus on regions like Western Asia, the Middle East, North Africa, and Sub-Saharan Africa. They will also learn about important cultural contributions and lasting achievements. By studying ancient history, students will better understand the roots of the modern world.
Sample Content Connections

Broad Topics • Cultural diffusion • Trade practices/ trade hub development • Expansion • Technological exchange • Nomadic herding • Trade • Architectural specialization • Agricultural specialization • Trade specialization • Military • Governance • Craftsmanship Early Civilizations 1. Western Asia (Mesopotamia, Anatolia, Levant) • Agriculture: Fertile Crescent farming (wheat, barley, dates); irrigation along the Tigris and Euphrates. • Trade: Long-distance trade in metals (tin, copper), textiles, and luxury goods. • Economy: Palace and temple economies, taxation in grain and labor.

2. Middle East (Overlap with Western Asia but includes Persia, Arabia) • Nomadic and settled economies: Mix of pastoralism (Bedouins) and urban centers. • Trade routes: Controlled key overland and maritime trade (Incense Route, Persian Royal Road). • Empire economics: Persian Empire used standardized coinage and administrative divisions. North Africa (Egypt, Carthage, Berber regions) • Nile agriculture: Predictable floods supported grain production and population growth. • State control: Centralized economy in Egypt with corvée labor and redistribution. • Trade and seafaring: Carthage dominated Mediterranean trade in grain, metals, and slaves. 3. Sub-Saharan Africa (Nok, Ghana, Nubia, Aksum) • Mining and metallurgy: Gold, iron, and salt were central to wealth. • Trans-Saharan trade: Camel caravans connected this region to North Africa and beyond. • Agriculture and pastoralism: Varied by region—yam, millet, sorghum, cattle.

Mediums of Exchange: barter, trade, progression of currency development Resources: Caravans/camels, public works projects, trade routes. Market Civilizations • Mesopotamia – Specialization of labor; development of irrigation systems; wealth accumulation-armies, construction projects • Ancient Egypt – construction labor force; Nile River - predictable flooding and transportation; Pharaohs controlled resources • Ancient Persia – satrapies for regional governance and resource management; Achaemenids organized mineral extraction and trade; Darius the Great - standardized currency • Ancient Arabia – Nomadic tribes; camel caravans connecting distant places/cultures; trading hubs – Mecca and Medina • Kingdom of Mali – skilled artisans/traders (Niger River); gold mines; wealth allowed for city development – Timbuktu, construction of mosques, education • Kush – south of Egypt • Nubia – rich gold mines/kings

Trade Barriers • War and conflict • Lack of infrastructure • Lack of technology • Geographic limitations • Cultural and linguistic barriers • Climate and environmental factors • Resource scarcity • Political boundaries and regulations Economic Impact of Conflict The Crusades (1096–1291) • Region: Middle East (especially modern-day Israel, Syria, Palestine) • Conflict: Series of religious wars between Christians and Muslims. • Economic Impact: • Trade routes between Europe and the Middle East expanded. • Cities like Damascus and Jerusalem suffered destruction but also saw increased economic activity. • Boosted exchange of goods (spices, silk), ideas, and technologies.

Mongol Invasions (1200s) • Region: Persia (modern-day Iran, Iraq) • Conflict: Mongols invaded and destroyed cities such as Baghdad. • Economic Impact: o Massive economic decline due to destruction of irrigation systems and trade centers. o Short-term loss of wealth, but long-term trade along the Silk Road was revived under Mongol rule. Arab Conquests (600s–700s CE) • Region: Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Algeria, Morocco • Conflict: Arab Muslim armies conquered much of North Africa. • Economic Impact: • Spread of Arabic language and Islamic banking systems. • Growth of trade across the Sahara and the Mediterranean. • Cities like Cairo became important economic centers. Roman Conquest of North Africa (146 BCE onward) • Region: Carthage and surrounding areas • Conflict: Rome defeated Carthage in the Punic Wars. • Economic Impact: • Carthage’s economy was destroyed. • Rome took control of trade in the western Mediterranean and expanded agriculture in the region.

Invasion of the Songhai Empire (1591) • Region: West Africa (Mali, Niger) • Conflict: Moroccan army invaded and defeated the Songhai Empire. • Economic Impact: • Collapse of the trans-Saharan trade network. • Decline of key trading cities like Timbuktu and Gao. • Weakened political and economic power in the region. Bantu Migrations & Regional Conflict (c. 1000 BCE–1700 CE) • Region: Central and Southern Africa • Conflict: Migration often led to conflict with existing groups over land and resources.

Bantu Migrations & Regional Conflict (c. 1000 BCE–1700 CE) (continued) • Economic Impact: • Spread of ironworking technology improved farming and tools. • New trade routes and markets were established. • Some regions faced food shortages or disruption due to clashes. Geography and Economic Specialization • Mesopotamia – Fertile land between two rivers; flat plains • Rich soil allowed for surplus farming (wheat, barley); surplus food supported job specialization (scribes, potters, metalworkers); location along trade routes encouraged trade with neighboring regions. • Phoenicia – Rocky coastline, limited farmland, access to the Mediterranean Sea. • Became expert shipbuilders, traders, and sailors; specialized in making purple dye and glass; built a strong economy based on maritime trade. • Ancient Egypt – Fertile land along the Nile, surrounded by deserts. • Nile floods provided reliable farming conditions (grain, papyrus); farmers, scribes, architects, and traders developed as specialized workers; surpluses allowed trade with Nubia and the Near East. • Kingdom of Ghana – Located between gold mines in the south and salt mines in the north. • Became a center for gold-salt trade across the Sahara; people specialized in mining, trading, blacksmithing, and governance; controlled trade routes and collected taxes, boosting wealth.

• Kingdom of Axum – Near the Red Sea, mountainous, with access to trade routes. • Traded goods like ivory, gold, and spices with Arabia and India; specialized in farming (terrace farming) and long-distance trade; developed a written language and minted their own coins for commerce.
Resources

Agriculture - C3 IDM: Students will examine sources related to the development of agriculture, the emergence of ancient writing in Mesopotamia, and the rise of social inequalities as they construct an argument in response to the compelling question “Was the development of agriculture good for humans?”

Ancient Trade Networks - OER - History project: Local networks might have been the most common and important types of networks in this period, but long-distance regional trade networks also connected societies across Afro-Eurasia and the Americas. Trade along these routes was slow and dangerous, but it allowed for the exchange of people, goods, ideas, and diseases across many regions. The networks changed the communities they touched and transformed production and distribution in every region.

4. Analyze how regional networks of exchange came into existence and how they became larger and more interconnected over time. 5. Evaluate how the sharing of goods and ideas such as metals and iron-making skills transformed societies. 6. Map regional trade networks to understand how communities were interconnected through trade and exchange.

Mali Wealth - C3 IDM: This inquiry focuses on understanding how the Kingdom of Mali became a center of wealth in West Africa. The questions, tasks, and sources in this inquiry asks students to analyze a variety of primary and secondary sources to determine the most important factor for generating wealth in Mali: geography, trade, or religion.

Nomadic Life - C3 IDM: This inquiry leads students through an investigation of prehistoric nomadic life. By investigating the compelling question “How do we know the past without written evidence?” students evaluate how nomads communicated, where they lived, and how they defined their needs based on the places they lived. The formative

performance tasks build on knowledge and skills through the course of the inquiry and help students develop understanding of nomadic life to compare with agrarian life. Students create an evidence-based argument about how non- written artifacts support understanding of nomadic life during prehistoric times.

Geography of Western Asia, the Middle East, North Africa, and Sub- Saharan Africa • Landforms • Climate • Natural resources • Fertile Crescent • Deserts • Rivers – Nile, Tigris, Euphrates, • Mountains • Seas – Mediterranean, Black, Aegean, Red Social, Cultural, Economic, and Political Geographic Characteristics • Monumental architecture • Trade routes • Political boundaries • City-states

Geographic Features: flooding (predictable/unpredictable), soil (fertile/unfertile), natural barriers (coast/desert), valuable resources (gold/salt) Decisions: Positive • Agriculture: Crop rotation, terrace farming, irrigation • Technology: Metallurgy, wheel, plow, arch, calendar, The Royal Road, Maritime development and trade Negative • Soil erosion from farming and mining • Dam construction affecting natural water cycle • Over-irrigation • Resource depletion – forests, minerals, water over-extraction

Interaction Effects: • Trade • cultural or linguistic exchanges • migration • religious conversion • conquest • Colonization Migrations: Indo-European: Roughly 4000–1000 BCE • Region: Originating from the Pontic-Caspian Steppe (modern-day Ukraine and southern Russia), Indo-European-speaking peoples migrated in multiple waves across Europe and into Asia. • Key Movements: • To Europe: Into the Balkans, Central Europe, and eventually Western Europe (Celts, Italic, Germanic groups) • To South Asia: Around 1500 BCE, the Indo-Aryans moved into the Indian subcontinent, contributing to the Vedic culture • To Anatolia and Iran: Hittites (in Anatolia) and Iranians (Medes, Persians) in the Iranian Plateau

Semitic: From around 3000 BCE onward • Region: Originating in the Arabian Peninsula and Near East, Semitic peoples spread throughout the Fertile Crescent, Levant, and Northeast Africa. • Key Movements: Akkadians in Mesopotamia (~2300 BCE) Semitic: From around 3000 BCE onward (continued) • Amorites, Assyrians, and Babylonians in the Near East • Phoenicians along the Levantine coast, later establishing colonies like Carthage (~1200–800 BCE) • Arabs expanding from the Arabian Peninsula, especially in later periods (including Islamic expansions in the 7th century CE) Bantu: Circa 1000 BCE to 1700 CE • Region: Originated in West-Central Africa (modern-day Cameroon/Nigeria area) and gradually spread throughout Sub- Saharan Africa. • Key Movements: • Migrated south and east into the Congo Basin, Great Lakes region, and as far as Southern Africa • Spread agriculture, ironworking, and Bantu languages, which now dominate much of Sub-Saharan Africa.

Berber: Ancient to Medieval (starting before 1000 BCE) • Region: Indigenous to North Africa (Maghreb region: modern Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya) • Key Movements: • Prehistoric spread across the Sahara when it was more habitable (Green Sahara period, ~7000–3000 BCE) • Interactions with Phoenicians, Romans, Vandals, and Arabs • Berbers played a key role in the spread of Islam across North Africa and into Al-Andalus (Spain) during the 7th–8th centuries CE. Nubian Movements: From ~2500 BCE through Classical Antiquity • Region: Upper Nile region, primarily in what is now southern Egypt and northern Sudan. • Key Movements: • Early Nubian cultures like Kerma (~2500–1500 BCE) • Kingdom of Kush (1000 BCE–350 CE), which at one point ruled over Egypt as the 25th Dynasty (ca. 747–656 BCE) • Nubians moved between Nubia and Egypt frequently due to trade, warfare, and political alliances • Later Christian Nubian kingdoms (e.g., Nobatia, Makuria) resisted Islamic expansion for centuries.

Persian Empire: Primary expansion 550–330 BCE (Achaemenid Empire) • Region: Originating in Persia (modern Iran) and expanding across Southwest Asia, Central Asia, the Caucasus, the Indus Valley, and into Egypt and parts of Greece. • Key Movements: • Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Empire (~550 BCE), conquering Media, Lydia, Babylon; Under Darius I and Xerxes, expansion reached its peak; Included a diverse range of peoples; the empire used roads and communication systems to link its territories. Impact of geography on settlement patterns: • Nile River • Tigris and Euphrates Rivers • Niger River • Fertile plains • City development – Sumer, Timbuktu, Persepolis, Babylon

Impact of geography on settlement patterns: (continued) • Coastal regions • Deserts • Mountains • Arabian Peninsula • Red Sea • Mecca • Medina • Israel • Palestine Environmental Characteristics • Rivers and waterways • Deserts and trade routes • Geographical features • Climate and agricultural practices • Nomadic farming/herding

Cultural Characteristics • Religious and cultural centers • Intellectual hubs • Cultural Diffusion • Trade network expansion • Technology transfer • State formation • Urbanization • Migration • Innovation and technological exchange • Trade and economic practices • Language and communication • Political and social structures • Pyramids and Ziggurats • Cultural exchange • Political power dynamics • Economic growth

Natural Disturbances: • Saharan Expansion • Halocene Climate Optimum – increase of aridity • Flooding – Tigris and Euphrates • Earthquakes – Anatolia and Levant Man-made transformations: • Agriculture – Long-term irrigation • Empire building – Akkadians, Assyrians, Persians, Egyptians; roads, gridded cities, military garrisons, trade networks • Conflicts and invasions • Spread of religion – pilgrimage routs, mosques
Resources

Ancient Agrarian Societies: Nubia and Ancient Egypt - OER - History Project: In this reading, students will learn about the Nile River Valley. Best known for pyramids and mummies, communities in this area, such as Egypt and Nubia, were founded long before the first pyramid.

Ancient Egypt - OER- History Project: Ancient Egypt was the site of some of the world’s oldest agrarian societies. Over 5,000 years ago, Egyptian pharaohs first rose to power and built mighty empires and astounding monuments. For 3,000 years, Egyptian pharaohs ruled the lands of the Nile River Valley. The Nile River was the key to Egypt’s success. In this article [with guiding questions], you’ll learn about how the river shaped Ancient Egypt and the people who lived there from c. 3400 to 30 BCE.

Ancient Hebrews - C3IDM: This C3 Inquiry leads students through an investigation of ancient Hebrew history and Judaism by using various sources that consider the historical and theological foundations, as well as issues related to geography and place. By investigating the compelling question, students examine the history of the ancient Hebrew people, the principles that form the foundation of Judaic thought, the connection of history and religion to Israel, and the geographic variance in religious practices. By completing this inquiry, students begin to understand issues revolving around the factors that help to form a people’s identity, as well as the fluidity of defining a group within any predetermined criteria.

Building the Pyramids of Ancient Egypt - PBS learning Media: In this interactive lesson supporting literacy skills, students learn how historians think the pyramids were built and why they were built—as doorways to the afterlife for the pharaohs. Students develop their literacy skills as – OER – Big History Project. They explore a social studies focus on ancient Egyptian society and how those at the top organized the rest of the population in order to build these amazing structures. During this process, they read informational text, learn and practice vocabulary words, and explore content through videos and interactive activities.

Egyptian Flooding - C3 IDM: This inquiry focuses on the impact of the flooding of the Nile River on ancient Egypt, specifically the costs and benefits of the flooding. Through examination and analysis of various photographs, videos, and article excerpts, students will consider how these sources can be used to convey the impact of flooding on multiple groups of people in ancient Egypt.

Egypt’s Pyramids: Monuments with a Message - National Endowment for the Humanities: By introducing students to artifacts and archaeology, this lesson considers pyramids as artifacts and examines the scale of these great structures and asks what clues pyramids give us about the ancient Egyptians.
Marco Polo lessons from the National Endowment for the Humanities (grades 6-8 adaptable curriculum):

• On the Road with Marco Polo: From Venice to Hormuz: Marco Polo's father and uncle returned to Venice when he was 15 years old. Two years later, when they set off again for China, they decided to take Marco with them. Students will take a “virtual” trip with Marco Polo from Venice to China and back. The first leg of the journey ends at Hormuz. • On the Road with Marco Polo: A Boy in 13th Century Venice: Marco Polo was one of the first Europeans to travel to China. Marco grew up in the 13th century in Venice, an important trading city in Italy. Here, students learn about the Venice of Marco Polo's time. • On the Road with Marco Polo: From Hormuz to Venice: Marco Polo was on the last leg of his journey home from China to Venice. After visiting several seaports in India, he and his party sailed across the Arabian Sea and to the mouth of the Persian Gulf, landing at the port city of Hormuz, where they decided to travel eastward across Asia following a land route.

Trekking to Timbuktu Teacher and Student Versions of Lessons 1-8 - National Endowment for the Humanities: For many people, Timbuktu is a metaphor for the mysterious, the remote, or the unobtainable. But the Malian city of Timbuktu was, in fact, once a thriving center of commerce and intellectual activity. In the lessons of this unit, students will learn about the geography of Mali and the early trade networks that flourished there. They will study how the spread of Islam influenced the cultures and economies along the Niger River. They will find out about the three kingdoms that evolved in ancient and medieval West Africa.

Emerging Governance • Origins: Centralization of authority – Code of Hammurabi, influence of trade, coordination of agricultural activities, interactions with neighboring cultures, maintenance of order, resource management, deterrence, belief systems, resource allocation. • Structures: Development of legal principles, influence of legal codes, Hammurabi’s Code, Islamic Law in Mali, 10 Commandments, communication infrastructure, patriarchy, city-state, pharaonic monarchy, monarchy, republic, oligarchy, kingdom, tribal councils, empires, caliphs Structures of Early Governance • Kingdom of Mali – Mansu Musa’s Reign; Islamic Golden Age; Code of Ur- Nammu; Code of Hammurabi; Ancient Arabia; Kingdom of Axum; Achaemenid Empire – Cyrus the Great; Mesopotamia; Ancient Egypt – Ma’at; Darius the Great Archaeological Sites • Western Africa/Middle East: Gobekli Tepe, Uruk, Tell Brak • North Africa: Nabta Playa, Giza Pyramids and Saqqara • Sub-Saharan Africa: Jenne-Jeno, Great Zimbabwe Comparisons • Tools, shelter, diet, use of fire, cave paintings, artifacts, clothing, rituals, daily life, gender roles.

Historical Origins of Religion • Migrations of the ancient Israelite tribes from Mesopotamia to the land called Canaan; the role of Abraham and Moses in Hebrew history. • History of ancient Israel and early Christianity • Monotheistic religion (e.g., the belief in one God, the Ten Commandments, the emphasis on individual worth and personal responsibility, the belief that rulers and the ruled must adhere to the same moral obligations) • The Hebrew Bible’s accounts of the history of early Israel; Torah • The emergence of Christianity as a distinct religion, with roots in Judaism • The central features of Christianity (e.g., the belief in a messiah who could redeem humans from sin, the concept of salvation, the belief in an Old and a New Testament in the Bible, the life and teachings of Jesus). • Islam’s historical relationship to Judaism and Christianity as monotheistic religions. • The life and teachings of Muhammad (570-c. 632 CE) and the significance of the Qur’an as the primary source of Islamic belief.

Rise • Trade and economic prosperity • Cultural achievements • Military power, conquests, and expansions Fall • Internal conflict • External invasions/war/conquests • Internal dissent • Environmental factors Innovations/lasting impacts: • Mathematics/number system • Communication – hieroglyphics/cuneiform • Human anatomy • Government/leadership structure • Culture (e.g., religion/beliefs, accepted practices/traditions) • Specialization of labor • Mastery of food supply • Technology • Economic systems • Education • Communication systems (e.g., spoken language, alphabetic and/or numeric systems, hieroglyphics, illustrations)
Innovations/lasting impacts: (continued) • Military tactics • Maritime power and trade • Architecture • Trade and diplomacy • Legal code • Astronomy • Human Rights (Cyrus Cylinder)
Resources

Cave Art: Discovering Prehistoric Humans through Pictures - National Endowment for the Humanities: By studying paintings from the Cave of Lascaux (France) and the Blombos Cave (South Africa), students will discover that pictures can be a way of communicating beliefs and ideas and can give us clues today about what life was like long ago.

Egyptian Symbols and Figures: Hieroglyphs - National Endowment for the Humanities: In this adaptable 6-8 lesson, students will examine the art and history of ancient Egypt through the oldest writing system in the world. This lesson teaches students how to understand and write Egyptian hieroglyphs.
Into the Field: Archaeology - PBS Learning Media: A collection of archaeology videos and lesson plans for classroom or home use.

Life in Old Babylonia: The Importance of Trade - National Endowment for the Humanities: Trade was critical to Old Babylonia, where many highly prized natural resources were scarce but agricultural goods were in surplus. Trade became integral to the economy and the culture. In this lesson, students explore the trade industry in Old Babylonia and its far- flung influence.

Refugee - C3 IDM: This inquiry leads students through an investigation of how we respond to the needs of refugee communities. With the example of King Najashi (in the 7th century Kingdom of Aksum, modern Eritrea), students an

historical instance of a national leader extending compassion to a refugee community. Students examine contemporary examples of national leaders who do and do not demonstrate care to refugee or immigrant communities. To close the inquiry, students consider how local activist take actions related to refugee populations with the example late hip-hop artist and activist Nipsey Hussle whose father was an Eritrean refugee. By connecting a historical example to a modern context, students use world history to construct an argument and take informed action around the compelling question: When should refugees be allowed refuge? (Grades 6-8)

The Cuneiform Writing System in Ancient Mesopotamia: Emergence and Evolution - National Endowment for the Humanities: The earliest writing systems evolved independently and at roughly the same time in Egypt and Mesopotamia, but current scholarship suggests that Mesopotamia’s writing appeared first. That writing system, invented by the Sumerians, emerged in Mesopotamia around 3500 BCE. This lesson plan is designed to help students appreciate the parallel development and increasing complexity of writing and civilization in Mesopotamia.

The Phoenicians and the Beginnings of the Alphabet - National Endowment for the Humanities: This is an adaptable K-5 lesson where students learn about the Phoenicians as a trading people who invented the first form of our alphabet.

body_standards: Grade 6 - World Geography and Ancient Civilization II - Latin America, South
and East Asia, Oceania, Latin America, and Europe (Draft)
Inquiry Process (K-12): Students act as social scientists as they ask questions, think critically, solve problems, and share conclusions.
C3 Indicators (6-8):
Constructing Compelling and Supporting Questions: D1.1, 2, 3; His. 12
Gathering and Evaluating Sources: D2. His. 6, 10, 12, 13; D3. 1, 2, 3
Communicating and Critiquing Conclusions: D2. His. 16; D4. 1, 2, 4
Overarching Themes:
• Emerging Governance • Trade and Exchange • Mastering Environments • Connecting Worlds
Civics
Theme: Emerging Governance
Civic and Political Institutions
D2.Civ.2.6-8. Explain specific roles played by citizens (such as voters, jurors, taxpayers, members of the armed forces, petitioners, protesters, and office-holders).

D2.Civ.3.6-8. Examine the origins, purposes, and impact of constitutions, laws, treaties, and international agreements. D2.Civ.5.6-8. Explain the origins, functions, and structure of government with reference to the U.S. Constitution, state constitutions, and selected other systems of government.
Sample C3 Indicator Connections
Students will be able to identify those aspects of our democratic government that derived from early civilizations.
Participation and Deliberation: Applying Civic Virtues and Democratic Principles
D2.Civ.10.6-8. Explain the relevance of personal interests and perspectives, civic virtues, and democratic principles when people address issues and problems in government and civil society.

Students will be able to identify how early civilizations fostered social responsibility. Students will be able to identify similarities and differences in civic virtues held in early civilizations and those today. Students will be able to identify rights, responsibilities, and privileges of individuals in various early civilizations.
Rules, Processes, and Laws

D2.Civ.12.6-8. Assess specific rules and laws (both actual and proposed) as means of addressing public problems. D2.Civ.14.6-8. Compare historical and contemporary means of changing societies and promoting the common good.
Students will be able to explain how early civilizations established law and order.
Continue
Continue
Economics
Theme: Connecting Worlds
Economic Decision Making
D2.Eco.1.6-8. Explain how economic decisions affect the well-being of individuals, businesses, and society.

Students will be able to examine factors that influenced economic decisions within early civilizations. Students will be able to explain how early civilizations addressed similar and different economic issues.
Exchange and Markets
D2.Eco.3.6-8. Explain the roles of buyers and sellers in product, labor, and financial markets.
D2.Eco.6.6-8. Explain how changes in supply and demand cause changes in prices and quantities of goods and services, labor, credit, and foreign currencies.
D2.Eco.7.6-8. Analyze the role of innovation and entrepreneurship in a market economy.

Students will be able to explain how markets in early civilizations facilitated the exchange of goods, services, and labor. Students will be able to explain human, natural, and capital resources in early civilizations.
Continue
The Global Economy
D2.Eco.14.6-8. Explain barriers to trade and how those barriers influence trade among nations.
D2.Eco.15.6-8. Explain the benefits and the costs of trade policies to individuals, businesses, and society
Students will explain how the costs and benefits of trade between early civilizations contributed to cultural development, economic growth, and interdependence.
Continue
Continue
Continue
Continue
Geography
Theme: Shaping Civilizations
Geographic Representations: Views of the World
D2.Geo.3.6-8. Use paper based and electronic mapping and graphing techniques to represent and analyze spatial patterns of different environmental and cultural characteristics.
Students will be able to identify locations and characteristics (environmental and cultural) of various societies and early civilizations to help them explain patterns and relationships.
Human-Environment Interaction: Place, Regions, and Culture
D2.Geo.4.6-8. Explain how cultural patterns and economic decisions influence environments and the daily lives of people in both nearby and distant places.
D2.Geo.5.6-8. Analyze the combinations of cultural and environmental characteristics that make places both similar to and different from other places.
Students will compare and contrast the physical, environmental, and human characteristics of different early civilizations.
Human Population: Spatial Patterns & Movement
D2.Geo.7.6-8. Explain how changes in transportation and communication technology influence the spatial connections among human settlements and affect the diffusion of ideas and cultural practices.
D2.Geo.9.6-8. Evaluate the influences of long-term human-induced environmental change on spatial patterns of conflict and cooperation.

Students will evaluate the positive and negative effects of long-term human activities—such as settlement, agriculture, and early technologies—on the environment and sustainability of early civilizations. Students will analyze how transportation systems, land use, and resource management practices in early civilizations contributed to both the growth and decline of those societies.
Global Interconnections: Changing Spatial Patterns
D2.Geo.10.6-8. Analyze the ways in which cultural and environmental characteristics vary among various regions of the world.
D2.Geo.11.6-8. Explain how the relationship between the environmental characteristics of places and production of goods influences the spatial patterns of world trade.
Students will be able to explain how the environmental and cultural features of early civilizations influenced economic activities and expansion.
History
Theme: Building Societies
Change, Continuity, and Context
D2.His.1.6-8. Analyze connections among events and developments in broader historical contexts.
D2.His.2.6-8. Classify series of historical events and developments as examples of change and/or continuity.

Students will be able to explain patterns of change in early civilizations (e.g., rise and fall of empires). Students will explain the social, political, economic, and environmental influences that contributed to major changes in early civilizations and assess how these influences shaped long-term outcomes.
Continue
Perspectives
D2.His.4.6-8. Analyze multiple factors that influenced the perspectives of people during different historical eras.
D2.His.5.6-8. Explain how and why perspectives of people have changed over time.
D2.His.6.6-8. Analyze how people’s perspectives influenced what information is available in the historical sources they created.
Students will be able to compare and contrast perspectives in early civilizations over time (e.g., caste system).
Causation and Argumentation
D2.His.14.6-8. Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past.
D2.His.15.6-8. Evaluate the relative influence of various causes of events and developments in the past

Students will be able to identify and explain multiple causes and effects of key events and developments in early civilizations. Students will be able to explain the environmental impacts of human innovation on early civilizations.
body_examples: Overview

In grade 6, students will examine how movement and migration impacted the interactions between expanding civilizations through conquest and trade, including the physical and political geography and ancient societies of South and East Asia, Oceania, Latin America, and Europe. Students will note how geography, power, wealth, and religion influence culture, change, and development within civilizations as they examine how the perspectives of political science, economics, geography, history, and archaeology apply to the study of regions and countries. Students will develop an appreciation of cultural contributions (art, music, literature, architecture) and lasting achievements in science and technology. Grade 6 concludes with a study of government in Greece and Rome, which serves as a prelude to the study of civics in grade 8. Through an understanding of ancient history, students will develop an appreciation for the foundations of the modern world.
Sample Content Connections

Ancient Greece • City-states with various forms of government – democracy in Athens, oligarchy in Sparta; varied structures – assemblies, councils, magistrates for defense, civil life and participatory governance Roman Republic and Empire • Republic with elected officials; transitioned to emperor rule; elected officials (senate, consul) later emperors for legal justice and military expansion • Legal systems

Cross-cutting concepts: • Religion • Community collaboration • Moral codes • Education • Maya – collective labor, personal sacrifice for the greater good, religious rituals, social hierarchies • Inca – lit’a (labor), community-based agriculture and resource management, adherence to Inca code, loyalty to state, worship of state deities • Aztec – mandatory military service, communal projects, Aztec principles, reverence for gods • Ancient China – meritocracy, filial piety, respect for authority/family values • Ancient India – dharmic duties, philosophies, non-violence, diversity, tolerance • Oceania – communal/cooperative labor • Ancient Greece – civic participation/engagement, philosophical discourse, military duty, laws • Ancient Rome – military service, taxes, adherence to Roman principles, duty, loyalty, participation

Cross-cutting concepts: • leadership role • cultural and philosophical values • infrastructure development • legal and administrative reforms • religious influence • centralized authority • punishment • deterrence • codification of social norms Regional Connections • Maya, Aztec, Inca: Highly religious, hierarchical, and centralized. Changes came from elite or divine interpretations. • Ancient Greece and Rome: Provided the roots of democratic and legal principles still seen today. • China and India: Influenced by philosophy/religion (Confucianism, Hinduism), blending centralized and localized governance. • Oceania: More localized, oral tradition-based governance, with strong environmental and spiritual connections.

Civilizations • Maya – Law/rules codified in hieroglyphs, enforced by kings; Religious and social order through kings and priests; city-state specific; severe punishments, order maintained; theocratic-monarchy; elite councils • Inca – Centralized under Sapa Inca; no written laws but quipu records; unity, labor, infrastructure; strict top-down governance; mit'a labor system; social stability, but little personal freedom; autocratic; centralized bureaucracy; resource control; religious/social order. • Aztec – Codified laws; many in Codex Mendoza; war, tribute, religious order; military and religious enforcers; centralized from Tenochtitlán; harsh penalties; strict social hierarchy; emperor advised by noble councils; codification of crimes, imperial authority. • Ancient China – Legalism, Confucianism; written codes (e.g., Qin and Han laws); harmony, obedience, order; imperial bureaucracy, scholar-officials; dynastic cycle; public works, exams; centralized monarchy; civil service; meritocratic/bureaucratic governance. • Ancient India – Dharma and Manusmriti; caste-based laws; social hierarchy, religious duty; local assemblies and royal courts; rigid caste system, but order preserved; mixed: monarchies, republics, village panchayats; religious diversity, moral principles. • Oceania – Oral laws; kapu system (sacred prohibitions); maintain divine order, resource control; chiefs enforced spiritual taboos; social cohesion but limited mobility; chiefdoms; consensus in councils; adherence to tradition, cultural practices. • Ancient Greece – Written laws; e.g., Draco, Solon; justice, equality (esp. in Athens); citizen assemblies, courts; flourishing of democracy, but instability; varied: democracy (Athens), oligarchy (Sparta); democratic laws, civic participation.

• Ancient Rome – Twelve Tables, Justinian Code; order, justice, imperial control; Magistrates, Senate, Emperor; legal legacy - rights for some, repression for others; Republic (Senate), then autocracy (Empire); justice, protection, legal uniformity.
