Ancient Greece and Rome - Core Knowledge: Free downloadable curriculum; Scroll to bottom of page to download individual PDF documents: Teacher Guide and Student Reader. Guide provides activities, assessments and literary selections.
Can You Read Shang? The Story of China - PBS Learning Media: In this activity, students use the Can You Read Shang? quiz to learn about the structure of Shang writing and how it differs from English.

Maya, Aztec, and Inca Civilizations - Core Knowledge: Free downloadable curriculum; Scroll to bottom of page to download individual PDF documents: Teacher Guide and Student Reader. Guide provides activities, assessments and literary selections; Grade 5 level.

Which Emperor Are You? The Story of China - PBS Learning Media: In this activity, students use the Which Emperor Are You? quiz to explore the nature of leadership in Chinese history. After completing this lesson, students will be able to describe and evaluate the leadership qualities of emperors and empresses in China’s history. Emperor Backgrounds.

Cross-cutting concepts: • Agrarian societies to trade networks • Urbanization • Technological advances in agriculture • Manufacturing • Transportation • Increased productivity • Economic interdependence • Complex social structures • Farming techniques, water management, resource allocation – including labor, city- state alliances, navigation and exploration, short vs. long-distance trade (Silk Road), sustainability, investments – infrastructure, military

• Barter and exchange, Commodity money, precious metals, transition to metal coins • Economic specialization, labor systems – slave labor, caste systems, bureaucracies, craftsmen, artisans, trade guilds; natural resources – agriculture, mining, fishing, timber; trade networks. Maya – Primarily barter system; cacao beans and obsidian used as a form of currency. Inca – No formal money system; used quipu (knotted strings) for record-keeping; relied heavily on mit’a labor tax and barter. Aztec – Barter-based; cacao beans and cotton cloth (called quachtli) used as currency. Ancient China – Early use of cowry shells; later, bronze coins; during the Zhou and Qin dynasties, round coins with square holes became common. Ancient India – Barter system early on; later, silver and copper coins were introduced by the Maurya and Gupta Empires. Oceania – Mostly barter; some used shell money (e.g., in Solomon Islands); trade occurred between islands for resources. Ancient Greece – Used coins (silver, bronze); Athens’ currency was the drachma; trade was significant in city-states.

Ancient Rome – Coin-based economy with denarii (silver) and aurei (gold); trade and taxes were monetized. Human, natural and capital resources: • Maya: Farmers, builders, astronomers, scribes; maize, cacao, limestone, jade; temples, pyramids, tools • Inca: Terraced farmers, engineers, runners (chasquis); gold, silver, potatoes, llamas; roads, bridges, quipu, agricultural tools • Aztec: Warriors, traders, artisans, priests; Lake Texcoco, obsidian, cacao, maize; Chinampas, temples, market infrastructure • Ancient China: Farmers, silk workers, soldiers, scholars; silk, jade, tea, rice, metals; Great Wall, iron tools, paper, plows • Ancient India: Farmers, traders, metalworkers, priests; cotton, spices, precious gems, fertile land; irrigation, tools, temples, urban planning (Harappa) • Oceania: Fishermen, navigators, farmers; fish, coconuts, volcanic soil, wood; canoes, fishing nets, communal structures • Ancient Greece: Philosophers, artisans, sailors, soldiers; olives, grapes, marble, silver; ships, temples, coin minting, tools • Ancient Rome: Soldiers, builders, farmers, engineers; timber, iron, olives, wine, marble; aqueducts, roads, coliseums, military tools

Cross-cutting: Cultural exchange – colonization conquests, trade, spread of religion; economic impact – trade; political changes – development of city-states, rise and fall of empires • Geographic barriers – mountainous terrain, islands, lakes, varied/vast landscapes, deserts • Lack of technology/transportation – limited advancements • Infrastructure – not well-developed • Internal strife, external invasions, military campaigns disrupt • Political barriers – wars, closed borders • Cultural/language differences Incas (South America – Andes Mountains) • Barriers: Steep mountains, lack of wheeled vehicles, no written language. • Impact: Trade was mostly local. Used llama caravans and built roads and bridges to connect their empire.

Aztecs (Central Mexico) • Barriers: Swampy land (Lake Texcoco), surrounded by rivals. • Impact: Built chinampas (floating gardens) to create fertile farmland on swampy lakebeds; Constructed causeways, dikes, and canals to connect their island capital and control flooding; Developed strong military alliances (Triple Alliance) to defend against and dominate neighboring rivals. Mayas (Mesoamerica – jungles) • Barriers: Dense rainforests, lack of rivers for easy transport. • Impact: Trade was by foot or canoe, often limited in distance. Cities traded luxury goods like jade and cacao. Ancient China • Barriers: Deserts (Gobi), mountains (Himalayas), oceans. • Impact: Limited early contact with the West but eventually created the Silk Road to trade goods like silk and porcelain. Ancient India • Barriers: Himalayas, monsoon seasons. • Impact: Mountains blocked northern trade, but rivers and seas enabled trade with Mesopotamia and East Africa. Major center for spice and textile trade. Ancient Greece • Barriers: Mountains divided city-states, poor farmland. • Impact: Encouraged sea trade and colonization. Greeks became skilled sailors trading olive oil, wine, pottery.

Ancient Rome • Barriers: Few natural barriers within empire, but external threats and pirates. • Impact: Created roads and protected sea routes. Controlled trade across Europe, Asia, and Africa Ancient Oceania (Pacific Islands) • Barriers: Vast ocean distances, limited natural resources. • Impact: Used canoes and star navigation to trade items like obsidian, shells, and food. Trade was inter-island and risky. War and conflict can: • Damage trade and reduce wealth • Destroy farmland and cities • Increase taxes or tribute to fund armies • Shift power between regions or leaders • Sometimes lead to new resources through conquest Incas: • Conflict Impact: Civil war weakened the empire just before Spanish arrival. • Economic Effects: War disrupted farming and the mita labor system, damaging food production and infrastructure; after conquest, Spanish took gold/silver.

Aztecs: • Conflict Impact: Constant warfare to collect tribute and captives. Economic Effects: Empire grew rich from tribute, but the system was unstable—many enemies joined the Spanish to overthrow the Aztecs, ending their economy. Mayas: • Conflict Impact: Frequent city-state wars. • Economic Effects: Wars weakened agriculture, led to abandoned cities, and disrupted long-distance trade. Likely contributed to the collapse of some major cities. Ancient China: • Conflict Impact: Long periods of war, like the Warring States Period. • Economic Effects: War destroyed farmland and displaced people, but also pushed innovation in infrastructure (roads, canals, walls). Unified under empires like the Han helped restore trade. Ancient India: • Conflict Impact: Invasions (e.g., by Persians, Greeks, Huns). • Economic Effects: Some wars hurt trade routes like the Silk Road; others, like the Maurya Empire's unification, boosted trade and taxes. War created shifts in power and economic stability.

Ancient Greece: • Conflict Impact: Wars between city-states (l Peloponnesian War) and with outsiders (like Persians). Economic Effects: Wars drained resources, destroyed crops, and disrupted trade. Athens, once rich, lost power and wealth after the Peloponnesian War. Ancient Rome: • Conflict Impact: Frequent wars of conquest and later civil wars. • Economic Effects: Early conquests brought wealth and slaves, growing the economy. But later wars drained resources, ruined trade, and contributed to Rome's decline. Oceania: • Conflict Impact: Small-scale tribal wars and resource competition. • Economic Effects: Limited warfare due to isolation, but conflicts could damage canoes, crops, or cause population loss, reducing trade and food security.
Resources

Economics in Ancient India - PBS Learning Media: Students will read a short history of the Indus Valley Civilization and its trading patterns. They will complete a chart with notes from the reading and address a prompt that requires them to analyze these trading patterns.

Cross-cutting concepts – geographic diversity, cultural uniqueness; resource utilization • Maya – present day Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, Honduras, El Salvador; river valleys, rainforests, limestone plateaus; city-states, architecture, hieroglyphics, trade, agriculture • Inca – Andes, including present-day Peru, Ecuador, Chile, Bolivia; mountains, high- altitude plateaus; terraced agriculture, architecture, engineering, labor system • Aztec – valley of Mexico, present day Mexico City; mountains, lakes, volcanoes; floating gardens, calendar, temples • Ancient China – Eastern Asia, mountains, plains, rivers; river valleys, Himalayas; agricultural innovations, Great Wall, Silk Road, Confucianism, Daoism, Legalism • Ancient India – South Asia, including present-day India, Pakistan, Bangladesh; Ganges River basin, diverse geography, Hinduism, Buddhism, arts, science, caste system • Oceania – Central and South pacific, including Hawaii; tropical climate, volcanic activity, diverse ecosystem; traditions and rituals, navigation/seafaring, agriculture • Ancient Greece – southern Europe including Balkan and islands in Aegean; Mediterranean climate; city-states, art, literature, architecture • Ancient Rome – Italian peninsula, later empire covered parts of Europe, Africa, Middle East; Mediterranean climate; republican governance

Cross-cutting concepts: • water management – terraced farming, aqueducts, irrigation • agricultural practices – terraced farming, slash and burn, irrigation systems • trade and transportation – access to rivers, seas, roads

Cross cutting concepts: Trade and cultural exchange, language, cultural assimilation • Culture (e.g., religion/beliefs, accepted practices/traditions) • Specialization of labor • Mastery of food supply • Economic systems • Education • Communication systems (e.g., spoken language, alphabetic and/or numeric systems, hieroglyphics, illustrations) • Technological advancements: metallurgy, weaponry, tools • Engineering and architecture: grid layouts, urban planning, roads, pyramids, monuments, temples, palaces, floating gardens, printing, papermaking, seed drill, plow • Agricultural advancements: terrace farming, irrigation • Military: weaponry, strategy, gunpowder • Government: meritocracy, leadership structure, urban planning, legal systems • Medicine • Astronomy • Philosophy

• Cultural exchange – colonization conquests, trade, spread of religion, cultural diffusion, migrations, blending of religious ideas, caste system developed (India) • Economic impact – trade; new roads and cities built, increase in farming/agricultural practices • Political changes – development of city-states, rise and fall of empires, wars/conquests
Resources

Ancient Math and Music - PBS Learning Media: Explore how Pythagoras and Plato found mathematics in music and nature in this video from NOVA: The Great Math Mystery. The ancient Greeks identified three pleasing musical intervals: an octave, a fifth, and a fourth. Pythagoras discovered that the beautiful musical relationship between the notes was also a mathematical relationship: the harmonious sounds are produced by vibrating strings with particular ratios of string length. Plato believed geometry and mathematics exist in their own ideal world and that certain shapes (now known as the Platonic solids) were associated with the classical elements from which the world was made - earth, fire, air, water, and the universe; discussion questions provided.

Chinese Innovation - C3 IDM: This IDM is described as being for grades 3-5 but can be utilized in Grade 6 with minimal adaptation. This inquiry provides students with an opportunity to examine nine of China’s most impactful innovations and their contributions to the modern world. These innovations and inventions fall into three categories: 1) Communication innovations, including written language, paper, and printing; 2) Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math (STEM) innovations, including the compass, the Great Wall of China, gunpowder, and fireworks, and; 3) Economic innovations, including common currency, silk, and the Silk Road.

Mapping Populations: The Ancient World - PBS Learning Media: Students will study choropleth maps of the ancient world, and the population density changes from 3000 BC to 1 CE. Then, they will fill out a chart about the major influential factors in population density, and answer questions about the map.

Nomadic Life - C3 IDM: This inquiry leads students through an investigation of prehistoric nomadic life. By investigating the compelling question “How do we know the past without written evidence?” students evaluate how nomads communicated, where they lived, and how they defined their needs based on the places they lived. The formative performance tasks build on knowledge and skills through the course of the inquiry and help students develop understanding of nomadic life to compare with agrarian life. Students create an evidence-based argument about how non- written artifacts support understanding of nomadic life during prehistoric times.

Where in China Is…? - PBS Learning Media: In this activity, students examine and plot different locations that hold historical importance. Students will also use the interactive game Where in China is...? to study and test their knowledge of Chinese geography.

Writings of the Ancient Maya - PBS Learning Media: In this interactive lesson supporting literacy skills, students are introduced to the ancient Mayan civilization through their writings. Students develop their literacy skills as they explore a social studies focus on the destruction of many Mayan writings by the Spanish and what archaeologists have learned from the writings that remain. During this process, they read informational text, learn and practice vocabulary words, and explore content through a video and interactive activities.

Cross-cutting Concepts: religion, agriculture, infrastructure, social governmental hierarchies, cultural achievements Maya – City-states with kingship; ruled by divine kings to maintain order, oversee economy, conduct religious rituals; King, nobles, priests, commoners • Agriculturally based society with complex city planning, monumental architecture, hieroglyphic writing; knowledge of astronomy Inca – Centralized ruler with supreme leader (Sapa) with bureaucratic system; rulers seen as descendants of gods; purpose to control vast territories, maintain order, manage resources • Advanced agriculture, extensive roads, labor system for largescale projects Aztec – Centralized emperor, aided by council of nobles and military leaders; empire expanded through conquest; purpose to govern conquered territories, conduct religious rituals • Advanced agriculture, monuments, extensive trade

Ancient China – Dynastic rule with emperors as political and religious leaders; concept of Mandate of Heaven, maintain social harmony, conduct rituals, civil service exams Advanced bureaucracy, Confucian influence, Great Wall, science and technology Ancient India (Maurya and Gupta) – Emperor Ashoka (Maurya), regional rulers (Gupta); religious philosophies governed to uphold dharma, protect, economic prosperity; administrative units and decentralization • Math, medicine, art, governance influence by Buddhism and Hinduism Oceania – Chiefdoms/chiefs ruling over extensive family units to maintain order, economy, religious ceremonies; chiefdoms, priests, warriors, commoners • Navigational skills, long-distance voyages, religious practices, complex social structures Ancient Greece – City-states with various forms of government (democracy in Athens, oligarchy in Sparta); varied structures – assemblies, councils, magistrates for defense, civil life and participatory governance • Philosophy, literature, political experimentation, architecture Roman Republic and Empire – Republic with elected officials; transitioned to emperor rule; elected officials (senate, consul) later emperors for legal justice and military expansion • Legal systems, engineering (aqueducts, roads)

• Religion/Culture (new beliefs can lead to peace or conflict; diversification) • Leaders (good or bad rulers affect people’s trust; resource management, governance) • Invasions/Conquests (often bring new culture or destroy old ones; external and internal threats) • Trade and Travel (new ideas spread; trade networks; disease spread) • Technology and Writing (how people learn and remember things; engineering, military advances; seafaring/maritime abilities, cultural achievements, agricultural innovation)

Cross-cutting concepts: Trade and cultural exchange, language, cultural assimilation, colonization conquests, spread of religion; political changes – development of city-states, rise and fall of empires • Government/leadership structure • Culture (e.g., religion/beliefs, accepted practices/traditions) • Specialization of labor • Mastery of food supply • Technology • Economic systems • Education • Communication systems (e.g., spoken language, alphabetic and/or numeric systems, hieroglyphics, illustrations)
Resources

An Age of Empires and Interchange - History Project UC-Irvine: What were the effects of the exchanges on the Silk Road?” and “What is Hellenistic culture and how did it spread among regions in Afroeurasia?” are just two of the 6th grade Curricular Resources provided by the History Project, which allows students to study the characteristics of the ancient civilizations (social, political, religious, economic, and cultural), and how they were able to grow in size, complexity, and power.

Angkor What? Angkor Wat! - National Endowment for the Humanities: Beginning in the 9th century, the Khmer empire, which was based in what is today northwestern Cambodia, began to gather power and territory in mainland Southeast Asia. It would grow to be one of the largest empires in Southeast Asian history. In this lesson, students will learn about Angkor Wat and its place in Cambodian, and Southeast Asian, history. Students will attempt to ‘read’ the temple, in a way which resembles the reading of a primary document, to gain insight into this history.

Aztec - C3 IDM: This annotated inquiry is listed as for 9th grade, but the compelling question, “What Do the Buried Secrets of Tenochtitlán Tell Us About the Aztecs?” and the staging question, where students look at photographs of the excavation of Tenochtitlán in 2012, can be used/adapted for 6th graders to formulate questions about the Aztec city.

Feudal Japan - Core Knowledge: Scroll to bottom of page to download individual PDF documents: Teacher Guide (p. 77-153) and Student Reader. Guide provides activities, assessments and literary selections; focused on grade 5.

Marco Polo, Ibn Battuta, and Zheng He-Early Connectors - PBS Learning Media: In this lesson, students will explore the adventures of these three world travelers. After viewing three short videos about their journeys, students will analyze photographs of a city that all three travelers visited, write a log entry describing a sighting of Zheng He’s fleet of ships, and then read excerpts from Marco Polo’s and Ibn Battuta’s accounts of their journeys. The lesson will conclude with students writing a short play in which the three travelers meet and share stories of their adventures.

Native America - PBS Learning Media: This Native America collection reaches back 15,000 years, examining ancient city planning and early systems of science and spirituality and extends to present-day exploration of Indigenous knowledge and language preservation; focus on Incas and Aztecs with video clips and discussion questions.

The Story of India - PBS.org: From ancient to modern times, India has played a central role in human history. The Story of India offers educational resources for teachers on this web site. The lessons are designed for high school world history
but can be adapted for lower grades as needed and many of the resources are aligned for either grades 5-12 or 7-12. Provides photos gallery, timeline, and lesson plans.

World History - OER Project: OER provides a collection of free activities, lesson plans, and other teaching resources related to topics in World History - such as Economic Networks and Trade, Cross Cultural Exchange, and Shifting Populations. These can be adapted for 6th graders or identified through a search of Middle School specific lessons.

body_standards: Grade 7 – Vermont and the U.S. – From Reconstruction to the Civil Rights
Movement (Draft)
Inquiry Process (K-12): Students act as social scientists as they ask questions, think critically, solve problems, and share conclusions.
C3 Indicators (6-8):
Constructing Compelling and Supporting Questions: D1.1, 2, 3; His. 12
Gathering and Evaluating Sources: D2. His. 6, 10, 12, 13; D3. 1, 2, 3
Communicating and Critiquing Conclusions: D2. His. 16; D4. 1, 2, 4
Overarching Themes:
• Civics – Grades 6 and 8, and woven into History • Disparities and Opportunities • Regional Differences and Migration Patterns • Conflict and Conciliation
Civics
Theme: Power and Rights
Economics
Theme: Disparities and Opportunities
Economic Decision Making
D2.Eco.1.6-8. Explain how economic decisions affect the well-being of individuals, businesses, and society.
Sample C3 Indicator Connections
Students will be able to explain how technology and the growth of industry transformed American society. Students will be able to identify the rise of labor and economic movements.
Continue Students will be able to identify how economic growth and decline have positively and negatively impacted Vermonters and the nation.
Exchange and Markets
D2.Eco.3.6-8. Explain the roles of buyers and sellers in product, labor, and financial markets.
D2.Eco.6.6-8. Explain how changes in supply and demand cause changes in prices and quantities of goods and services, labor, credit, and foreign currencies.
D2.Eco.8.6-8. Explain how external benefits and costs influence market outcomes.
D2.Eco.9.6-8. Describe the roles of institutions such as corporations, non-profits, and labor unions in a market economy

Students will be able to explain how industry and trade impact the economy and people of Vermont and the nation. Students will be able to explain how economic systems and policies affected different racial and social groups from Reconstruction to the Modern Civil Rights era.
Continue
The National Economy
D2.Eco.12.6-8. Explain how inflation, deflation, and unemployment affect different groups.
D2.Eco.13.6-8. Explain why standards of living increase as productivity improves.
Students will be able to explain the changing role of government in people’s lives over time. Students will be able identify ways the federal government has influenced the economy.
Geography
Theme: Regional Differences and Migration Patterns
Geographic Representations: Views of the World
D2.Geo.1.6-8. Construct maps to represent and explain the spatial patterns of cultural and environmental characteristics.

D2.Geo.2.6-8. Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics.
D2.Geo.3.6-8. Use paper based and electronic mapping and graphing techniques to represent and analyze spatial patterns of different environmental and cultural characteristics.

Students will analyze and interpret maps to explain how cultural, political, and societal factors influence the spatial distribution of populations, and evaluate how mapping practices impact representation, resource allocation, and social equity.
Human-Environment Interaction: Place, Regions, and Culture
D2.Geo.4.6-8. Explain how cultural patterns and economic decisions influence environments and the daily lives of people in both nearby and distant places.
D2.Geo.6.6-8. Explain how the physical and human characteristics of places and regions are connected to human identities and cultures.
Students will be able to explain how geography influenced the culture of the country.
Human Population: Spatial Patterns and Movements
D2.Geo.7.6-8. Explain how changes in transportation and communication technology influence the spatial connections among human settlements and affect the diffusion of ideas and cultural practices.
D2.Geo.8.6-8. Analyze how relationships between humans and environments extend or contract spatial patterns of settlement and movement.
D2.Geo.9.6-8. Evaluate the influences of long-term human-induced environmental change on spatial patterns of conflict and cooperation.

Students will be able to explain the impact - both intended and unintended - of geographic expansion. Students will be able to explain the impact of westward expansion on Native American communities. Students will be able to explain how immigration and urbanization influenced the country during the post- Reconstruction era.
Continue
Continue
Global Interconnections: Changing Spatial Patterns
D2.Geo.12.6-8. Explain how global changes in population distribution patterns affect changes in land use in particular places.

Students will be able to analyze migration patterns to understand the relationships among major events, government policies, and private action in the US from Reconstruction to the modern civil rights era. Students will be able to explain the diffusion of ideas, technologies, and cultural practices in the US from Reconstruction to the modern civil rights era.
History
Theme: Growth and Struggles
Change, Continuity, and Context
D2.His.1.6-8. Analyze connections among events and developments in broader historical contexts.
D2.His.2.6-8. Classify series of historical events and developments as examples of change and/or continuity.
D2.His.3.6-8. Use questions generated about individuals and groups to analyze why they, and the developments they shaped, are seen as historically significant.

Students will be able to describe how Reconstruction programs transformed social relations in the South. Students will be able to explain how citizenship in a democratic society affords its members equal access to certain rights, liberties, and protections under the law.

Students will be able to explain strategies used in societal reforms and efforts to address discrimination after the Civil War. Students will be able to explain how laws and civic action expanded or restricted civil rights between Reconstruction and the civil rights era. Students will be able to explain causes and effects of conflicts within the United States between Reconstruction and the civil rights era. Students will be able to identify common sources of international conflict.
Perspectives
D2.His.4.6-8. Analyze multiple factors that influenced the perspectives of people during different historical eras.
D2.His.5.6-8. Explain how and why perspectives of people have changed over time.

Students will be able to explain movements and reforms and their social, political, and economic impacts. Students will be able to identify factors that led to the civil rights movement. Students will be able to analyze examples of conflict, compromise, cooperation, and the pursuit of social justice from multiple perspectives over time from Reconstruction to the civil rights era.
Continue Students will be able to identify how U.S. has cooperated with other nations on issues over time.
Causation and Argumentation
D2.His.14.6-8. Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past.
D2.His.15.6-8. Evaluate the relative influence of various causes of events and developments in the past.

Students will be able to explain US reactions to conflicts both at home and abroad from Reconstruction to the civil rights era. Students will be able to explain historic events to recognize power, authority, religion, economics, and governance as they relate to oppression and impact on groups in America from Reconstruction to the civil rights era.
body_examples: Overview

In grade 7, students will build on their knowledge of Vermont and U.S. politics, geography, economics, and peoples as they re-visit the sectional conflicts over slavery that continued into Reconstruction and beyond and led to the long struggle in the 19th and 20th centuries for civil rights. Grade 7 content spans decades; takes students through Reconstruction, industrialization, and world wars, and allows students to dig into critical topics and America’s role in them, such as human rights, the Holocaust, genocide, women’s suffrage, and atomic weaponry. By the end of grade 7, students will have a broad understanding of the roles that politics and power have played both locally and on a world stage; be aware of their changing cultural and physical environments; and gain keen insight as to the ways in which individuals, businesses, governments, and societies make decisions. This broad journey provides a framework for understanding and will allow for deeper analysis of history in high school.
Sample Content Connections

Reconstruction - Progressive Era: Business leaders (Vanderbilt, Mellon, Carnegie, Rockefeller, J.P. Morgan); limited competition and maximization of profits; Gilded Age; industrialization; technological breakthroughs – steam engines, railroads, Bessemer steel, electrical power, telephonic communication Great Depression and New Deal: New Deal programs; mass unemployment; growth of unions WWII to Modern Civil Rights Era: Taft-Hartley Act; increased strikes; economic justice, United Farm Worker’s Bureau

Economic Movements: Labor unions; women in the workforce (pink collar); safety in the workplace (laws, child labor laws); Knights of Labor; American Federation of Labor; Congress of International Organizations strikes (Great Railroad Strike of 1877, Haymarket Riot); Cesar Chavez (farm workers’ rights); A. Philip Randolph (Black worker rights) History and the Economy: Buying on margin, speculation, Great Depression, Gold Rushes, Dust Bowl, war manufacturing, post World War II economic boom, industrial boom(s) and decline(s), economic panics of 1800s, stock market crashes

Individuals and Groups Affected: Indentured servants, enslaved people, Free Blacks, sharecroppers/tenant farmers, women homesteaders, women in the workforce (Rosie the Riveter), entrepreneurs, farmers, mill workers, miners, loggers. Policies/Systems: Black Wall Street, Great Migration, American Indian fur trade, New Deal Programs, farming/agriculture, tourism. Sharecropping and Tenant Farming (Post-Civil War – early 1900s) Economic System: Southern agricultural system where formerly enslaved people and poor white farmers worked land in exchange for a share of the crops. • Effect: African Americans remained in poverty and debt due to unfair contracts; Landowners had more power; limited opportunity for Black economic advancement. Segregated Labor and Low-Wage Jobs (Jim Crow Era) Economic Policy/Practice: Racial segregation in employment; "last hired, first fired." • Effect: African Americans and other minorities often denied skilled jobs, union membership, or fair wages; women, especially women of color, were restricted to low- paying domestic or service jobs. New Deal Programs (1930s) Economic Policy: Government relief programs during the Great Depression (e.g., Social Security, housing assistance, job creation programs). • Effect: Helped many, but excluded farm workers and domestic workers, which affected Black and Latinx workers. Housing programs supported segregation through practices like redlining, denying loans to Black families.

GI Bill After WWII (1944 onward) Economic Policy: Gave returning veterans benefits like college tuition, home loans, and job training. • Effect: White veterans accessed college and bought homes, helping to build middle- class wealth. Black veterans were often denied benefits due to local racism, leaving them economically disadvantaged. Civil Rights Era Economic Focus (1960s) Economic Ideas: “Freedom from poverty” and economic justice became central to the Civil Rights Movement. Examples: Poor People’s Campaign (organized by MLK Jr.) demanded fair wages, jobs, and housing. Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Voting Rights Act of 1965 aimed to end discrimination, which had long limited economic mobility for Black Americans.

Reconstruction – Gold standard; not much government control over economy or major efforts for tax/spend – Panic of 1873, Panic of 1893; Freedman’s Bureau; land redistribution Progressive Era – Federal Reserve creation, decisions led to 1929 Great Depression; anti- trust laws, Interstate Commerce Commission; Child Labor laws Great Depression – FDR’s New Deal – government spending; jobs programs – WPA, CCC; Social Security; Taxes raised on wealthy; Wagner Act of 1935; Fair Labor Standards Act WWII/post WWII – War production; GI Bill 1960s-1970s – Kennedy tax cuts; Johnson’s Great Society/War on Poverty – fought poverty/boost economy; Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC)
Resources

Fair Labor Practices, Current and Historical- New Jersey: Then and Now - PBS Learning Media: Working conditions in the Paterson silk industry and the farms of the Pinelands varied for the immigrant and seasonal laborers. Labor movements and leaders like Elizabeth Gurley Flynn in Paterson and Elizabeth White at Whitesbog worked to improve the conditions of workers including fair hours, conditions, and benefits. This lesson will examine the labor conditions of historical industries in New Jersey while comparing these with modern fair labor practices and issues both in the country and around the world.

Gilded Age and Progressive Era - Bill of Rights Institute: In these three units - with 8 lessons and 2 videos - students will respond to the following inquiry: “How did Americans at the turn of the 20th century address the rapid technological, demographic, and economic changes around them?” Provide students an in-depth look at this formative period in United States history. Through primary-source-based activities and engaging narratives, students will be exposed to this fascinating period and analyze its numerous parallels to today.

Industrial Revolution: Uncovering America - PBS Learning Media: How did the Industrial Revolution change the United States? What makes industrialization possible? How does art reflect the varying experiences within a capitalist economy? In suggested activities, students consider multiple viewpoints of images from the Industrial Revolution; research and evaluate arguments for and against capitalism; and investigate their own community to create a portrait of their local industry.

The Industrial Age in America: Robber Barons and Captains of Industry - National Endowment for the Humanities: In this lesson students will be able to evaluate the actions taken by various captains of industry and robber barons of the time.

The Industrial Age in America: Sweat Shops. Steel Mills, and Factories - National Endowment for the Humanities: In this lesson, students will analyze the working conditions that led to the Haymarket Affair, the Homestead Strike, and the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire and the actions taken by the managers and workers involved in the incidents, and evaluate the significance of the featured events to the labor movement, the industrialists involved, and the attitude of the American people toward working conditions in the United States.
• Political maps • Census maps • Apportionment • Gerrymandering • Redlining • Homestead Act Black Codes/Jim Crow • Plessy v. Ferguson • Voting Laws • Great Migration • Louisiana Purchase

• Enslaved labor was used to transform the Southern landscape for cotton, sugar, and tobacco farming. • Environmental destruction and land exhaustion in the South led to westward expansion. • The South was more rural and dependent on agriculture; the North was more urban and industrial. These differences influenced how Reconstruction played out in each region. • Places in the North and South both had industrializing economies, but at different scales and with different labor systems. • In the South, slavery shaped a distinct human and cultural landscape before the Civil War. • After the war, freed Black communities began building churches, schools, and political organizations—changing the human geography. • Urbanization and migration (especially the Great Migration) moved Black communities into Northern cities, shifting demographics and political power; segregation, Harlem Renaissance.

Geographic Expansion – Louisiana Purchase, Westward Expansion, Annexation of Alaska and Hawaii, Gadsden Purchase, Kansas-Nebraska Act, Annexation of Texas, US Territories, Possession of Philippines Impacts of Expansion – roads, city growth, businesses and industry, railroads, land grants, pollution, ecosystems, loss of native lands, access to natural resources Policies/Acts • Homestead Act (1862) and its long-term effects, Indian Removal policies and the continuation of forced relocations • The Dawes Act (1887) – broke up tribal lands, encouraged assimilation • Reservation system and loss of traditional homelands • Battle of Little Bighorn (1876) and Wounded Knee Massacre (1890) • Boarding schools and the effort to "Americanize" Native children Examples of U.S. Immigration after Reconstruction: Massive immigration after 1870 and how new social patterns, conflicts, and ideas of national unity developed amid growing cultural diversity

Southern and Eastern European Immigration (1880s–1920s) • Who: Italians, Poles, Russians, Greeks, Jews, and others • Why: Escaping poverty, persecution (especially Jews from Russia), and seeking economic opportunity • Impact: Settled in cities (e.g., New York, Chicago, Boston); filled industrial jobs (factories, steel mills, garment industry); faced discrimination and sparked nativist backlash; helped build American infrastructure and culture Chinese Immigration • Who: Chinese immigrants, mostly men • Why: Seeking work during the Gold Rush and to build the Transcontinental Railroad • Impact: Post-Reconstruction Issues: After Reconstruction, many stayed and worked in the West; Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882: first major federal law restricting immigration by nationality Irish Immigration (Continued from pre-Civil War era) • Who: Irish Catholics • Why: Escaping poverty and political unrest • Impact: Became politically active in urban centers; took part in labor movements and political machines like Tammany Hall German Immigration • Who: German immigrants, both skilled workers and farmers • Why: Escaping war, seeking religious freedom or land; in Midwest (Ohio, Wisconsin, etc.) • Impact: Influenced American beer brewing, education, and farming techniques

Scandinavian Immigration • Who: Norwegians, Swedes, Danes • Why: Land and opportunity; settled in Midwest and Great Plains • Impact: Helped develop farming communities and contributed to American agrarian culture Middle Eastern and North African Immigration (late 1800s–early 1900s) • Who: Primarily Lebanese and Syrian Christians • Why: Religious freedom and escaping Ottoman rule • Impact: Became merchants, shopkeepers, and community leaders

Migration Influences: Black Codes/Jim Crow; Supreme Court Cases - Plessy v. Ferguson; Voting Laws; Westward expansion; Homestead Act; Transcontinental railroad; Manifest destiny; Great migration; Redlining; Dust Bowl migration; Second Great Migration; White Flight Diffusion of Ideas: Abolition, Suffrage, Women’s rights, civil rights Spread of Technology: Railroads, radio and television, cars and highways Spread of Cultural Practices: Harlem Renaissance, food and music, traditions (immigrant/indigenous)
Resources

A Cheyenne Odyssey - Mission US: A Public Media Project: Mission US is an award- winning media project that immerses young people in transformational moments in US history; teacher guide. In “A Cheyenne Odyssey,” players become Little Fox, a Northern Cheyenne boy whose life is changed by the encroachment of white settlers, railroads, and U.S. military expeditions. As buffalo diminish and the U.S. expands westward, players experience the Cheyenne’s persistence through conflict and national transformation.

A Cold Reception: Anti-Immigrant Sentiment in the United States - PBS Learning Media: This media-enhanced lesson plan will use video from Dr. Henry Louis Gates Jr.'s PBS series Faces of America to explore the hostile reception immigrants have often received from anti-immigrant "nativists" in an America not always eager to accept them and the change they represent.

A People on the Move- Great Migrations - PBS Learning media: In this lesson, students will contextualize the Great Migration (1910–1940) to better understand its importance and impact on Black Americans and the country. Students will discuss the concepts of resistance and cultural flourishing in the context of the Great Migration. Additionally, students will participate in historical research and presentation, as well as creative expression, to dive deeper into the challenges and triumphs of this historical moment.

City of Immigrants - Mission US: A Public Media Project: Mission US is an award- winning media project that immerses young people in transformational moments in US history; teacher guide. In “City of Immigrants,” players navigate New York’s Lower East Side as Lena, a young Jewish immigrant from Russia. Trying to save money to bring her parents to America, she works long hours in a factory for little money and gets caught up in the growing labor movement.

Hunter-Dunbar Expedition - C3 IDM: This inquiry leads students through an investigation of the Hunter-Dunbar expedition, commissioned by President Thomas Jefferson after the purchase of the Louisiana Territory from France. By investigating the compelling question “Is the Hunter-Dunbar Expedition Worth Remembering?” students evaluate the contributions Dr. George Hunter and William Dunbar made in the discovery and cataloguing of natural resources, geographic features, and Native American groups in the lower portion of the Louisiana Territory (present-day Arkansas). The formative performance tasks build on knowledge and skills through the course of the inquiry and help students draw evidence from articles, charts, graphs, and maps while justifying their reasoning in writing.

Immigration and Displacement: Uncovering America - PBS Learning Media: In this set of artworks and suggested activities, students will explore the motivations of immigration and causes of displacement throughout American history, practice telling stories, investigate transformational journeys, and reflect on the American dream.

Population Profile of Our New Nation: A Comparison of the 1790 and 1800 Censuses - Statistics in Schools: In this activity, students will refer to the 1790 and 1800 censuses to compare the total population with the population of enslaved people, drawing conclusions from the data.

Promised Land - C3 IDM: This inquiry leads students through an investigation of immigration experiences in the United States. By investigating the compelling question “Is America the ‘Promised Land’ for the world’s immigrants?” students evaluate the motivating factors and deterrents for immigration to the United States both in the past and present. The formative performance tasks help students build on knowledge and skills through the course of the inquiry and allow students to recognize the push/pull factors for immigrants throughout our history.

They’re Coming to America: Immigrants Past and Present - PBS Learning Media: In this lesson, students explore the history of this nation of immigrants. In the introductory activity, students identify their own countries of heritage, as well as those of their classmates. Students then identify ethnic groups that migrated to the United States during various historic waves of immigration. In the learning activities, students watch video segments from Faces of America to develop an understanding of key motivations for immigration and explore online resources to examine specific immigrant experiences from various points in American history. In the culminating activity, students utilize their historical knowledge and examination of case studies to develop a brief narrative summarizing the experiences, aspirations, and emotions of a hypothetical immigrant to then the past or the present.

Up from the Dust - Mission US: A Public Media Project: Mission U.S. is an award- winning media project that immerses young people in transformational moments in U.S. history; teacher guide. In “Up from the Dust,” players take on the roles of twins Frank and Ginny Dunn, whose family wheat farm is devastated by the Great Depression and Dust Bowl. As they experience the hardships of the 1930s, players learn about Americans’ strategies for survival – as individuals, communities, and a nation.

Strategies/approaches to Affect Change: Picketing; Boycotts; Lawsuits; Sit-ins; Voting; Marches; Holding elected office; Lobbying; Armed resistance; Hunger strike; Advertising; Social media campaigns; Walk-outs Organizing Societal Reforms Temperance Movement; Mental health/healthcare; Prison reform; Immigration rights; Sovereign rights of Indigenous tribes; Abolitionism; Voting; Labor conditions; Integration of public accommodations; American Indian Movement (AIM); Asian American Political Alliance; Affirmative action; Gerrymandering; Civil Rights Act of 1964; Voting Rights Act of 1965; NAACP Limits to Civil Rights Poll taxes; literacy test; grandfather clauses; Supreme Court cases - Plessy v. Ferguson “separate but equal”, Korematsu v. US; Jim Crow Laws; Klux Klan (KKK); Black Codes

Expansion of Rights Suffrage; 13th, 14th, and 15th amendments; Freedman’s Bureau; NAACP; Naturalization; Brown v. Board of Education Causes and Effects of National Conflict: Population redistribution; State’s rights; Slavery; Land expansion; Land disputes; Annexation; Federalism; Taxation without representation; Congressional representation; Political balance in congress; Discrimination; Disenfranchisement; Civil Rights; Civil Rights legislation; Wage and labor disputes; Environment; Resource allocation Examples of Conflicts (National/International) Federalist/Anti-Federalists; Indigenous rights; National Bank; Labor unions; Internment camps; Domestic and international wars; Indian removal; Suffrage; Spanish-American War; Economic impacts of war; Great Depression; World Wars; Cold War; Korean War Common Sources of International Conflict: • Trade/economic policy • Border disputes/U.S. expansion • Human rights • Holocaust – History of Antisemitism; Pre-war Jewish life; WWI and rise of fascism; US response; Eugenics; Bystanders; Upstanders; Nuremburg trials; Creation of UN • Genocide examples - Indigenous peoples; Armenia; Mao Tse-Tung’s Cultural Revolution; The Rape of Nanking

Movements/Reforms: • Progressive Era – Women’s Suffrage movement, Prohibition (18th and 21st Amendments), Muckrakers and investigative journalism • Legal challenges – Brown v. Board of Ed, Civil Rights Act of 1964, Voting Rights Act of 1965 • Social Movements – sit-ins, marches, Montgomery Bus Boycott Factors the Led to Civil Rights Movement: segregation and Jim Crow laws; lack of voting rights; violence and injustice; wars and returning Black veterans; growth of non-White middle class; media awareness; Supreme Court cases Conflict, Compromise, Cooperation: class, gender, religious, regional, and racial; Class conflict and labor movement; AFL-CIO; Gender and suffrage movements; Korematsu v. US; Civil Rights movement; Civil Rights Act of 1964; Indian reorganization Act of 1934; Voting Rights Act International Cooperation: Considerations: Nation-states, Interaction among nation-states; U.S. relations with other nation-states; Major governmental, nongovernmental international organizations; Impact of the American concept of democracy, individual rights on the world; The influence of other nations on American politics, society; Effects of significant world political, demographic, environmental developments, and trends on the United States; The United Nations - purpose and function.

Examples: • International Trade and Diplomacy (Post-Civil War): After the Civil War, the U.S. worked to rebuild trade with Europe and expand into new global markets. Example: U.S. opened trade relationships in Asia and Latin America, helping grow its economy. • Spanish-American War and Treaty of Paris (1898): U.S. and Spain signed a peace treaty after war; U.S. gained Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines. • World War I (1917–1918): U.S. joined the Allied Powers (Britain, France, etc.) to fight Germany. After the war, President Wilson promoted the League of Nations (an early idea of global cooperation), though the U.S. didn’t officially join. Example of international negotiation, though it also raised debates about U.S. imperialism. • World War II (1941–1945): The U.S. allied with the United Kingdom, Soviet Union, France, and China to defeat Nazi Germany and Japan. Major example of military and economic cooperation through the Allied Powers. • United Nations (Founded 1945): After WWII, the U.S. helped create the United Nations, a global organization for peace, health, and human rights. The U.S. became a permanent member of the UN Security Council. • Marshall Plan (1948): U.S. gave billions of dollars to help European countries rebuild after WWII. Goal: prevent the spread of communism and support global economic stability.

• Cold War Cooperation (1950s–60s): Cold War involved tension – the U.S. formed alliances like NATO with European nations to ensure collective security. • World War I: US initially neutral; German sub attacks • World War II: Pearl Harbor, Japanese internment, Holocaust, McCarthyism, nuclear weapons, space race, ‘red scare’, fear of communism; atomic bomb; post War NATO creation and Marshall Plan • Cold War: US v. USSR, capitalism v. Communism; proxy wars (Korea, and early Vietnam); McCarthyism • Korean War: containment of Communism; armistice • Vietnam War: containment of Communism; draft dodgers; chemical warfare; US Protests; first war on nightly news • Historic Events Recognizing Oppression: Reconstruction era; Disenfranchisement; Chinese Exclusion Act; Jim Crow laws; Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire; The Great Depression; Japanese Internment; Civil Rights movement
Resources

The American Revolution- PBS Learning Media: This Ken Burns series offers media clips with lessons for grades 6-8: “Demographics of the British Colonies”, Native Americans and British Colonial America: Sovereignty, Diplomacy, and Resistance”, and “Patriot, Loyalist Neutral: Differing Perspectives on the American Revolution”.

African Americans in the Gilded Age - Bill of Rights Institute: Constitutional amendments were ratified during and after the Civil War to protect the natural and civil rights of African Americans. Despite these legal protections, the condition of African Americans significantly worsened in the last few decades of the nineteenth century. In this 120-minute lesson, Students will trace and evaluate efforts to achieve equality and protect the natural rights of blacks during the period following the Civil War and analyze primary source documents and respond to a document-based question concerning efforts to achieve racial equality.

An Uphill Battle: Fighting Injustice on the Homefront During WWI - National Archives Harry S. Truman Museum: Students will rotate through four learning centers where they will read primary and secondary sources about injustices during World War I. This will culminate in brainstorming solutions to each type of injustice.

Civil Rights Movement: The Declaration’s Influence - PBS Learning Media: In this interactive lesson, students explore key speeches given by Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr., during the 1960s civil rights movement. They will analyze how he employed language to connect the movement to the Declaration of Independence and to justify its goals.

Fighting for the Right to Fight - The National World War II Museum: This middle school guide provides an introductory essay, profiles of prominent wartime African Americans, and three primary source-based lesson plans.

Korea’s Place in Teaching Social Studies - World History Digital Education. In partnership with the National Council for Social Studies (NCSS), the World History Digital Education Foundation offers a set of free resources for social studies teachers to incorporate lessons on the history, geography, economy, and civic society of the Republic of Korea. The Learning Module is composed of four modules: History, Geography, Economics, and Civics; each content area provides inquiry lessons, resources, and activities.

No Turning Back - Mission US: A Public Media Project: Mission U.S. is an award- winning media project that immerses young people in transformational moments in US history; teacher guide. Estimated time: 2-2.5 hrs. The year is 1960. You are 16-year-old Verna Baker, born and raised in the Mississippi Delta. As you move to the city of Greenwood to
start high school, a movement for civil rights is gaining momentum. How will you take part in the struggle for freedom and equality?

Prisoner in My Homeland - Mission U.S.: A Public Media Project: Mission U.S. is an award-winning media project that immerses young people in transformational moments in U.S. history; teacher guide. ESTIMATED TIME: 1.5-2 HOURS The year is 1941. You are 16-year-old Henry Tanaka. When the government forces you and 120,000 other innocent Japanese Americans into camps, how will you react?

Pushing Towards Civil Rights - iCivics: This curriculum unit covers the following topics for either grades 6-8 or 9-12: Slavery, Civil War, Reconstruction, Jim Crow Era, Progressive Era, Women’s Suffrage, Civil Rights Movement, Black Power Movement. Lessons and “Quests” are aligned to the C3 standards; videos, additional resources, and infographics also provided. All resources are free, but teachers need to create an educator account.

Reconstruction: Middle School Inquiry - American Battlefield Trust: In this inquiry lesson, students will respond to the question “What are the outcomes of the period known as Reconstruction?” Students will develop a hypothesis, search for evidence in multiple primary and secondary sources, and complete a graphic organizer. Two opportunities for assessment are provided: storyboard and inquiry response (oral or written).

Teach- United States Holocaust Memorial Museum - The USHMM provides the fundamentals of Teaching the Holocaust, Teaching Materials by Topic, Online teaching Resources, Professional Development, Videos, Poster Sets, and general support for teaching the Holocaust in a non-partisan manner.

Teaching with Historic Places - National Parks Service: Place-based learning puts “place” – a historic structure, an archaeological site, a cultural landscape, or National Park – at the center of the story. By rooting the study of the past in the physical geography, the Teaching with Historic Places program help learners more deeply connect to their local community as well as communities across the country. Find lessons archived by time period, state, or various themes- such as African American History, American Presidents, Civil Rights, and Conservation.

The Lost Promise of Reconstruction and the Rise of Jim Crow, 1860-1896 - Bill of Rights Institute: This lesson asks students to look at primary source documents as they consider the following question: To what extent did Founding principles of liberty, equality, and justice become a reality for African Americans from Reconstruction to the end of the nineteenth century? The Civil War ended slavery, and African Americans were in a position to claim their natural rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. But would that happen?

The National WWI Museum and Memorial - Search this site by topic (i.e., economics, geography, politics), resource type (i.e., curriculum, lesson plan, video), and grade-band for classroom materials focused on teaching about WWI.

The Vermont 250th in the Classroom - The purpose of this document is to provide lessons and resources to engage students in learning about the founding of the nation and the critical role that Vermont and Vermonters played in the War for Independence and the legacy they left on America. Members of the 250th Education Committee have identified lessons and resources that align with the four themes established by the Vermont 250th Commission on which to focus the commemoration of the Semiquincentennial; suggested grades have also been provided for upper Elementary, Middle, and High school students.

Voting Trends in America, 1964-2020 - Statistics in Schools: This activity is designed to be part of a unit on the U.S. Constitution, as it focuses on U.S. voting trends. Students will analyze bar and line graphs showing the percentages of people (by race, age, sex, region, and education) who voted in elections between 1964 and 2020. Students will use these data to respond to the question “Who votes in American elections?”

Wilmington 1898 Education - PBS Learning Media: A variety of interactive resources and lessons that tell the story of the people, communities, and actions that defined the city of Wilmington, North Carolina in the decades following the Civil War, as well as the political factors that led to the only successful coup in U.S. history. Designed to accompany the PBS NC-produced American Experience episode "American Coup: Wilmington 1898," this collection includes segments from that film, as well as original videos and animations.

Women’s Suffrage - Learning for Justice: In this lesson, students will understand that until the Nineteenth Amendment was ratified, use primary and secondary sources to understand the ways that women advocated for the right to vote, and evaluate the importance of the federal government in securing women's right to vote.

Women’s Suffrage in the United States - Teach a Girl to Lead- Rutgers University: The goal of this module is to provide resources and information about the history of women’s vote in the U.S. Looking at the women’s suffrage movement provides a framework for exploring the changing role of women in politics and society in the 19th and 20th centuries. The history of suffrage offers an opportunity to examine women’s roles at critical points in the nation’s history, and to think about the impact of women’s voting behavior on politics in our time.

Choices in Little Rock - Facing History and Ourselves - This unit examines attempts to integrate Little Rock Central High School in 1957. It explores the impact of the choices of the Little Rock Nine as well as those of leaders, the media, and community members.

The Individual and Society - Facing History and Ourselves - How does our society shape the way we define ourselves and others? Explore some of the dilemmas people experience when others perceive them differently than they define themselves.
